chapters.title: Book I
paragraphs: Yesterday I went down to the Piraeus with Glaucon, son of Ariston. I wanted to pray to the goddess Bendis, the Thracian Artemis, and I was also curious to see how they would celebrate this new festival. The local procession was delightful, and the Thracian one was equally impressive, if not more so. After we finished our prayers and watched the spectacle, we turned back toward the city. Just then, Polemarchus, son of Cephalus, spotted us from a distance and sent his servant running after us. The servant grabbed my cloak from behind and said: Polemarchus wants you to wait.
I turned around and asked where his master was.
He's right there, said the boy, coming after you. Just wait a moment.
Of course we'll wait, said Glaucon. A few minutes later Polemarchus arrived, along with Adeimantus, Glaucon's brother, Niceratus the son of Nicias, and several others who had been at the procession.
Polemarchus said to me: It looks like you and your friend are already heading back to the city, Socrates.
You're not wrong, I said.
But look how many of us there are, he said. Do you see?
Of course.
Well, are you stronger than all of us? Because if not, you'll have to stay right here.
Couldn't we persuade you to let us go instead? I said.
Can you persuade people who refuse to listen? he said.
Certainly not, said Glaucon.
Well then, we're not going to listen. Count on that.
Adeimantus added: Hasn't anyone told you about the torch-race on horseback tonight in honor of the goddess?
On horseback! I said. That's something new. Will the riders carry torches and pass them to each other during the race?

Yes, said Polemarchus, and there's also a nighttime festival that you really should see. We'll head out after dinner and watch it. There will be plenty of young people around, and we can have a good conversation. So stay, and don't be difficult.
Glaucon said: Well, since you insist, I suppose we have to.
Very good, I said.

So we went with Polemarchus to his house. There we found his brothers Lysias and Euthydemus, along with Thrasymachus from Chalcedon, Charmantides from Paeania, and Cleitophon the son of Aristonymus. Cephalus, Polemarchus's father, was also there. I hadn't seen him in a long time and thought he had aged considerably. He was sitting in a cushioned chair with a garland on his head, having just been offering sacrifices in the courtyard. Other chairs were arranged in a semicircle, and we sat down beside him. He greeted me warmly and said:

You don't come to see me often enough, Socrates. If I could still get around, I wouldn't ask you to come to me. But at my age, I can barely make it to the city, so you should visit the Piraeus more often. I'll tell you something: the more the body's pleasures fade, the more I enjoy and value good conversation. So don't turn me down. Make this house your regular stop and spend time with these young men. We're old friends, and you'll feel right at home.

I said: Actually, Cephalus, there's nothing I enjoy more than talking with older people. I think of them as travelers who have gone ahead on a road I may have to walk myself, and I want to ask them whether the path is smooth or rough. So let me ask you, since you've reached what the poets call the 'threshold of old age' — is life harder toward the end? What's your experience?

I'll tell you how I see it, Socrates, he said. People my age tend to flock together — birds of a feather, as the saying goes. And at our gatherings, the usual complaints go something like this: 'I can't eat, I can't drink, the pleasures of youth and love are gone. Those were the good days, and now life is barely worth living.' Some grumble about how their relatives mistreat them, and they go on and on about all the miseries old age has brought them. But Socrates, I think they're blaming the wrong thing. If old age were really the cause, then I and every other old person would feel the same way. But that's not my experience, nor the experience of others I've known. I remember the old poet Sophocles. Someone asked him, 'How does love treat you in old age, Sophocles? Are you still the man you were?' He replied, 'Quiet! I'm delighted to have escaped that — it's like escaping from a mad and savage master.' I've thought about his words many times since, and they seem just as wise now as when he first said them. Old age really does bring a deep sense of calm and freedom. When the passions loosen their grip, then, as Sophocles said, we're freed not from one mad master but from many. The truth is, Socrates, these regrets and complaints about relatives all come from the same source — not old age, but people's characters. Someone with a calm and contented nature will barely feel the weight of aging, but for someone with the opposite temperament, youth and old age are both a burden.

I was fascinated and wanted to keep him going, so I said: Yes, Cephalus, but I suspect most people aren't convinced when you say this. They think old age sits lightly on you not because of your temperament, but because you're rich. Wealth, as everyone knows, is a great comfort.

You're right, he said. They're not convinced, and there's something to what they say — but not as much as they think. I could answer them the way Themistocles answered the man from Seriphos who was insulting him, saying he was famous only because he was Athenian, not because of any merit of his own: 'If you had been from my country, or I from yours, neither of us would be famous.' The same applies to those who aren't rich and resent old age. The honest truth is that old age isn't easy for a good person who's poor, but a bad person who's rich can never find peace with himself either.
May I ask, Cephalus — did you mostly inherit your fortune, or did you earn it yourself?

Earn it? Well, Socrates, you want to know how much I've earned? When it comes to making money, I fall somewhere between my father and my grandfather. My grandfather, whose name I carry, doubled and tripled what he inherited — ending up with roughly what I have now. But my father Lysanias reduced the estate to less than its current value. I'll be satisfied if I leave my sons not less than what I received, but maybe a little more.

That's exactly why I asked, I said. I noticed you don't seem particularly attached to money, which is usually a trait of those who inherited their wealth rather than those who made it. People who've built their own fortunes develop a second kind of love for money — they love it as their own creation, the way authors love their own books or parents love their children, on top of the normal appreciation everyone has for money's practical usefulness. That makes them tedious company, because all they can talk about is the glory of wealth.
That's true, he said.
It really is. But let me ask you one more thing: what do you consider the greatest benefit you've gained from being wealthy?

Something that most people wouldn't easily believe, he said. You see, Socrates, when a person starts to feel that death is approaching, fears and concerns enter his mind that never bothered him before. The stories about the underworld and punishment for wrongs done in this life — stories he used to laugh at — now torment him with the thought that they might be true. Whether from the frailty of age or because he's drawing closer to that other world, he sees these things more clearly. Suspicions and anxieties crowd in on him, and he starts to reflect on any wrongs he may have done to others. If he finds the total is large, he wakes up in terror like a child from a bad dream, filled with dread. But for the person with a clear conscience, as Pindar beautifully puts it, sweet hope is the kind nurse of his old age:

'Hope,' he says, 'nourishes the soul of the one who lives in justice and holiness. She is the nurse of old age and the companion of his journey — hope, which has the greatest power to sway the restless human heart.'

What wonderful words! And the greatest blessing of wealth — not for everyone, but for a good person — is that he's never had to cheat or defraud anyone, whether on purpose or by accident. When he departs for the next world, he carries no anxiety about offerings owed to the gods or debts owed to people. Wealth contributes enormously to this peace of mind. So weighing everything up, I'd say that for a person of good sense, this is wealth's greatest advantage.

Well said, Cephalus. But on the subject of justice itself — what exactly is it? Just telling the truth and paying back what you owe? Isn't that too simple? Aren't there exceptions? Suppose a friend lent me his weapons while he was sane, and then comes to collect them when he's lost his mind. No one would say I should return them, or that it would be right to always tell the full truth to someone in that state.
You're absolutely right, he said.
So telling the truth and repaying debts isn't a correct definition of justice.
That's right, Socrates — at least if we're to believe Simonides, said Polemarchus, jumping in.
Well, said Cephalus, I'm afraid I have to leave now. I need to attend to the sacrifices. I'll hand the discussion over to Polemarchus and the rest of you.
Isn't Polemarchus your heir? I said.
He certainly is, Cephalus said with a laugh, and went off to his sacrifices.
So tell me then, heir to this argument — what did Simonides say about justice that you believe is true?
He said that paying back what you owe is just, and I think he was right.

I'd be reluctant to doubt such a wise and inspired man, but while his meaning may be clear to you, it's anything but clear to me. He surely doesn't mean, as we were just discussing, that I should return weapons or anything else to someone who's out of his mind — even though a deposit is certainly a debt.
True.
So when the person asking isn't in his right mind, I shouldn't give it back?
Certainly not.
Then when Simonides said repaying debts was justice, he didn't mean cases like that?
Certainly not. He thinks a friend should always do good to a friend, never harm.
I see — so you're saying that returning gold to someone when it would actually harm them, if the two are friends, isn't really repaying a debt. Is that what you think Simonides meant?
Yes.
And what about enemies? Should we give them what we owe them too?
Absolutely, he said. An enemy owes an enemy what's appropriate — which is to say, something bad.
So Simonides, in his poetic way, was speaking in riddles about justice. What he really meant was that justice is giving each person what's appropriate to them, and he called this a 'debt.'
That must have been what he meant, he said.
All right then! And if we asked him what appropriate thing does medicine give, and to whom, what do you think he'd say?
He'd say medicine gives drugs, food, and drink to human bodies.
And what appropriate thing does cooking give, and to what?
Seasoning to food.
And what does justice give, and to whom?
If we follow the pattern of the other examples, Socrates, then justice is the skill of giving good to friends and harm to enemies.
Is that what he means?
I think so.
And who is best at helping friends and harming enemies when they're sick?
A doctor.
And who does that best when they're at sea, facing danger?
A ship's captain.
So in what kind of situation is a just person best at helping friends and harming enemies?
In war — fighting against enemies and forming alliances with friends.
But when a person is healthy, Polemarchus, there's no need for a doctor, right?
No.
And someone who isn't on a voyage doesn't need a captain?
No.
So is justice useless in peacetime?
I'm far from saying that.
You think justice is useful in peace as well as in war?
Yes.
Like farming is useful for growing grain?
Yes.
And shoemaking for making shoes?
Yes.
So what similar practical use does justice have in peacetime?
It's useful in business dealings, Socrates — in contracts.
By contracts, you mean partnerships?
Exactly.
But in a game of checkers, is a just person a more useful partner than a skilled player?
The skilled player.
And for laying bricks and stones, is the just person a better partner than a builder?
Not at all.
Then in what kind of partnership is the just person a better partner than, say, a musician is when playing music?
In a financial partnership.
Yes, Polemarchus, but not when you're actually using the money. You wouldn't want a just man as your advisor when buying a horse — you'd want someone who knows about horses, right?
Certainly.
And when buying a ship, you'd want a shipbuilder or a captain?
True.
So when is the just person more useful when it comes to money?
When you want to keep a deposit safe.
You mean when the money isn't being used — when it's just sitting there?
Exactly.
So justice is useful when money is useless?
That seems to follow.
And when you want to keep a pruning hook safe, justice is useful. But when you want to actually use it, you need the skill of a gardener?
Apparently.
And when you want to store a shield or a lyre safely, justice is helpful. But when you want to use them, you need a soldier or a musician?
Certainly.
So for everything else too — justice is useful when things aren't being used, and useless when they are?
That seems to be where we've ended up.
Then justice isn't worth much, is it? But let's consider another angle. Isn't the person who's best at throwing a punch in boxing also best at blocking one?
Certainly.
And the person who's best at preventing disease is also best at causing it?
True.
And the best guard of a military camp is the one best at launching a surprise attack on the enemy?
Certainly.
So anyone who's good at guarding something is equally good at stealing it?
That seems to follow.
So if the just person is good at keeping money safe, he's also good at stealing it.
That's what the argument implies.
So the just man turns out to be a kind of thief! You must have picked this up from Homer, who praises Odysseus's grandfather Autolycus as being
'the best of all men at theft and deception.'
So you and Homer and Simonides all agree that justice is a kind of theft — practiced 'for the good of friends and the harm of enemies.' Is that what you were saying?
No, definitely not that. Though honestly, I'm not sure anymore what I was saying. But I still stand by the idea that justice means helping friends and harming enemies.
Well, here's another question. When we say 'friends' and 'enemies,' do we mean people who truly are, or just people who appear to be?
Surely, he said, we love those we think are good and hate those we think are bad.
But don't people often misjudge? Many who seem good aren't really, and vice versa?
That's true.
So for those people, the good become their enemies and the bad their friends?
And in that case, it would be right for them to help the bad and harm the good?
Apparently.
But the good are just and wouldn't do wrong?
True.
So by your reasoning, it's just to harm people who've done nothing wrong?
No, Socrates — that conclusion is clearly immoral.
Then perhaps we should say: do good to the just and harm to the unjust?
That sounds better.

But consider this: many people are poor judges of character. They have friends who are actually bad people, and enemies who are actually good. In those cases, they'd be right to harm the good and help the bad — which is the exact opposite of what we said Simonides meant.
You're right, he said. I think we need to correct our use of 'friend' and 'enemy.'
What was the mistake, Polemarchus?
We assumed that a friend is whoever seems good or is thought to be good.
And how should we correct it?
We should say that a true friend is someone who both seems good and actually is good. Someone who only seems good but isn't is an apparent friend, not a real one. And the same goes for enemies.
So you're saying the good are our friends and the bad are our enemies?
Yes.

And instead of our original simple claim that justice means helping friends and harming enemies, we should now say: it's just to help friends who are genuinely good and to harm enemies who are genuinely bad?
Yes, that seems right to me.
But should a just person harm anyone at all?
Of course — he should harm those who are both wicked and his enemies.
When horses are harmed, do they get better or worse?
Worse.
Worse in terms of what makes horses good — not in terms of what makes dogs good?
Yes, as horses.
And dogs that are harmed get worse as dogs, not as horses?
Of course.
And wouldn't people who are harmed become worse in terms of what makes people good?
Certainly.
And isn't justice what makes people good?
Absolutely.
So people who are harmed necessarily become more unjust?
That follows.
But can a musician use music to make people unmusical?
Of course not.
Or a horseman use horsemanship to make bad riders?
Impossible.
Then can a just person use justice to make people unjust? Or more broadly, can good people use their goodness to make others bad?
No, that's impossible.
Just as heat can't produce cold?
It can't.
Or drought produce moisture?
No.
The good can't harm anyone?
Impossible.
And the just person is good?
Certainly.
Then harming a friend or anyone else isn't the work of a just person, but of an unjust one?
I think what you say is completely true, Socrates.

So if anyone claims that justice means paying debts, where good is the debt owed to friends and harm is the debt owed to enemies — that's not wise. It's simply not true, since we've shown that harming others can never be just.
I agree, said Polemarchus.
Then you and I are ready to take on anyone who attributes that saying to Simonides or Bias or Pittacus or any other wise man?
I'm ready to fight alongside you, he said.
Shall I tell you who I think actually came up with it?
Who?

I think it was Periander, or Perdiccas, or Xerxes, or Ismenias of Thebes, or some other rich and powerful man who had an inflated opinion of himself, who first said justice means 'helping your friends and harming your enemies.'
That's very likely true, he said.
Yes. But if this definition of justice has also fallen apart, what other one can we propose?

Several times during the discussion, Thrasymachus had tried to seize control of the argument, but the others kept shutting him down because they wanted to hear how things would play out. When Polemarchus and I paused, though, he couldn't contain himself any longer. He gathered himself up and came at us like a wild animal going in for the kill. We were honestly terrified.

He shouted at the whole group: What nonsense is this, Socrates? Why are you two bowing and scraping to each other like idiots? If you really want to know what justice is, don't just ask questions — answer them! And don't try to score points by tearing down other people's answers. Give your own! And I won't accept vague answers like 'duty' or 'advantage' or 'profit' or 'gain' or 'interest.' I want precision and clarity.

I was shaken by his words. I couldn't look at him without trembling. In fact, I believe that if I hadn't looked at him before he spoke, I would have been struck speechless. But because I saw his fury building, I was able to meet his eye first and reply.

Thrasymachus, I said with a slight tremor, don't be so hard on us. If Polemarchus and I went wrong somewhere in the argument, I promise it wasn't on purpose. If we were searching for gold, we wouldn't deliberately undermine each other and waste our chance of finding it. So why, when we're searching for justice — something far more precious than gold — would you accuse us of going easy on each other instead of doing our best to find the truth? No, my friend, we're genuinely trying. It's just that we can't seem to manage it. You who know everything should pity us rather than be angry.

How typical of Socrates! he said with a scornful laugh. That's your signature irony! Didn't I predict this? Didn't I tell everyone that you'd refuse to give your own answer and instead play your little games of irony and evasion?

You're a clever man, Thrasymachus, I said. You know perfectly well that if you ask someone 'What numbers make twelve?' but then forbid them from saying 'twice six' or 'three times four' or 'six times two' or 'four times three,' saying 'none of that nonsense' — well, obviously no one could answer you. But suppose that person replied, 'Thrasymachus, what do you mean? If one of those forbidden answers is the right one, should I deliberately give a wrong answer instead? Is that what you want?' What would you say to that?
As if the two situations were comparable! he said.
Why shouldn't they be? I said. And even if they're not really comparable but only seem so to the person being asked, shouldn't he still say what he thinks, regardless of whether you or I disapprove?
So I suppose you're going to give one of those forbidden answers?
I might, I said, if after thinking it over I find one of them convincing. Despite the risk.
But what if I give you a different answer about justice, he said, one that's better than all of those? What penalty would you deserve?
The penalty that fits someone who's ignorant — to learn from someone who's wise. That's the penalty I deserve.
How delightful — learn, but pay nothing!
I'll pay when I have the money, I said.
But you do have money, Socrates, said Glaucon. Don't worry about money, Thrasymachus — we'll all chip in for Socrates.
Right, said Thrasymachus, so Socrates can do what he always does: refuse to answer himself and just pick apart everyone else's answer.

But my good friend, I said, how can anyone answer who knows nothing — and admits it? And who's been told by an authority like you not to say what little he thinks he knows? You're the one who claims to have knowledge and can share it. So please, do us all a favor and enlighten us.

Glaucon and the others backed me up, and Thrasymachus — as anyone could see — was actually eager to speak. He thought he had a brilliant answer and wanted to show it off. But first he made a show of insisting that I answer. Finally he gave in and said: Behold the wisdom of Socrates — he refuses to teach and goes around learning from everyone else, without even saying thank you.

That I learn from others is absolutely true, I said. But that I'm ungrateful — that I completely deny. I have no money, so I pay in praise, which is all I have. And you'll see soon enough how eagerly I praise anyone who seems to speak well. I expect you'll speak very well.
Listen then, he said. My position is that justice is nothing other than the interest of the stronger. Now, why don't you praise me? Of course you won't.

Give me a moment to understand you first, I said. Justice, you say, is the interest of the stronger. What exactly do you mean by that? Surely you don't mean that because Polydamas the wrestler is stronger than us and finds that eating beef builds his strength, eating beef is therefore right and just for us too, even though we're weaker?
That's a disgusting distortion, Socrates. You're deliberately taking my words in the worst possible way.
Not at all, I said. I'm just trying to understand. Please be clearer.
Well, he said, haven't you noticed that governments come in different forms? There are tyrannies, democracies, and aristocracies.
Yes, I know.
And in each state, the government holds the power?
Certainly.

Each type of government makes laws that serve its own interests — democracies make democratic laws, tyrannies make tyrannical laws, and so on. By making these laws, they define 'justice' for their citizens, and anyone who breaks these laws is punished as a lawbreaker and an unjust person. That's what I mean: in every state, the principle of justice is the same — it's whatever serves the interest of the ruling power. And since the government has the power, the only reasonable conclusion is that everywhere, justice is the interest of the stronger.

Now I understand you, I said. Whether you're right or not, I'll try to figure out. But let me point out that you've used the word 'interest' in your definition — the very word you told me not to use. You've just added 'of the stronger.'
A minor addition, he said.

Maybe minor, maybe not. We'll see. But first, let's determine whether what you're saying is actually true. We both agree that justice involves some kind of interest, and you add 'of the stronger.' I'm not sure about that addition, so let's examine it.
Go ahead.
I will. First, tell me: do you agree that it's just for citizens to obey their rulers?
I do.
But are rulers infallible? Or do they sometimes make mistakes?
Of course they make mistakes.
So when they make laws, they sometimes get it right and sometimes get it wrong?
True.
When they get it right, the laws serve their interests. When they make mistakes, the laws go against their interests. Agreed?
Yes.
And their citizens must obey these laws — that's what you call justice?
Of course.
Then by your own argument, justice is sometimes not the interest of the stronger, but the opposite?
What do you mean? he asked.
I'm just following your logic. Haven't we agreed that rulers sometimes make mistakes about what's in their own interest, and that obeying them is justice?
Yes.

Then you've also admitted that justice sometimes works against the interest of the stronger — because when rulers mistakenly pass laws that harm themselves, and their subjects obey those laws, the weaker are doing what actually hurts the stronger. Isn't that the inescapable conclusion, wisest of men?
That's perfectly clear, Socrates, said Polemarchus.
Sure, said Cleitophon, jumping in, if you're allowed to be his witness.
No witness is needed, said Polemarchus. Thrasymachus himself admitted that rulers sometimes command what's not in their own interest, and that obeying them is justice.
True, Polemarchus — Thrasymachus said that doing what rulers command is just.

Yes, Cleitophon, but he also said justice is the interest of the stronger. And having accepted both claims, he also acknowledged that rulers sometimes command things that harm themselves. Which means justice is just as much the injury as the interest of the stronger.
But, said Cleitophon, what he meant by 'interest of the stronger' was what the stronger believed to be his interest. That's what the weaker had to do, and that's what he called justice.
Those weren't his words, said Polemarchus.

Never mind, I said. If that's what he wants to say now, let's go with it. Tell me, Thrasymachus: did you mean that justice is whatever the stronger thinks is in his interest, whether it actually is or not?
Absolutely not, he said. Do you think I'd call someone 'the stronger' at the very moment when he's making a mistake?
Well yes, I said. That's what I thought you meant when you admitted that rulers aren't infallible and sometimes get things wrong.

You argue like a nitpicking lawyer, Socrates. Do you call someone a doctor when he's making a medical mistake? Or a mathematician when he's getting the math wrong? Sure, we say 'the doctor made an error' or 'the mathematician got it wrong,' but that's just a manner of speaking. In reality, none of them make mistakes insofar as they are what we call them. They only go wrong when their skill fails them, and at that point they've stopped being true practitioners. No genuine craftsman or expert ever errs while truly practicing his craft. So to be perfectly precise — since you love precision — the ruler, insofar as he truly is a ruler, is infallible. And being infallible, he always commands what's in his own interest, which his subjects must carry out. So as I said from the start: justice is the interest of the stronger.
Well, Thrasymachus, do I really seem to you to argue like a nitpicking lawyer?
You certainly do, he said.
And do you think I'm deliberately trying to trip you up?
I don't just think it — I know it. But it won't work. You'll never beat me through argument alone.

I wouldn't dream of trying, my friend. But to avoid misunderstanding: when you speak of the 'ruler' or 'stronger' whose interest the weaker must serve, do you mean this in the loose, everyday sense, or in this strict, precise sense?
In the strictest possible sense, he said. Now try to trip me up if you can. I'm not asking for mercy. But you'll never manage it.
Do you really think I'm crazy enough to try shaving a lion? I said.
Well, you just tried it, he said, and failed.
Enough of this sparring, I said. Let me ask you something: in this strict sense you're talking about, is a doctor a healer of the sick or a moneymaker? Remember, I'm asking about the true doctor.
A healer of the sick, he said.
And a ship's captain — the true captain — is he a commander of sailors or just another sailor?
A commander of sailors.
The fact that he happens to sail on the ship doesn't matter. We don't call him a sailor. He's called a captain because of his skill and authority over the crew.
Exactly, he said.
Now, every craft has its own particular interest?
Certainly.
And each craft exists to serve and provide for that interest?
Yes, that's its purpose.
And the interest of any craft is its own perfection — nothing more?
What do you mean?

Let me illustrate. If you asked me whether the body is self-sufficient or has needs, I'd say: Obviously the body has needs. It can get sick and require treatment — and that's precisely why medicine exists, to serve the body's interests. Am I right?
Quite right, he said.

But does the art of medicine itself have any deficiency? Does any craft need some other craft to look after its interests, and that one still another, in an endless chain? Or do crafts only need to look after their subject matter, having no defects of their own? A craft, insofar as it's truly practiced, is pure and complete — it only concerns itself with its subject. Think carefully about this and tell me if I'm wrong.
You're right, he said.
So medicine doesn't serve the interests of medicine — it serves the interests of the body?
True, he said.
And horsemanship doesn't serve itself but serves the horse? No craft looks after itself, because it has no needs — it looks after its subject?
True, he said.
But surely, Thrasymachus, crafts have authority over their subjects?
He agreed, though with considerable reluctance.
Then no craft or science serves the interest of the stronger or ruling element, but only the interest of the weaker — its subject?
He tried to contest this too, but finally gave in.
So a true physician doesn't consider his own good in prescribing treatment, but the good of his patient — since a real doctor is a ruler over human bodies, not a moneymaker. We agreed on that?
Yes.
And a true captain is a ruler of sailors, not just a fellow sailor?
That was agreed.
And such a captain will work for the benefit of his sailors, not for his own benefit or the benefit of his rank?
He gave a grudging yes.

So, Thrasymachus, no ruler of any kind, insofar as he is truly a ruler, considers or pursues his own interest. He always considers the interest of his subjects and what their craft requires. Everything he says and does is directed toward their benefit.

When we reached this point in the argument and everyone could see that the definition of justice had been completely demolished, Thrasymachus, instead of responding, said: Tell me, Socrates, do you have a nanny?
Why do you ask that, I said, when you should be answering?
Because she lets you walk around with a runny nose. She hasn't even taught you to tell the shepherd from the sheep.
What do you mean by that? I said.

I mean that you naively believe shepherds and cowherds care for their animals for the animals' own good, rather than for themselves or their masters. And you think that political rulers, if they're truly rulers, never think of their citizens as sheep to be exploited, and that they aren't always calculating their own advantage day and night. You're so completely wrong about justice and injustice that you don't even realize justice is actually another person's good — the advantage of the ruler and stronger party, and the loss of the weaker subject. Injustice is the opposite: the unjust man rules over the truly simple and just, and his subjects serve his happiness, which is very far from their own. Think about it, you extremely naive Socrates: the just person always comes out worse than the unjust. First, in private business: whenever a just person partners with an unjust one, the unjust person always ends up with more when the partnership dissolves. Second, in public life: when there's a tax, the just person pays more on the same income; when there's something to collect, the just person gets nothing while the unjust person takes a lot. When either holds public office, the just person neglects his own affairs, suffers losses, and gains nothing, while also being resented by friends and family for refusing to use his position to give them illegal favors. Everything is reversed for the unjust person. I'm talking about injustice on a grand scale, where its advantages are clearest. And this is most obvious in tyranny, which by force and fraud seizes everything — sacred and profane, public and private — all at once. If someone got caught doing any one of these crimes individually, he'd be punished and disgraced — called a temple-robber, kidnapper, burglar, swindler, or thief. But when a man not only steals citizens' property but enslaves the citizens themselves, instead of these ugly names he's called blessed and happy — not just by his own people but by everyone who hears about it. People condemn injustice not because they're afraid of committing it, but because they're afraid of suffering it. So, Socrates, injustice on a large enough scale has more strength, freedom, and power than justice. As I said at the start: justice is the interest of the stronger, while injustice is what actually profits the individual.

After this tirade, having drenched us with words like a bathhouse attendant drenching his customers, Thrasymachus was ready to leave. But the group wouldn't let him go. They insisted he stay and defend his position. I added my own plea: Thrasymachus, you brilliant man, you can't just throw out an idea like that and then walk away! Are you really going to leave before you've properly taught us — or learned yourself — whether your claims are true? Do you think deciding how a person should live is a trivial matter — how each of us can live the best possible life?
Do I seem to think it's trivial? he said.

That's exactly how you seem, I said. Or maybe you just don't care about us at all — whether we live better or worse lives for not knowing what you claim to know. Please, friend, don't hoard your knowledge. There are many of us here, and any benefit you give will be well repaid. I'll tell you openly: I'm not convinced. I don't believe injustice is more profitable than justice, even when it has free rein and faces no opposition. Suppose there is an unjust man who can get away with anything through force or fraud — that still doesn't convince me of injustice's superiority. Others here may feel the same way. So if we're wrong, use your wisdom to show us why we should prefer injustice over justice.
And how am I supposed to convince you? he said. If what I just said didn't persuade you, what more can I do? Should I force the argument into your heads?

God forbid! I said. Just be consistent. Or if you change your position, do it openly without trying to deceive us. Look, Thrasymachus: let's go back to something you said earlier. You defined the true physician in a very precise way, but you weren't equally precise about the shepherd. You said the shepherd tends sheep not for the sheep's benefit but for profit — like a banquet planner or a meat merchant, not a true shepherd. But the art of shepherding is only concerned with the good of the flock, since the art itself is already complete when it fulfills its purpose. That's what I was saying about rulers too. The art of ruling, whether in public or private life, can only be concerned with the good of those being governed. Yet you seem to think rulers actually enjoy holding power.
I don't just think it — I'm certain of it.

Then why, in smaller offices, do people refuse to serve without pay, unless they understand that governing benefits the governed, not the governor? Answer me this: don't different crafts differ precisely because each has its own distinct function? Please say what you really think, so we can make some progress.
Yes, that's what distinguishes them, he said.
And each craft provides its own specific benefit, not just a general one? Medicine gives health, navigation gives safety at sea, and so on?
Yes.

And the craft of earning pay has its own specific function: providing wages. We don't confuse it with other crafts, just as we don't confuse navigation with medicine because a ship's captain happens to improve his health on a voyage. You wouldn't call navigation the art of medicine, would you?
Certainly not.
And you wouldn't say that the art of payment is medicine just because someone happens to be healthy when they get paid?
Of course not.
And you wouldn't call medicine the art of earning money just because a doctor collects fees while healing?
No.
And we've agreed that each craft's benefit belongs specifically to that craft?
Yes.
Then if there's some benefit all practitioners share in common, that must come from something they all use in addition to their specific craft?
True, he said.
So when a craftsman benefits from getting paid, the advantage comes from his additional use of the craft of wage-earning, not from his own specific craft?
He agreed, though reluctantly.

The pay doesn't come from practicing medicine or building or any other specific craft. Medicine provides health, building provides houses, and a separate activity — earning wages — provides the pay. Each craft does its own work and benefits its subject, but does the craftsman personally benefit unless he's also paid?
Apparently not.
But does that mean he provides no benefit when he works for free?
Of course he provides a benefit.

So now it's clear, Thrasymachus: no craft or government serves its own interests. As we said before, each governs and serves its subjects, the weaker party, not the stronger. It attends to their good, not the rulers'. That's exactly why no one willingly takes on the task of governing — because no one wants to fix other people's problems without compensation. In practicing his craft and giving orders, the true practitioner always has his subjects' interests in mind, not his own. That's why rulers must be paid in one of three ways: money, honor, or a penalty for refusing.
What do you mean, Socrates? said Glaucon. I understand money and honor as payments, but what's this about a penalty?
You don't understand the payment that most motivates the best people to govern? Surely you know that ambition and greed are considered disgraceful?
Of course.

That's why good people won't govern for money — they don't want to be called mercenaries for openly demanding pay, or thieves for secretly helping themselves to public funds. And they won't do it for honor either, since they're not ambitious. So they need to be compelled by the threat of a penalty. Perhaps that's why seeking office voluntarily, instead of waiting to be called upon, is considered shameful. And the worst penalty for refusing to govern is being governed by someone worse than yourself. It's the fear of this, I think, that drives good people to accept office — not because they want to, but because they must, and because they can't find anyone better or even equal to hand the job to. In a city of entirely good people, avoiding office would be as fiercely contested as seeking it is now. That would prove the true ruler doesn't naturally pursue his own interest but his subjects'. Everyone who understood this would rather receive benefits than take on the burden of conferring them. So I completely reject Thrasymachus's claim that justice is the interest of the stronger. But we can return to that later. What strikes me as far more important is his claim that the unjust life is better than the just life. Which do you think, Glaucon? Which life do you prefer?
I think the just life is more rewarding, he said.
Did you hear all the advantages of injustice that Thrasymachus listed?
I heard them, he said, but I'm not convinced.
Shall we try to show him he's wrong?
Absolutely, he said.

Well, if we both make long speeches listing the advantages of our respective positions, we'll need judges to weigh them. But if instead we proceed as we've been doing — reaching agreement step by step — we can be both judges and advocates ourselves.
Agreed, he said.
Which approach do you prefer? I asked.
The step-by-step method.
All right, Thrasymachus, let's start from the beginning. You say that perfect injustice is more profitable than perfect justice?
Yes, that's exactly what I say, and I've given my reasons.
So how would you classify each of them? Would you call one a virtue and the other a vice?
Of course.
I assume you'd call justice the virtue and injustice the vice?
How charming! As if I'd say that, when I've just argued that injustice is profitable and justice is not.
Then what would you say?
The opposite, he said.
You'd call justice a vice?
No — I'd call it noble naivety.
And injustice — would you call that wickedness?
No, I'd call it good judgment.
So in your view, the unjust are wise and good?

Yes — at least those who can practice injustice perfectly and have the power to dominate entire cities and nations. Though perhaps you thought I was talking about pickpockets. Even petty crime has its advantages if you don't get caught, but they're nothing compared to what I'm describing.
I understand what you mean, Thrasymachus, but I'm still amazed that you classify injustice with wisdom and virtue, and justice with their opposites.
That's exactly what I do.

That's a much harder position to challenge. If you'd said injustice is profitable while admitting it's shameful and wrong — as most people would — we could argue on common ground. But since you actually call injustice honorable and strong, and you attribute to the unjust all the qualities we normally give to the just, there's nothing holding you back.
You've read me perfectly, he said.
Well, I won't shy away from following the argument wherever it leads, as long as you're being sincere. And I do believe you're being genuine, not just playing with us.
Whether I'm sincere or not, what's that to you? Just refute the argument.
Fair enough. But would you answer one more question? Does the just person try to outdo other just people?
Not at all — if he did, he wouldn't be the charmingly simple creature that he is.
And would he try to do more than what's just?
No.
What about outdoing unjust people — would he see that as fair or unfair?
He'd think it fair and would try, but he wouldn't succeed.
That's not the point, I said. I'm just asking whether the just person, while not claiming more than another just person, would claim more than an unjust one?
Yes, he would.
And the unjust person — does he try to outdo the just person and take more than what's just?
Of course — he tries to outdo everyone.
So the unjust person competes with both the unjust and the just, trying to come out ahead of everyone?
True.
Let me put it this way: the just person doesn't try to outdo his equals, only those unlike him. The unjust person tries to outdo everyone, equals and unequals alike?
That's a perfect way to put it, he said.
And you say the unjust person is wise and good, and the just person is neither?
Exactly right, he said.
And the unjust person resembles the wise and good, while the just person doesn't?
Well, of course, he said. A person resembles those of his own kind.
Each one is like his own kind?
Obviously, he said.
Good. Now, Thrasymachus, consider the crafts. You'd agree that one person is a musician and another isn't?
Yes.
And which is wise and which is foolish?
The musician is wise, the non-musician foolish.
And wise in the areas where he's skilled, and foolish where he's not?
Yes.
The same goes for doctors?
Yes.
Now, my excellent friend, when a musician tunes a lyre, does he try to outdo or surpass another musician in tightening the strings?
I don't think he would.
But he would try to surpass a non-musician?
Of course.
And a doctor — in prescribing food and medicine, does he try to outdo another doctor or the practice of medicine itself?
No.
But he would try to surpass a non-doctor?
Yes.

Think about knowledge and ignorance in general. Does any person with knowledge try to claim more or do more than another person with the same knowledge? Wouldn't he do and say the same thing as his equal in the same situation?
I suppose that's undeniable.
And the ignorant person? Wouldn't he try to outdo both the knowledgeable and the ignorant?
I suppose so.
And the knowledgeable person is wise?
Yes.
And the wise person is good?
True.
So the wise and good person doesn't try to outdo his equals — only those who are unlike him and his opposites?
So it seems.
While the bad and ignorant person tries to outdo everyone?
Yes.
But didn't we say, Thrasymachus, that the unjust person tries to outdo both equals and unequals? Weren't those your exact words?
They were.
And you also said the just person doesn't try to outdo his equals, only his unequals?
Yes.
Then the just person resembles the wise and good, and the unjust person resembles the ignorant and bad?
That seems to follow.
And each person is like what he resembles?
That was agreed.
So it turns out that the just person is wise and good, and the unjust person is ignorant and bad.

Thrasymachus conceded all these points, though not smoothly as I'm recounting them, but with extreme reluctance. It was a hot summer's day, and the sweat was pouring off him. And then I witnessed something I'd never seen before: Thrasymachus blushing. Now that we'd established that justice is virtue and wisdom, and injustice is vice and ignorance, I moved on.
All right, I said, that's settled. But weren't we also saying that injustice has power? Do you remember?

I remember, he said, but I don't accept your conclusions, and I have a reply. But if I started to make it, you'd accuse me of speechmaking. So either let me speak at length, or if you'd rather keep asking questions, go ahead — I'll just say 'very good' like people do to old women telling stories, and nod along.
Not if it goes against what you really think, I said.
Fine, he said, I'll go along with you to keep you happy, since you won't let me speak freely. What more do you want?
Nothing at all. If that's what you're going to do, go ahead. I'll ask the questions.
Proceed.

Then let me go back to a question I raised before, so we can examine the relationship between justice and injustice in an orderly way. We heard the claim that injustice is stronger and more powerful than justice. But now that we've identified justice with wisdom and virtue, it's easy to see that justice must be stronger, since injustice is ignorance. Nobody could dispute that anymore. But I want to approach this from a different angle, Thrasymachus. Would you agree that a state can be unjust — that it might try to enslave other states, or might already hold them in subjection?
Of course, he said. And the most perfectly unjust state would be the most likely to do so.
I know that's your position. But my question is: can a state exercise this power without any justice at all, or does it need at least some justice?
If you're right that justice is wisdom, then it needs justice. But if I'm right, then it doesn't.
I'm delighted, Thrasymachus, that you're not just nodding but actually giving excellent answers.
I'm just being polite, he said.

Very kind of you. Now tell me: do you think that a state, or an army, or a band of robbers and thieves, or any group of criminals could accomplish anything if they constantly cheated and betrayed each other?
Obviously not, he said.
But if they refrained from betraying each other, they'd work together more effectively?
Yes.
Because injustice produces division, hatred, and conflict, while justice creates harmony and cooperation. Isn't that right, Thrasymachus?
Fine, I agree — I don't want to fight with you.

That's generous of you. But tell me this: if injustice breeds hatred wherever it exists — among slaves or free people — won't it set them against each other and make them incapable of working together?
Certainly.
And if injustice exists between just two people, won't they quarrel and become enemies to each other and to the just?
They will.
And if injustice takes root in a single person, does it lose its natural power, or keep it?
Let's say it keeps its power.

And isn't the nature of that power such that wherever injustice takes hold — whether in a city, an army, a family, or any group — it first makes that group incapable of united action through internal conflict, and then makes it an enemy to itself and to everything just? Isn't that right?
Yes, certainly.

And isn't injustice equally destructive within a single person? It makes him incapable of action because he's at war with himself, and it makes him an enemy to himself and to the just. True, Thrasymachus?
Yes.
And my friend — surely the gods are just?
Let's say they are.
Then the unjust person will be the enemy of the gods, while the just person will be their friend?
Go ahead, enjoy your victory and feast on the argument. I won't oppose you — I don't want to upset everyone here.

Then let me finish my feast. We've already shown that the just are wiser, better, and more capable than the unjust, and that the unjust are incapable of real cooperation. In fact, when we said that unjust people can sometimes act effectively together, that wasn't strictly true. If they were completely unjust, they'd turn on each other instantly. There must have been some remnant of justice in them that held them together — otherwise they'd have destroyed each other along with their victims. They were only half-villains, because completely unjust people would be completely incapable of action. That, I believe, is the truth, not what you originally said. But whether the just also live better and happier lives than the unjust — that's a separate question we still need to examine. I think they do, based on what we've discussed, but the stakes are too high to settle this casually. Nothing less than the right way to live is on the line.
Go on.
I'll continue by asking: would you say a horse has a specific function?
Yes.
And isn't the function of a horse — or anything else — the task that only it can do, or that it does better than anything else?
I don't follow, he said.
Let me explain. Can you see with anything other than your eyes?
No.
Or hear with anything other than your ears?
No.
So we can rightly say that seeing and hearing are the specific functions of these organs?
Yes.
Now, you could cut a vine branch with a dagger or a chisel or various other tools?
Of course.
But not as well as with a pruning hook designed for the job?
True.
So we can call pruning the specific function of the pruning hook?
Yes.
Now you should have no trouble understanding what I meant. The function of something is the task that either only it can do, or that it does better than anything else.
I understand, he said, and I agree.
Good. And doesn't everything with a function also have a corresponding excellence? Take the eyes again — don't they have a function?
They do.
And an excellence as well?
Yes.
The ears have a function and an excellence too?
True.
And the same holds for everything else — each has its own function and its own excellence?
That's right.
Now, can the eyes perform their function well if they lack their proper excellence and have a deficiency instead?
Obviously not — if they're blind, they can't see.
I mean more generally: doesn't everything perform its function well through its own proper excellence, and badly through its defect?
Certainly, he said.
And the same goes for ears that have lost their excellence — they can't fulfill their function?
True.
And this principle applies to everything?
I agree.

Good. Now, doesn't the soul have a function that nothing else can perform? Things like deliberating, governing, making decisions, and living itself — can these be assigned to anything other than the soul?
Nothing else.
And living is one of the soul's functions?
Absolutely, he said.
And the soul has its own excellence too?
Yes.
Can the soul perform its functions well when deprived of its proper excellence?
It cannot.
So a defective soul must be a poor governor and director of life, while a good soul does these things well?
Necessarily.
And didn't we agree that justice is the soul's excellence, and injustice is its defect?
We did.
Then the just soul and the just person will live well, and the unjust person will live badly?
That's what your argument proves.
And the person who lives well is happy, while the one who lives badly is unhappy?
Certainly.
So the just person is happy, and the unjust person is miserable?
So be it.
But happiness is an advantage, and misery isn't.
Obviously.
Then injustice can never be more profitable than justice, my dear Thrasymachus.
Well, Socrates, he said, let this be your entertainment for the evening of the festival.

And I have you to thank for it, I said, since you've become gentle and stopped being hostile. Still, I haven't been properly entertained — but that's my own fault, not yours. Like a greedy diner who snatches a taste of each new dish before properly finishing the last, I jumped from one topic to the next without ever discovering what I was looking for — the nature of justice itself. I abandoned that inquiry to ask whether justice is a virtue and a form of wisdom or a vice and ignorance. And then when the question came up about whether injustice is more profitable than justice, I couldn't resist chasing that either. The result of this entire discussion is that I know nothing at all. Since I don't know what justice is, I can hardly know whether it's a virtue or not, or whether the just person is happy or miserable.

chapters.title: Book II
paragraphs: I thought the discussion was over with those words, but it turned out to be only the beginning. Glaucon, who's always the most combative person in any room, wasn't satisfied with Thrasymachus's surrender. He wanted to see the fight through to the end. So he said to me: Socrates, do you actually want to persuade us that being just is always better than being unjust, or do you just want to seem like you've persuaded us?
I'd genuinely like to persuade you, I said, if I could.

Well, you certainly haven't succeeded. Let me ask you something: how would you classify different kinds of goods? Aren't there some we value purely for their own sake, regardless of consequences — like harmless pleasures and enjoyments that delight us in the moment, even though nothing comes of them afterward?
Yes, I agree there's a category like that.
And isn't there a second category of goods that we value both for themselves and for their results — things like knowledge, sight, and health?
Certainly.

And wouldn't you recognize a third category — things like exercise, medical treatment, and various ways of earning money? These benefit us, but we find them unpleasant. No one would choose them for their own sake, only for the rewards or results they produce.
Yes, there's that third category too. But why do you ask?
Because I want to know which category you'd place justice in.
In the highest category, I said — among those goods that anyone who wants to be happy would value both for their own sake and for their results.

That's not how most people see it. They put justice in the unpleasant category — something you pursue for the sake of rewards and reputation, but that's disagreeable in itself and best avoided if possible.
I know that's how people think, and that's the position Thrasymachus was just defending when he praised injustice and criticized justice. But I'm too stubborn to be convinced by him.

I want you to hear my argument too, he said, and then we'll see if you and I agree. Thrasymachus seems to me like a snake that was charmed by your voice sooner than it should have been. But to my mind, the true nature of justice and injustice still hasn't been made clear. Setting aside their rewards and consequences, I want to know what they are in themselves — how they work within the soul. So if you don't mind, I'll revive Thrasymachus's argument. First, I'll explain the common view of what justice is and where it comes from. Second, I'll show that everyone who practices justice does so reluctantly, out of necessity, not because they see it as good. Third, I'll argue that there's good reason for this view, since the life of the unjust person really is far better than the life of the just person — or so they say. I don't personally believe this, Socrates, but I'm genuinely confused. I hear Thrasymachus and countless others arguing this way, and it overwhelms me. On the other hand, I've never heard anyone defend the superiority of justice over injustice in a truly satisfying way. I want to hear justice praised for what it is in itself. You're the person I'm most likely to hear this from. So I'm going to praise the unjust life as powerfully as I can, and the way I argue will show you how I want to hear you praise justice and condemn injustice in return. Does this plan work for you?
Absolutely. I can't imagine a topic I'd rather discuss.
Wonderful, he said. Then I'll begin, as I proposed, with the common account of justice's nature and origin.

The popular view goes like this: by nature, doing injustice is good, and suffering injustice is bad. But the harm of suffering it outweighs the benefit of doing it. So after people have experienced both — doing and suffering injustice — and can't manage to get one without the other, they decide it's better to make an agreement: nobody will do injustice, and nobody will suffer it. That's where laws and social contracts come from. Whatever the law commands, people call 'lawful' and 'just.' This, they say, is the origin and essence of justice: it's a compromise between the best situation (committing injustice without punishment) and the worst (suffering injustice without recourse). Justice sits in the middle — tolerated not as something genuinely good, but as the lesser evil, valued only because people lack the power to be unjust successfully. Anyone truly worthy of the name 'man' would never agree to such a deal if he had the power to break it. He'd be crazy to. That, Socrates, is the common account of justice's nature and origin.

Now, to show that people practice justice only because they lack the power to be unjust, imagine this thought experiment. Give both the just and the unjust person complete freedom to do whatever they want, and then watch where their desires lead them. You'll catch the just person doing exactly the same thing as the unjust one — pursuing self-interest, which every creature naturally considers good. Only the force of law diverts people onto the path of justice. The kind of freedom I'm describing is best illustrated by the legendary power of Gyges' ancestor, a shepherd serving the king of Lydia. One day there was a great storm and earthquake that opened a chasm in the ground where he was tending his flock. Amazed, he climbed down and discovered, among other wonders, a hollow bronze horse with doors. He looked inside and saw a corpse, larger than any human, wearing nothing but a gold ring. He took the ring and climbed back out. Later, at the shepherds' monthly meeting to report on the flocks, he was sitting with the others and happened to turn the ring's setting inward on his hand. Instantly, he became invisible to everyone else, and they started talking about him as if he'd left. Astonished, he turned the setting outward and reappeared. He tested this several times with the same result — inward meant invisible, outward meant visible. He arranged to be chosen as a messenger to the king's court, and once there, he seduced the queen, conspired with her against the king, killed him, and took the kingdom. Now imagine two such rings — one on the just person's finger, one on the unjust person's. No one, it is claimed, has such an iron will that he would remain just. No one would keep his hands off other people's property when he could take whatever he wanted from the marketplace, enter any house and sleep with anyone he chose, kill or free anyone from prison — in short, move through the world like a god among mortals. The just person would end up acting exactly like the unjust one; they'd both end up in the same place. This, people say, is powerful proof that no one is just willingly — only out of necessity. Whenever someone thinks they can get away with injustice, they're unjust. Everyone believes deep down that injustice is far more profitable than justice, and anyone who argues as I've been doing would say they're right. If you could imagine someone with the power of invisibility who never did anything wrong or touched what wasn't his, everyone watching would think him a pathetic fool — though they'd praise him to each other's faces, out of fear that they themselves might become victims of injustice. But enough of that.

Now, to properly judge the life of the just and unjust, we need to isolate each in pure form. Here's how: let the unjust person be completely unjust, and the just person completely just. Strip away nothing from either; equip both perfectly for their respective lives. First, the unjust person: let him be like other master craftsmen — a skilled captain or doctor who knows his own abilities, stays within his limits, and recovers quickly from any misstep. Let the unjust person commit injustice skillfully and stay hidden, because the highest achievement of injustice is to seem just while being completely unjust. Getting caught means you're nobody. So give our perfectly unjust man the greatest reputation for justice while committing the most unjust acts. If he stumbles, let him recover. Let him speak persuasively when his deeds come to light, use force when needed, backed by courage, strength, money, and friends. Now place the just person beside him — noble and simple, wanting, as Aeschylus says, to be good rather than to seem good. In fact, there must be no seeming at all, because if he appears just, he'll receive honors and rewards, and then we won't know whether he's just for justice's own sake or for the rewards. So strip him of everything except justice itself. Imagine him in the opposite situation from the other: let him be the best of men but thought the worst. Let him be tested this way — will the fear of disgrace and its consequences shake him? Let him persist in justice until death, being just but seeming unjust. When both have reached the extreme — one of justice, one of injustice — let us judge which is happier.
Good heavens, Glaucon! I said. You're polishing these two characters like statues for a competition!

I'm doing my best, he said. And now that we know what each looks like, it's easy to trace the life that awaits each. Let me describe it — and if the language seems harsh, remember, Socrates, that these aren't my words. I'll put them in the mouths of those who praise injustice. They'll tell you that the just person who seems unjust will be whipped, racked, chained, have his eyes burned out, and finally be impaled. Then he'll understand that he should have aimed to seem just rather than to actually be just. The words of Aeschylus apply far better to the unjust person than the just one, they'll say. For the unjust person pursues reality, not appearances — he wants to truly be unjust, not merely seem so:
'His mind has a soil deep and fertile, from which spring his wise designs.'

First, because he's thought to be just, he rules the city. He can marry whomever he wants and give his children in marriage to whomever he chooses. He trades and deals freely, always to his own advantage, since he has no scruples about injustice. In every contest, public or private, he wins at others' expense and grows rich. From his gains he benefits his friends and harms his enemies. He makes lavish sacrifices and generous gifts to the gods, honoring gods and men far more grandly than the just person ever could. So naturally, they say, the gods are more likely to favor him. And that's how, according to this argument, gods and men unite to make the unjust life better than the just one.
I was about to respond to Glaucon when his brother Adeimantus interrupted: Socrates, you don't think that's the whole argument, do you?
What else is there? I said.
The strongest point hasn't even been mentioned, he said.

Well then, as the proverb says, 'Let brother help brother.' If Glaucon's argument has any gaps, help him fill them — though I must say, what he's already said is enough to knock me down and leave me unable to defend justice.

Nonsense, he said. But let me add something more. There's another side to Glaucon's argument about the praise and blame of justice that needs to be stated to bring out his full meaning. Parents and teachers always tell their children to be just — but why? Not for justice's own sake, but for the reputation and rewards it brings. They want their children to seem just so they can win the offices, marriages, and advantages that Glaucon listed among the benefits the unjust gain from a reputation for justice. These people put even more weight on appearances than the others, and they throw in divine favor too, claiming that heaven showers blessings on the righteous. They cite the noble Hesiod and Homer as proof. Hesiod says that for the just, the gods make the oaks—
'Bear acorns at their crown and bees in their hollows, and their woolly sheep are heavy with fleece,'
and many other similar blessings. Homer says something very similar about one whose reputation is—
'Like that of a blameless king who, godlike, upholds justice; for him the dark earth yields wheat and barley, his trees bend with fruit, his sheep never fail to breed, and the sea provides him fish.'

Even grander are the gifts that Musaeus and his son promise the just in the afterlife: they picture the righteous lying on couches at an eternal feast, permanently drunk, wearing garlands — as if an eternity of drunkenness were the highest reward of virtue. Some extend the rewards even further, saying that the descendants of the faithful and just will survive to the third and fourth generation. That's how they praise justice. As for the wicked, they bury them in mud in Hades and make them carry water in a sieve. While they're still alive, they heap on them the same punishments that Glaucon described as the fate of the just person who seems unjust. That's the extent of their imagination. That's their way of praising one and condemning the other.

Now, Socrates, consider yet another way people talk about justice and injustice — not just poets but prose writers too. Everyone declares that justice and virtue are admirable but difficult and burdensome, while the pleasures of vice and injustice are easy to get and only frowned upon by law and public opinion. They say dishonesty is usually more profitable than honesty. They're perfectly happy to call wicked people blessed and honor them in public and private when they're rich and powerful, while looking down on anyone who's weak or poor, even while admitting they're better people. But the most extraordinary thing is what they say about virtue and the gods: they claim the gods send suffering to many good people and happiness to the wicked. And wandering prophets go to the doors of the rich and persuade them that they have power, granted by the gods, to atone for a person's sins or their ancestors' sins through sacrifices and rituals, with celebrations and feasts. They also promise to harm any enemy, just or unjust, for a small fee, using magic and incantations that supposedly bind the gods to do their bidding. They cite poets as their authority, paving the way to vice with Hesiod's words—
'Vice can be had in abundance, easily; the path is smooth and she lives nearby. But before virtue the gods have placed hard work,'
and a long, steep road. Then they cite Homer as proof that the gods can be swayed by humans, since he says—
'The gods themselves can be turned; men sway them with sacrifices and gentle prayers, with offerings and the aroma of burnt fat, when they have sinned and transgressed.'

They produce stacks of books by Musaeus and Orpheus — supposedly children of the Moon and the Muses — and perform rituals based on these texts, persuading not just individuals but entire cities that sins can be atoned for through sacrifices and pleasant diversions, which serve both the living and the dead. These latter rituals they call 'mysteries,' claiming they save us from the torments of the afterlife — but if we neglect them, terrible things await.

He continued: Now, Socrates, when young people hear all this about virtue and vice, and about how gods and humans view them, what effect do you think it has on their minds? I mean the clever ones, who flit like bees from flower to flower, drawing conclusions about how they should live to make the best of life. Such a young person would probably say to himself, echoing Pindar—
'Shall I climb to the higher tower by justice, or by crooked paths of deceit, and there build my fortress for life?'

Because what people say is this: if I'm truly just but don't also seem just, there's no profit in it — only obvious pain and loss. But if I'm unjust while maintaining a reputation for justice, a heavenly life is promised to me. Since, as the wise men show, appearance dominates truth and is the lord of happiness, I should devote myself entirely to appearance. I'll construct an elaborate facade of virtue as my front entrance, while behind it I'll keep the subtle, crafty fox, as Archilochus, that greatest of sages, recommends. Someone objects that concealing wickedness is often difficult. I reply: nothing great is easy. But the argument points this way if we want to be happy — this is the path to follow. For concealment, we'll form secret societies and political clubs. There are teachers of rhetoric who train us to persuade courts and assemblies. So partly through persuasion and partly through force, we'll make illegal gains and escape punishment. But still, someone insists, the gods can't be deceived or coerced. Well, what if there are no gods? Or what if they don't care about human affairs? In either case, why worry about hiding anything? And even if gods do exist and do care about us, we only know about them from tradition and the poets — the very same authorities who say gods can be influenced by 'sacrifices and soothing prayers and offerings.' Either believe both claims or neither. If the poets speak truly, then we should be unjust and use the proceeds of injustice to make offerings. If we're just, we may escape divine punishment but we'll miss out on the gains of injustice. If we're unjust, we keep the gains, and by praying and sacrificing, we can appease the gods and avoid punishment. 'But there's an afterlife where we or our descendants will pay for our crimes.' Yes, my friend, comes the reply, but there are mystery rites and gods of atonement with great power. Mighty cities confirm this, and the children of gods, who were their poets and prophets, say the same.

On what basis, then, should we choose justice over the worst kind of injustice? If we combine injustice with a carefully maintained appearance of virtue, we'll do well with both gods and humans, in this life and the next — at least according to the most numerous and authoritative voices. Knowing all this, Socrates, how can any person of superior intelligence, or wealth, or rank, or power, be willing to respect justice instead of laughing when they hear it praised? Even if someone could disprove everything I've said and show that justice truly is best, such a person wouldn't be angry at the unjust but would readily forgive them, knowing that people aren't just voluntarily — unless perhaps some divine nature has inspired a hatred of injustice in them, or they've arrived at the truth through genuine knowledge. Otherwise, no one chooses justice freely. People only blame injustice when they're too cowardly, too old, or too weak to practice it themselves. And the proof? The moment such people gain power, they become as unjust as they can.

The root cause of all this, Socrates, is what my brother and I pointed out at the start: among all the supposed champions of justice — from the ancient heroes whose memories survive to the people of our own time — not one has ever condemned injustice or praised justice except in terms of the reputation, honors, and rewards that come from them. No one has ever properly described what justice and injustice actually are in themselves, operating invisibly within the soul, unseen by any human or divine eye. No one has shown that justice is the soul's greatest good and injustice its greatest evil. If this had always been the message — if you had taught us this from childhood — we wouldn't need to guard against each other's injustice. Each person would be his own guard, afraid that by doing wrong he'd be harboring the greatest of evils within himself. I'm sure Thrasymachus and others would make the same argument I've been making, or even stronger ones, about justice and injustice — crudely distorting their true nature, in my view. But I'm making this case as forcefully as I can, Socrates — I'll be honest with you — because I want to hear you argue the opposite. Show me not just that justice is superior to injustice, but what effect each has on its possessor that makes one inherently good and the other inherently evil. And please, as Glaucon asked, set aside reputations. Unless you strip away false reputations and add on true ones for both justice and injustice, we'll say you're praising the appearance of justice, not the reality. We'll think you're just telling us to keep injustice hidden, and that you secretly agree with Thrasymachus that justice is someone else's good and the interest of the stronger, while injustice profits the individual at the expense of the weaker. You've admitted that justice belongs to the highest category of goods — those valued for their results but even more for themselves, like sight, hearing, knowledge, or health, or any other genuine, natural good rather than a merely conventional one. So in your praise of justice, focus on this one thing: the essential good and evil that justice and injustice work in those who possess them. Let others praise justice for its rewards and condemn injustice for its punishments. I can tolerate that from other people. But from you, who have spent your entire life examining this question — unless you tell me otherwise — I expect something better. Not only prove that justice is better than injustice, but show what each does to its possessor that makes one good and the other evil, whether or not gods and humans can see it.

I had always admired Glaucon and Adeimantus for their intelligence, but hearing these words I was truly delighted. I said: Sons of a remarkable father — that admirer of Glaucon's wasn't wrong when he wrote those elegiac verses after you distinguished yourselves at the battle of Megara:
'Sons of Ariston,' he sang, 'divine offspring of an illustrious hero.'

The description fits perfectly. There's something genuinely extraordinary about arguing so powerfully for the superiority of injustice while remaining unconvinced by your own arguments. And I do believe you're unconvinced — I can tell from your character, because if I judged only from your speeches, I'd be suspicious of you. But the more I trust you, the more I struggle with how to respond. I'm torn two ways. On one hand, I feel unequal to the task — my inability is proven by the fact that my earlier argument against Thrasymachus, which I thought showed justice's superiority over injustice, didn't satisfy you. On the other hand, I can't refuse to help while I still have breath and words. I'd feel it was almost a sacrilege to stand by while justice is being attacked and not lift a finger in its defense. So I'd better offer what help I can.

Glaucon and the others begged me not to drop the question but to press on with the investigation. They wanted to discover, first, the true nature of justice and injustice, and second, their relative benefits. I told them honestly that this would be a serious inquiry requiring sharp eyes. Since we're not exactly brilliant, I said, maybe we should adopt this method: suppose a nearsighted person was asked to read small letters from a distance, and someone pointed out that the same letters existed somewhere else, larger and easier to read. Wouldn't it be a stroke of luck to read the large letters first and then check whether the small ones were the same?
Absolutely, said Adeimantus. But how does this relate to our inquiry?
I'll tell you, I said. Justice, which we're investigating, is sometimes spoken of as a quality of an individual, but also as a quality of an entire state.
True, he said.
And a state is larger than an individual?
It is.

Then justice is likely to exist on a larger scale in a state and be easier to see. So I suggest we first look for justice in the state and then examine it in the individual, moving from the larger to the smaller and comparing them.
That's an excellent idea, he said.
And if we imagine a state being created from scratch, we'll see justice and injustice coming into existence along with it.
Probably so.
And once the state is complete, we'll have a better chance of finding what we're looking for?
Much better.
But should we actually try to construct one? It'll be an enormous undertaking. Think about it.
I have thought about it, said Adeimantus, and I'm eager for you to go ahead.
A state comes into existence, I said, because no person is self-sufficient — we all have many needs. Can you think of any other origin for a state?
No other.
So because we have many needs and require many people to meet them, we gather together in one place as partners and helpers. This community of people is what we call a state.
Exactly, he said.
And people exchange goods and services with each other because they believe the exchange benefits everyone.
Very true.
Then let's build a state in our imagination from the ground up. Its true creator, of course, is necessity — the mother of invention.
Of course, he said.
Now, the first and greatest necessity is food — the basic condition of life itself.
Certainly.
The second is shelter, and the third is clothing and such things.
True.
So how will our city provide for all these needs? We'll have one person as a farmer, another as a builder, another as a weaver — and should we add a shoemaker or other providers for bodily needs?
Exactly right.
The most basic state would need at least four or five people.
Clearly.

Now, how will they organize their work? Will each one contribute to a common supply — the farmer, for example, producing food for all four and spending four times as long farming? Or will each person work only for himself, spending a quarter of his time on food and the rest making his own house, clothes, and shoes, without bothering to share with others?
Adeimantus thought each person should focus on producing food rather than trying to do everything.
That's probably the better approach, I said. And hearing you say this reminds me that we're not all alike — people have different natural abilities suited to different tasks.
Very true.
And is work done better when someone practices many trades, or just one?
When he has just one.
And surely work suffers when it's not done at the right time?
No doubt.
