Because tasks don't wait around for the worker to get to them. The worker has to follow the work and make it his priority.
He must.
So things are produced more abundantly, more easily, and at higher quality when each person does the one thing that suits his nature, does it at the right time, and leaves everything else to others.
Undoubtedly.

Then we'll need more than four people. The farmer won't make his own plow or other farming tools if they're to be any good. Neither will the builder make his own tools — and he needs many. Same for the weaver and shoemaker.
True.
So carpenters, metalworkers, and many other craftsmen will join our little state, which is already starting to grow?
True.

And even if we add cattle herders, shepherds, and other herdsmen — so our farmers have oxen to plow with, our builders have draft animals, and our weavers and leather workers have wool and hides — our state still won't be very large.
True, but it won't be tiny either, with all these people.
Then there's the question of location. It's virtually impossible to find a place where everything the city needs is available locally.
Virtually impossible.
So there must be another group of citizens who import what's needed from other cities.
There must.
But if the trader goes empty-handed, with nothing that the other city wants, he'll come back empty-handed too.
That's certain.
So the city must produce not just enough for its own people, but enough in both quantity and quality to trade with those who supply what it lacks.
Very true.
Which means more farmers and more craftsmen?
Yes.
Not to mention the importers and exporters — the merchants?
Yes.
So we'll need merchants?
We will.
And if trade happens by sea, we'll need skilled sailors, and plenty of them?
Yes, plenty.
Now, within the city itself, how will people exchange what they produce? That was one of our main reasons for forming a community in the first place.
Obviously, through buying and selling.
Which means we'll need a marketplace and a currency system for exchange.
Certainly.
Now suppose a farmer or craftsman brings his goods to market at a time when no one wants to trade with him. Should he abandon his work and sit idle in the marketplace?

Not at all. There will be people who see this need and take on the role of salesmen. In well-run states, these are usually people who are physically weak and not much good for anything else. Their job is to stay in the marketplace, buying from sellers for cash and selling to buyers.
So this need creates a class of shopkeepers in our state. We use 'shopkeeper' for those who buy and sell in the marketplace, and 'merchant' for those who travel between cities to trade?
Yes, he said.
And there's another class of workers who aren't intellectually suited for skilled work but have strong bodies for physical labor. They sell their labor and are called wage-workers.
True.
So wage-workers will also be part of our population?
Yes.
So, Adeimantus, has our state now grown to maturity?
I think so.
Then where in it are justice and injustice? At what point in its creation did they arise?
Probably in the interactions between these citizens. I can't imagine they'd come from anywhere else.
You're probably right, I said. We should think it through carefully and not shy away from the inquiry.

Let's consider, then, how these people will actually live. They'll produce grain, wine, clothes, and shoes, and build houses. In summer they'll mostly work stripped down and barefoot; in winter they'll be well clothed and shod. They'll make bread from wheat and barley — fine loaves and cakes — and serve them on mats of reeds or clean leaves, while reclining on beds of yew and myrtle branches. They and their children will feast together, drinking wine, wearing garlands, singing hymns to the gods, and enjoying each other's company. And they'll be careful not to have more children than they can support, keeping an eye on both poverty and war.
But, said Glaucon, interrupting, you haven't given them anything to eat with their bread!

You're right, I forgot. Of course they'll have something to go with it — salt, olives, cheese, and they'll cook up roots and vegetables the way country people do. For dessert, we'll give them figs, chickpeas, and beans. They'll roast myrtle berries and acorns by the fire and drink in moderation. With a diet like that, they can expect to live in peace and good health to a ripe old age, and pass the same kind of life on to their children.
Sure, Socrates, he said — and if you were building a city of pigs, wouldn't you feed them the same way?
Well, what would you have, Glaucon? I said.
The normal comforts of civilized life, he said. People who want to live comfortably lie on couches, eat at tables, and enjoy the sauces and desserts we have today.

Ah, I see, I said. We're not just looking at how a simple state is formed, but a luxurious one. And that may not be a bad thing, actually, because in a luxurious state we're more likely to see how justice and injustice arise. In my view, the simple, healthy state is the true one. But if you want to examine a state in a fever, I have no objection. I suspect many people won't be satisfied with the simple life. They'll want couches, tables, and other furniture, plus delicacies, perfumes, incense, courtesans, and pastries — every variety of each. We'll have to go beyond basics like houses, clothes, and shoes. We'll need painters and embroiderers, gold and ivory and all sorts of materials.
True, he said.

Then we'll have to expand our borders, because the original healthy state won't be large enough anymore. We'll need to add a whole host of occupations that go beyond any natural need: hunters, actors, musicians of all kinds — poets with their entourages of performers, dancers, and producers — plus manufacturers of every kind of luxury item, including women's fashion. We'll need more servants too: tutors, nurses both wet and dry, hairdressers, barbers, pastry chefs, cooks, and even swineherd — who had no place in the simple state but are needed now. And there will be all sorts of other livestock, if people are going to eat meat.
Certainly.
And living this way, we'll need far more doctors than before?
Far more.
And the territory that was enough for the original population will now be too small?
Exactly.

So we'll need to take a slice of our neighbors' land for pasture and farming, and they'll want a slice of ours — assuming they've also gone beyond meeting basic needs and given themselves over to the unlimited pursuit of wealth?
That's inevitable, Socrates.
And so we'll go to war, Glaucon. Won't we?
Most certainly, he said.

Without deciding yet whether war does good or harm, we can at least say this: we've discovered war's origin, and it comes from the same causes that produce nearly all the evils in states, both public and private.
Undoubtedly.

So our state needs to be even larger. And this expansion won't be small — we'll need an entire army to go out and fight invaders for everything we have, including all the things and people we just described.
Why? he said. Can't they defend themselves?
No, I said — not if we were right about the principle we all agreed on when building the state: that one person can't practice many skills well.
Very true, he said.
And isn't warfare a skill?
Certainly.
A skill requiring as much dedication as shoemaking?
Absolutely.

We didn't let the shoemaker also be a farmer or weaver or builder, so that shoes would be well made. Each worker was assigned the one task he was naturally suited for, to do that and nothing else his whole life, never letting opportunities slip — and that's how he'd become good at it. Now, nothing is more important than having warfare done well. But is war so easy that a person can be both a warrior and a farmer, or a shoemaker, or anything else? No one becomes a good chess or checkers player just by playing casually — you have to dedicate yourself to it from an early age. And no tool makes someone a skilled fighter or defender who hasn't trained with it extensively. So how would someone who picks up a shield or any other weapon become a competent warrior overnight, regardless of the type of combat?
Yes, he said — tools that could teach people to use them would be priceless.
And the higher the guardian's duties, the more time, skill, training, and dedication they'll require?
No doubt, he said.
Won't they also need natural talent for the role?
Certainly.
Then it's our job to select people with the right natures for guarding the city, if we can?
It is.
And that selection won't be easy. But we must be brave and do our best.
We must.
Isn't a well-bred young person rather like a well-bred dog when it comes to guarding?
What do you mean?
I mean that both need to be quick to spot things, fast enough to chase down what they see, and strong enough to fight when they catch it.
All those qualities will certainly be needed, he said.
And a guardian must be brave if he's going to fight well?
Certainly.

And can a horse, a dog, or any creature be brave without spirit? Haven't you noticed how invincible and unstoppable spirit is — how its presence makes any creature absolutely fearless and unconquerable?
I have.
So we know what physical qualities our guardian needs.
True.
And the mental ones: his soul must be full of spirit?
Yes.
But won't these spirited natures tend to be aggressive — toward each other and everyone else?
That's a serious problem, he said.
Yet they need to be fierce toward enemies while gentle with friends. Otherwise they'll destroy themselves before any enemy can.
True, he said.
What do we do, then? How do we find a nature that's both gentle and high-spirited? These seem like opposites.
True.
And yet without both qualities, a person can't be a good guardian. But if combining them seems impossible, then being a good guardian is impossible.
I'm afraid you might be right, he said.
I was feeling stuck and began reviewing what we'd said. Then I said: No wonder we're confused, my friend. We've lost sight of the comparison we started with.
What do you mean?
There actually are natures that combine these seemingly opposite qualities.
Where do you find them?
In many animals, I said — and our friend the dog is a perfect example. Well-bred dogs are perfectly gentle with people they know and fierce with strangers.
Yes, I know.
So there's nothing impossible or unnatural about finding a guardian with the same combination?
Certainly not.
But wouldn't a good guardian also need to be something of a philosopher, in addition to being spirited?
I don't follow.
It's a quality you can actually see in dogs, and it's remarkable.
What quality?

A dog is angry whenever it sees a stranger, and welcomes anyone it knows — even if the stranger has never done it any harm and the friend has never done it any good. Hasn't that ever struck you as curious?
I never really thought about it before, but yes, that is exactly what they do.
And this instinct in dogs is actually quite charming. Your dog is a true philosopher.
Why?

Because it distinguishes friend from enemy purely by the test of knowing and not knowing. And any creature that determines what it likes and dislikes based on knowledge and ignorance must be a lover of learning.
Definitely.
And isn't the love of learning the same thing as the love of wisdom — which is philosophy?
They're the same, he said.
Then can we confidently say that a human being who is naturally gentle with familiar people must also be a lover of wisdom and learning?
We can safely say that.
So anyone who's going to be a truly good and noble guardian of the state must combine philosophy with spirit, speed, and strength?
Absolutely.

That's the nature we're looking for, then. Now that we've found it, how should these guardians be raised and educated? Exploring this question will surely shed light on our bigger inquiry — how do justice and injustice develop in states? We don't want to skip anything important, but we also don't want to drag this out forever.
Adeimantus said he thought the inquiry would be very useful.
Then we mustn't give up on it, my friend, even if it takes a while.
Certainly not.
Come on, then. Let's take our time and tell a story — the story of how our heroes should be educated.
Let's do it.
What should their education look like? Can we improve on the traditional system? It has two parts: physical training for the body and the arts for the mind.
True.
Should we start with the arts and move to physical training afterward?
By all means.
And when you say 'the arts,' does that include literature?
It does.
And literature can be either true or fictional?
Yes.
And children should be exposed to both kinds, starting with fiction?
I don't understand what you mean, he said.
You know that we start by telling children stories — stories that aren't entirely true but are mostly made up. And we tell them these stories before they're old enough for physical training.
Very true.
That's what I meant: we teach the arts before physical training.
Right, he said.
And you know that the beginning of anything is the most important part, especially with something young and impressionable. That's when character is being shaped and impressions are most deeply made.
Exactly.
So should we carelessly let children hear whatever stories anyone happens to invent, absorbing ideas that are often the exact opposite of what we'd want them to believe as adults?
We absolutely should not.

Then our first step must be to supervise the storytellers. We'll accept the good stories and reject the bad ones. We'll encourage mothers and nurses to tell children only the approved stories, shaping their minds with these tales even more carefully than they shape their bodies with their hands. Most of the stories currently in use will have to be thrown out.
What stories are you talking about? he said.
The larger ones will show us the pattern of the smaller, I said. Both types follow the same mold and share the same spirit.
Probably true, he said, but I still don't know which larger stories you mean.
The ones told by Homer, Hesiod, and the other poets — the great storytellers of humanity.
Which stories specifically, and what's wrong with them?
The most serious fault of all, I said: telling lies — and what's worse, ugly lies.
When does that happen?
Whenever gods and heroes are portrayed falsely — like a painter creating a portrait that looks nothing like the original.
Yes, he said, that kind of thing is certainly wrong. But which stories do you mean exactly?

First and foremost, I said, there's the greatest lie about the greatest beings — the ugly story Hesiod told about what Uranus did and how Cronus took revenge. Even if these stories were true, they certainly shouldn't be told casually to young, impressionable people. Ideally they should be buried in silence. But if they absolutely must be mentioned, only a select few should hear them in a secret ritual, after sacrificing not an ordinary pig but some enormous, nearly impossible victim — so that as few people as possible would hear them.
Yes, he said, those stories are deeply objectionable.

Exactly, Adeimantus. Those stories have no place in our state. We shouldn't tell a young person that in committing the worst crimes, he's simply following the example of the first and greatest of the gods, or that punishing a father for wrongdoing is nothing outrageous.
I completely agree, he said. Those stories are totally unfit to be repeated.

Nor, if we want our future guardians to consider fighting among themselves the most shameful thing imaginable, should anyone tell them about wars in heaven, or plots and battles among the gods — since these stories aren't even true. We should never mention the battles of the giants or embroider them on clothing. We should stay silent about the countless quarrels of gods and heroes with their friends and relatives. If we could make them believe it, we'd tell them that fighting among citizens is unholy and has never happened. That's what elders should teach children from the beginning, and as they grow up, the poets should compose in the same spirit. But the story of Hephaestus binding his mother Hera, or Zeus throwing him out for defending her when she was being beaten, and all the battles of the gods in Homer — none of these should be allowed in our state, whether they're meant allegorically or not. A young person can't distinguish allegory from literal truth, and whatever enters the mind at that age tends to become permanent and unchangeable. That's why the first stories children hear must be models of good character.
You're right, he said. But if someone asks us where to find such stories and what tales we're talking about — what do we say?

I said: You and I, Adeimantus, aren't poets at the moment — we're founders of a state. And founders need to know the general principles poets should follow and the boundaries they must respect, but composing the actual stories isn't our job.
Fair enough, he said. But what are these principles about how to portray the gods?
Something like this, I said: God must always be represented as he truly is, whether in epic, lyric, or tragic poetry.
Right.
And isn't God truly good? Shouldn't he be portrayed as such?
Certainly.
And nothing good is harmful?
No.
And what isn't harmful causes no hurt?
Of course not.
And what causes no hurt does no evil?
No.
And can what does no evil be a cause of evil?
Impossible.
And the good is beneficial?
Yes.
And therefore a cause of well-being?
Yes.
So the good is not the cause of everything — only of what's good?
Certainly.

Then God, if he is good, is not the cause of everything, as most people claim. He's the cause of only a few things — the good things. The many evils in human life must have some other source, not God.
That seems absolutely right to me, he said.
Then we must reject Homer and every other poet who foolishly says that two jars
'Sit on Zeus's threshold, one filled with good fates, the other with bad,'
and that the person who receives a mixture from Zeus
'Sometimes meets with misfortune, sometimes with good luck,'
while the person who gets only from the jar of bad fortune
'Is driven by savage hunger across the beautiful earth.'
And again—
'Zeus, who distributes both good and evil to us.'

And if anyone claims that the breaking of oaths and treaties — which was really Pandarus's doing — was arranged by Athena and Zeus, or that the gods' conflict was instigated by Themis and Zeus, we won't accept it. Nor will we let our young people hear Aeschylus say that
'God sows guilt among mortals when he wishes to utterly destroy a house.'

And if a poet writes about the sufferings of Niobe, or the house of Pelops, or the Trojan War, or any similar theme, we must either forbid him from saying these are God's doing, or if they are, he must explain them in the way we're requiring. He must say that God did what was right, and the punished were made better by their punishment. But the poet must never say that those who are punished are miserable because of God. He may say the wicked are miserable because they need punishment, and that receiving it from God benefits them. But that God, being good, causes evil to anyone — this must be firmly denied and must never be said or heard in any well-governed community, whether in verse or prose, by anyone young or old. Such a claim would be self-destructive, impious, and internally contradictory.
I agree, he said, and I'm ready to support that as a law.
Let this, then, be our first principle about the gods, which our poets and storytellers must follow: God is not the cause of everything, but only of what is good.
That works, he said.

Now, what about a second principle? Is God a kind of magician who appears deceptively in different shapes — sometimes actually changing form, sometimes creating illusions? Or is he one and the same, forever fixed in his own true nature?
I can't answer without thinking about it more, he said.
Well, if something changes, mustn't the change be caused either by the thing itself or by something else?
It must.

And things that are in their best condition are least susceptible to change from outside forces. Think about it: the healthiest, strongest body is least affected by food and drink; the most vigorous plant suffers least from wind, heat, and similar stresses.
Of course.
And the bravest, wisest soul is least disturbed by external influences?
True.
The same principle applies to manufactured things — furniture, houses, clothes. When well made, they're least affected by time and wear.
Very true.
So everything that's good, whether natural or crafted, is least subject to change from outside?
True.
But surely God and everything divine is perfect in every way?
Of course.
So God could hardly be forced by external influence to take many shapes?
Hardly.
But might he change himself voluntarily?
If he changes at all, he said, that must be how it happens.
And would he change himself for the better or for the worse?
If he changes at all, it can only be for the worse, since we can't suppose he's lacking in either virtue or beauty.
Exactly right, Adeimantus. And would anyone, whether God or human, voluntarily make himself worse?
Impossible.
Then it's impossible for God to want to change. Being, as we suppose, the fairest and best conceivable, each god remains absolutely and forever in his own form.
That necessarily follows, he said.
Then, my dear friend, let no poet tell us that
'The gods, disguised as travelers from foreign lands, walk through cities in all sorts of forms.'
And let no one slander Proteus and Thetis, or introduce Hera in a tragedy disguised as a priestess begging for alms
'For the life-giving daughters of Inachus, the river of Argos.'

And let's have no more of mothers scaring their children with corrupted versions of these myths, telling them that gods 'wander at night in the guise of strangers in various forms.' They should stop making cowards of their children while simultaneously blaspheming the gods.
Absolutely not, he said.
But even though the gods themselves don't change, might they use sorcery to make us think they appear in different forms?
Perhaps, he said.
But would God willingly deceive us, whether in word or action, or project a false image of himself?
I'm not sure, he said.
Don't you realize, I said, that what we might call the 'true lie' — if such an expression is allowed — is hated by both gods and humans?
What do you mean? he said.
I mean that no one willingly accepts deception in the deepest, most important part of himself, about the most important matters. That's where people are most terrified of harboring a falsehood.
I still don't understand, he said.

That's because you think I'm saying something profound, I said. But I'm simply saying this: being deceived in the soul about reality — being misinformed about the most fundamental truths in the most fundamental part of yourself — and holding onto that falsehood: that is what people truly hate above all else.
Nothing is more hateful to them.

And as I was saying, this kind of ignorance in the deceived person's soul is the 'true lie.' The lie expressed in words is just a kind of imitation — a shadow copy of the deeper deception in the soul, not a pure, unalloyed falsehood. Am I right?
Perfectly right.
So the true lie is hated not only by gods but by humans as well?
Yes.

But what about lies expressed in words? Aren't they sometimes useful and not hateful? For instance, when dealing with enemies. Or when friends are about to do something harmful in a fit of madness or delusion — then a verbal lie becomes useful, like a kind of medicine or preventive. And in mythology, which we were just discussing — since we don't know the truth about ancient times, we make our fictions as close to truth as possible, and that way they serve a purpose.
Very true, he said.
But do any of these reasons apply to God? Would God be ignorant about the past and need to resort to invention?
That would be absurd, he said.
So there's no lying poet in God?
I'd say not.
Or maybe he lies because he's afraid of enemies?
That's inconceivable.
Does he have friends who are foolish or insane?
No fool or madman can be a friend of God.
Then there's no reason whatsoever for God to lie?
None at all.
So the divine and superhuman is completely incapable of falsehood?
Yes.
Then God is perfectly simple and true in both word and deed. He doesn't change, and he doesn't deceive — not through signs, not through words, not through dreams, not through visions.
My thoughts exactly, he said.
Then you agree with me that this is the second principle for how we should write and speak about the gods: the gods are not shape-shifting magicians, and they don't deceive humanity in any way.
I do agree.
Then, although we admire Homer, we can't admire the deceptive dream Zeus sends to Agamemnon. Nor can we approve of the passage in Aeschylus where Thetis says Apollo, at her wedding,

'Sang of her beautiful children who would live long lives free from sickness. And when he had praised my destiny as blessed in every way by the gods, he raised a cry of triumph that cheered my heart. I believed that the divine words of Phoebus, full of prophecy, would not fail. Yet he himself — the very one who sang that song, the one who was there at the feast, the one who said all this — he is the one who killed my son.'

These are the kinds of claims about the gods that will provoke our anger. Anyone who says such things will be denied public performance, and we won't let teachers use them in educating the young. Our guardians must be, as far as humanly possible, true worshippers of the gods and godlike themselves.
I completely agree, he said, and I accept these principles as our laws.

chapters.title: Book III
paragraphs: So those are our principles of theology, I said. Certain stories should be told to our students from childhood, and others should not, if we want them to honor the gods, respect their parents, and value friendship with each other.
Yes, and I think our principles are right, he said.
But if they're going to be courageous, don't they need to learn other lessons too — lessons that will take away the fear of death? Can anyone be brave if he's terrified of dying?
Certainly not, he said.
And can a person be fearless of death, or choose death in battle over defeat and slavery, if he believes the underworld is real and terrible?
Impossible.

Then we need to control this category of stories too, and ask the poets not simply to demonize the world below but actually to praise it — making clear that their grim descriptions are false and harmful to our future warriors.
That will be our duty, he said.
Then, I said, we'll need to cut out many offensive passages, starting with lines like:
'I would rather be a serf on the land of a poor, landless man than rule over all the dead who have perished.'
We must also remove the verse about how Pluto feared
'That the grim, squalid halls the gods despise might be exposed to mortals and immortals alike.'
And again:
'Oh heavens! So in the house of Hades there really is a soul and a ghostly form, but with no mind at all!'
And about Tiresias:
'To him alone, even after death, Persephone granted reason — he alone has wisdom; the other souls are flitting shadows.'
And again:
'The soul, leaving the body, went down to Hades, mourning its fate, leaving behind its strength and youth.'
And again:
'The soul, shrieking, passed like smoke beneath the earth.'
And:
'As bats in the depths of a mysterious cave, when one drops from the cluster on the rock, fly shrieking and clinging to each other — so these souls moved together, shrieking as they went.'

We must ask Homer and the other poets not to be angry if we cut out these and similar passages. Not because they're bad poetry or unpleasing to hear — actually, the more poetically charming they are, the less suitable they are for the ears of boys and men who are meant to be free and who should fear slavery more than death.
Undoubtedly.

We'll also need to get rid of all those terrible, frightening names for the underworld — Cocytus, Styx, ghosts beneath the earth, bloodless shades, and every similar word that makes listeners shudder to their very core. I'm not saying these horrifying stories don't have some use, but there's a real danger that our guardians' nerves will be made too fragile and sensitive by them.
There is a real danger, he said.
Then they have to go.
True.
A different, nobler strain must be composed for us to hear.
Clearly.
And shall we also get rid of the weeping and wailing of famous heroes?
Those will go with the rest.
But should they? Think about it: our principle is that a good person won't consider death terrible for any other good person who is his friend.
Yes, that's our principle.
So he won't grieve for his dead companion as if something terrible had happened?
He won't.
And we also maintain that such a person is self-sufficient when it comes to his own happiness, and therefore least dependent on others.
True, he said.
So for him, the loss of a son or brother, or the loss of his fortune, is the least devastating of all.
Certainly.
And therefore he'll be the least likely to mourn, and will bear such misfortunes with the greatest calm.
Yes, he'll feel such a loss far less than others would.

Then we'll be right to remove the lamentations of famous men, and hand them over to women — and not even respectable women — or to men of inferior character. That way, those we're educating to be defenders of the country will be ashamed to do anything similar.
That's absolutely right.

So we'll once more ask Homer and the other poets not to show Achilles, the son of a goddess, first lying on his side, then on his back, then on his face, then leaping up and pacing in a frenzy along the barren shore, then scooping up ashes in both hands and pouring them over his head, weeping and wailing in all the various ways Homer describes. Nor should they show Priam, a man related to the gods, begging and groveling,
'Rolling in the dirt, calling out loudly to each man by name.'
And we'll insist even more strongly that they never show the gods themselves lamenting, saying things like:
'Ah, my suffering! Ah, that I bore the bravest of men, only to grieve!'
And if they must bring in the gods, they should at least not dare to so completely misrepresent the greatest of gods as to have him say:
'Oh heavens! With my own eyes I watch a dear friend chased around the city walls, and my heart aches.'
Or again:
'Woe is me, that fate decrees my beloved Sarpedon, dearest of mortals to me, must fall at the hands of Patroclus, son of Menoetius.'

Because, my dear Adeimantus, if our young people take these unworthy portrayals of the gods seriously instead of laughing at them as they should, they'll hardly think it beneath their own dignity — being merely human — to behave the same way. They won't feel any shame or self-control, and will break into weeping and wailing at the slightest provocation.
That's very true, he said.
Yes, and that's exactly what shouldn't happen, as our argument has just shown. We must stand by this conclusion until a better one disproves it.
It shouldn't happen.
Our guardians also shouldn't be prone to excessive laughter. When someone indulges in a fit of laughter beyond all measure, it almost always triggers an equally violent reaction.
I believe so.
Then people of worth, even mortals, must not be portrayed as overcome by laughter. And this applies even more to portrayals of the gods.
Much more so, as you say, he said.
So we won't allow Homer's description of how
'Uncontrollable laughter broke out among the blessed gods when they saw Hephaestus bustling about the hall.'
By your reasoning, we can't allow that.
If you want to attribute that reasoning to me, fine. But we certainly can't allow it.

Next, truth must be highly valued. If, as we were saying, lying is useless to the gods and useful to humans only as a kind of medicine, then its use should be restricted to doctors. Private citizens have no business with it.
Clearly not, he said.

Then if anyone has the privilege of lying, it should be the rulers of the state. They may lie to enemies or to their own citizens for the public good. But no one else should touch the practice. For a private citizen to lie to the rulers is a worse offense than for a patient to lie to his doctor, or an athlete to his trainer, or a sailor to his captain about what's happening on the ship.
Very true, he said.
So if the ruler catches anyone else in the state lying —
'Any craftsman, whether priest, doctor, or carpenter' —
he'll punish him for introducing a practice that's just as destructive to a state as it is to a ship.
Absolutely, he said, if our idea of the state is ever carried out.
Next, our young people must be self-disciplined?
Certainly.
And isn't self-discipline mainly about obedience to leaders and self-control over physical pleasures?
True.
Then we'll approve of passages like Diomedes' words in Homer:
'Friend, sit still and do as I say.'
And the lines that follow:
'The Greeks marched with fierce determination... in silent reverence for their commanders.'
And other sentiments of the same kind.
We will.
What about this line —
'You wine-soaked fool with the eyes of a dog and the heart of a deer!' —
and the insults that follow? Would you say that these or similar impertinent remarks from private citizens to their rulers, whether in verse or prose, are appropriate?
They are not.
They might be amusing, but they don't promote self-discipline. And so they're likely to be harmful to our young people. Wouldn't you agree?
Yes.
And then, having the wisest man in the world declare that nothing is more glorious than
'When the tables are loaded with bread and meat, and the wine-bearer carries wine from the bowl and pours it into the cups' —
is that fitting or conducive to self-discipline for a young person to hear? Or the line —
'The saddest fate of all is to die of hunger'?

What would you say about the story of Zeus, who, while all other gods and mortals were asleep and he alone was awake, lay making plans — but forgot them all in an instant because of his lust? He was so overwhelmed at the sight of Hera that he wouldn't even go inside, but wanted to lie with her right there on the ground, declaring he had never desired her so much, not even when they first came together
'Without their parents' knowledge.'
Or the tale of how Hephaestus, because of similar behavior, bound Ares and Aphrodite in chains?
I strongly agree, he said, that they should not hear that sort of thing.
On the other hand, any deeds of endurance performed or described by famous men — these our students should see and hear. For example:
'He struck his chest and rebuked his own heart: Bear up, my heart! You have endured far worse than this.'
Certainly, he said.
Next, we must not let our guardians be lovers of gifts or lovers of money.
Certainly not.
Nor should we sing to them about
'Gifts that sway the gods, gifts that sway mighty kings.'

Nor should we approve of Phoenix, Achilles' tutor, for advising his student to accept the Greeks' gifts and help them, but to refuse unless paid. Nor will we accept that Achilles himself was such a lover of money that he took Agamemnon's gifts, or that he only returned Hector's body after being paid, but wouldn't do it without payment.
No, he said, those are not sentiments we can approve.

Out of love for Homer, I hesitate to say it, but attributing these feelings to Achilles — or believing they're accurately attributed to him — borders on impiety. Nor can I accept his insolence toward Apollo, where he says:
'You have wronged me, most hateful of gods. I would take revenge on you if only I had the power.'

Or his defiance of the river-god, on whose divinity he was ready to lay hands. Or his offering of his own hair to the dead Patroclus — hair previously dedicated to the river Spercheius. Or that he dragged Hector's body around Patroclus's tomb and slaughtered captives at the funeral pyre. I cannot believe he did any of this, any more than I can let our citizens believe it. This was supposedly the student of the wise Chiron, son of a goddess and of Peleus — the gentlest of men, third in descent from Zeus. It's absurd to think he was so disturbed as to be torn between two incompatible passions: pettiness mixed with greed, combined with contempt for both gods and men.
You're absolutely right, he said.

And let's equally refuse to believe or allow the story that Theseus, son of Poseidon, and Pirithous, son of Zeus, attempted a terrible kidnapping — or that any hero or son of a god dared to do such impious and dreadful things as are falsely attributed to them. Let's make the poets say either that they didn't do these things, or that they weren't sons of gods — but not both at once. We won't let them try to convince our youth that the gods produce evil, or that heroes are no better than ordinary people. We've already proven that evil cannot come from the gods.
Absolutely not.

Furthermore, such stories will have a terrible effect on those who hear them. Everyone will start excusing their own vices once they're convinced that similar wickedness is constantly being committed by —
'The relatives of the gods, kin of Zeus himself, whose ancestral altar stands high on Mount Ida in the air,'
and who still have
'The blood of gods flowing in their veins.'
Therefore let's put an end to such tales, before they breed moral laxity among the young.
By all means, he said.

Now that we've determined which subjects should and shouldn't be covered, let's check whether we've missed anything. How to portray gods, spirits, heroes, and the underworld — all that has been settled.
Very true.
That leaves the question of how to portray human beings. That's obviously the remaining topic.
Clearly.
But we can't answer that question yet, my friend.
Why not?

Because, if I'm not mistaken, we'll have to say that poets and storytellers commit the gravest error when they tell us that wicked people are often happy and good people miserable, and that injustice is profitable when undetected while justice is a personal loss and someone else's gain. We'll forbid them from saying these things and command them to say the opposite.
Of course we will, he said.
But if you agree I'm right about this, then I can claim you've already accepted the principle we've been arguing for all along.
I accept your point.
We can't settle what should and shouldn't be said about human beings until we've discovered what justice is and how it naturally benefits whoever possesses it, whether or not he appears just.
Very true, he said.
That's enough about the content of stories. Let's now talk about style. Once we've covered both content and style, we'll have dealt with the topic completely.
I don't understand what you mean, said Adeimantus.
Then let me explain. Maybe I can make it clearer this way. You're aware that all mythology and poetry is a narration of events — past, present, or future?
Certainly, he said.
And narration can be straightforward storytelling, dramatic imitation, or a combination of both?
I still don't quite understand, he said.

I must be a terrible teacher, having so much trouble making myself clear! Like a bad public speaker, let me just take one part and use it as an illustration. You know the opening of the Iliad, where the poet tells how Chryses begged Agamemnon to release his daughter, how Agamemnon got furious, and how Chryses, having failed, called on Apollo to punish the Greeks. Up through the lines —
'And he prayed to all the Greeks, but especially to the two sons of Atreus, the leaders of the people' —

the poet is speaking in his own voice. He never pretends to be anyone else. But in what follows, he takes on the character of Chryses and does everything he can to make us think the speaker isn't Homer but the old priest himself. And he uses this double approach throughout his account of events at Troy, in Ithaca, and throughout the Odyssey.
Yes.
And it remains narrative both in the speeches he puts into characters' mouths and in the connecting passages between them?
Exactly.
But when the poet speaks in another person's voice, doesn't he adapt his style to match the character who's about to speak?
Certainly.
And this adaptation — through voice and gesture — to imitate the person whose character he's assuming, that's what we mean by dramatic imitation?
Of course.
So in those parts, the poet's narrative works through imitation?
Exactly.

But if the poet never hides behind characters and always appears as himself, then there's no imitation — it's pure narration. To make sure you understand and don't say 'I don't get it' again, let me show how the change works. If Homer had written, 'The priest came with a ransom for his daughter, begging the Greeks and especially the kings,' and then continued in his own voice instead of speaking as Chryses, it would have been narration rather than imitation. It would have gone something like this (I'm no poet, so I'll skip the meter): 'The priest came and prayed that the gods would grant the Greeks victory at Troy and a safe return home. He asked them to release his daughter and accept his ransom, out of respect for the god. The other Greeks agreed. But Agamemnon was furious and told him to leave and never come back, or the god's staff and garlands wouldn't protect him. His daughter would not be released, he said — she would grow old with him in Argos. He warned the old man to go and not provoke him if he wanted to get home safely. The old man left in fear and silence. Once he was away from the camp, he called on Apollo by his many names, reminding him of every temple he had built and every sacrifice he had made, and praying that the god would repay his devotion by punishing the Greeks with his arrows.' That's how it would read as pure narration.
I understand, he said.
Or you could imagine the opposite: the connecting passages removed, leaving only the dialogue.
I understand that too — you mean like in tragedy.

Exactly. So now you see what you didn't grasp before: that poetry and storytelling come in three forms. First, pure imitation — as in tragedy and comedy. Second, the poet speaking only in his own voice — as in the dithyramb. And third, a combination of both — as in epic poetry and various other forms. Do you follow?
Yes, now I see what you meant.
And remember what I said at the start: that we were done with content and could move on to style?
Yes, I remember.

What I meant was this: we need to decide about imitation. Should our poets be allowed to use it in their narratives? If so, in whole or in part? And if in part, which parts? Or should imitation be forbidden entirely?
You're really asking, I suspect, whether we should allow tragedy and comedy in our state?
Yes, but possibly more than that. I don't actually know yet — wherever the argument leads, that's where we'll go.
Let's follow it then, he said.

All right, Adeimantus. Should our guardians be imitators? Or hasn't this already been settled by the principle that one person can only do one thing well, and that trying to do many things means doing none of them well?
Certainly.
And the same applies to imitation: no one can imitate many things as well as one?
True.

Then the same person won't be able to live a serious life and also be a skilled imitator of many different characters. Even closely related forms of imitation can't be mastered by the same person — for instance, tragic and comic playwrights. Didn't you just call those forms of imitation?
Yes, and you're right that the same people can't do both successfully.
Any more than the same people can be both reciters and actors?
True.
And even comic and tragic actors are different people, though both are just imitators.
They are.
Human nature, Adeimantus, seems to be cut into even finer specializations. It's no better at imitating many things well than it is at doing many things well in real life.
Very true, he said.

So if we stick with our original principle that guardians must dedicate themselves entirely to maintaining the state's freedom — making that their sole profession and doing nothing else — then they shouldn't practice or imitate anything outside their role. If they do imitate, they should imitate from youth onward only characters suited to their calling: the courageous, self-disciplined, reverent, free-spirited, and the like. They should not study or practice imitating anything base or shameful, in case they end up becoming what they imitate. Haven't you noticed how imitations, when they start in youth and continue into later life, eventually become habits and a second nature, affecting body, voice, and mind?
Yes, certainly, he said.

Then we won't allow those we claim to care about — those who should grow into good men — to imitate a woman, whether young or old, quarreling with her husband, defying the gods in arrogant self-satisfaction, or suffering from grief, sorrow, or tears. And certainly not a woman who's sick, in love, or in labor.
Exactly right, he said.
Nor must they play the parts of slaves, male or female, performing the work of slaves?
They must not.

Nor bad people — whether cowards or others — who do the opposite of what we've prescribed: people who mock, ridicule, or insult each other drunk or sober, or who offend against themselves and others in word or deed, as such people do. Nor should they be trained to imitate the speech or actions of the mad or wicked. Madness, like vice, should be understood but not practiced or imitated.
Very true, he said.
Should they imitate metalworkers, or other craftsmen, or rowers, or the officers who direct them?
How could they, he said, when they're not even allowed to pay attention to such occupations?
And may they imitate horses neighing, bulls bellowing, rivers rushing, oceans roaring, thunder, and all such things?
No, he said. If we've forbidden imitating madness, they can't imitate the sounds of madness either.
So you're saying, I said, that there's one kind of narrative style suited to a truly good person when he has something to say, and another kind used by someone of opposite character and upbringing?
What are these two styles? he asked.

Imagine, I said, that a good and just person is telling a story and comes to something said or done by another good person. I think he'll willingly take on that role and not be embarrassed by this kind of imitation. He'll be most eager to play the good person acting wisely and firmly, and less so when portraying someone overcome by illness, love, or drink, or struck by some other misfortune. But when he comes to a character unworthy of himself, he won't seriously take on that role. He'll only do it briefly, if the character is doing something good. Otherwise, he'll be ashamed to practice imitating someone he's never tried to be. He finds such imitation beneath him, and his mind rebels against it — unless it's done as a joke.
That's what I'd expect, he said.
So his narrative style will be like what we illustrated from Homer: a mix of imitation and straightforward narration, but with very little imitation and a great deal of narration. Do you agree?
Certainly. That's the model such a speaker must naturally follow.

But there's another type who will narrate anything at all, and the worse his character, the more shameless he'll be about it. Nothing will be beneath him. He'll eagerly imitate everything — not as a joke, but in complete earnest and before a large audience. As I was saying, he'll try to reproduce thunder, wind, hail, creaking wheels and pulleys, the sounds of flutes, pipes, trumpets, and every kind of instrument. He'll bark like a dog, bleat like a sheep, or crow like a rooster. His entire art will consist of imitating voices and gestures, with very little actual narration.
Yes, that will be his style, he said.
So those are the two kinds of style?
Yes.

And you'd agree that one of them involves minimal variation? If you choose an appropriate melody and rhythm, a speaker using this style will stay pretty much the same throughout, keeping within a single mode of harmony (since the changes are slight) and a fairly consistent rhythm?
That's exactly right, he said.
Whereas the other style requires every kind of harmony and every kind of rhythm, since the style itself involves every kind of variation.
That's perfectly true, he said.
Don't these two styles, or a mixture of them, cover all forms of expression? No one can say anything except in one style, the other, or both combined.
They cover everything, he said.
So which should our state allow? All three styles? Or only one of the two pure forms? Or the mixed one?
If I had my way, I'd only admit the pure imitator of virtue.

Yes, Adeimantus, but the mixed style is also very charming. And the purely imitative style — the opposite of what you've chosen — is the most popular with children, their caretakers, and the general public.
I don't deny it.
But you'd argue it's unsuitable for our state, where human nature isn't split into many roles — each person does one thing only?
Yes, completely unsuitable.

And that's why, in our state alone, a shoemaker is just a shoemaker and not also a ship's captain; a farmer is just a farmer and not also a judge; a soldier is just a soldier and not also a trader — and so on throughout?
True, he said.

So if one of these versatile imitators comes along — so clever he can imitate anything — and offers to perform for us, we'll honor him like a sacred and wonderful being. But we'll also tell him that our state has no place for people like him. We'll anoint his head with perfume, crown him with a wreath of wool, and then send him off to another city. Because we intend to use, for the health of our souls, the rougher, stricter kind of poet or storyteller — one who imitates only the virtuous style and follows the models we established when we first began planning the education of our soldiers.
That's certainly what we'll do, if it's in our power, he said.
So now, my friend, the part of the arts and literature that relates to stories and myths is complete. We've covered both content and style.
I think so too, he said.
Next comes melody and song.
Obviously.
By now, everyone can already see what we should say about them, if we're going to be consistent with ourselves.
I'm afraid, said Glaucon, laughing, that 'everyone' doesn't quite include me. I can't say right now what the rules should be, though I can probably guess.
At the very least, you know that a song has three elements: words, melody, and rhythm? That much I can assume?
Yes, he said, you can assume that much.
And as for the words, there won't be any difference between words that are set to music and words that aren't? Both must follow the same rules we've already established?
Yes.
And the melody and rhythm must follow the words?
Certainly.
We said, when discussing content, that we have no need for songs of lamentation and sorrow?
True.
And which musical modes express sorrow? You're the musical one — you tell me.
The mixed Lydian and the full-toned Lydian, and modes like them.
Then those must be banned. They're of no use even to women of good character, let alone men.
Certainly.
Next, drunkenness, laziness, and self-indulgence are completely inappropriate for our guardians.
Completely.
And which modes are soft and associated with drinking?
The Ionian and the Lydian, he said. They're called 'relaxed' modes.
Do those have any military use?
None at all, he said. That leaves you with only the Dorian and Phrygian.

I don't know the technical details of musical modes, I said, but I want two: one that suits a brave person in danger or facing death, meeting misfortune with steady resolve and endurance. And another for peacetime, when there's no pressure — when someone is trying to persuade God through prayer, or teaching and advising others, or willingly accepting guidance, and when, having achieved his goal, he acts with moderation and wisdom rather than being carried away by success. These two modes — one for hardship and one for freedom, one for courage and one for self-discipline — those are the ones I want us to keep.
And those, he said, are exactly the Dorian and Phrygian modes I was just talking about.
So if these are the only modes allowed in our songs and melodies, we won't need complex multi-note scales?
I suppose not.
Then we won't support the makers of elaborate multi-stringed instruments or complex tuning systems?
Certainly not.

And what about flute-makers and flute-players? Will you let them into our state, given that the flute is the most varied of all instruments? Even those elaborate multi-mode compositions are really just imitations of the flute.
Obviously not.
That leaves the lyre and the harp for use in the city, and a simple pipe for the shepherds in the countryside.
That's the logical conclusion.
We're really just preferring Apollo and his instruments over Marsyas and his, I said. Nothing unusual about that.
Not at all, he said.
And so, by the dog of Egypt, without even realizing it we've been purging the state that we earlier called luxurious.
And wisely so, he said.

Then let's finish the purging. After modes come rhythms, and the same principles apply. We shouldn't aim for complex meters and every possible rhythm, but rather discover which rhythms express a courageous and well-ordered life. Once we find them, we'll match the rhythm and melody to words of the same character — not the other way around. Identifying which specific rhythms these are will be your job — you can teach me, just as you've taught me about modes.

Well, he said, I can't really tell you specifically. I know there are three basic types of rhythm from which meters are built, just as there are four notes that form all harmonies. But I can't tell you which rhythms express which kinds of life.

Then we'll consult Damon about this, I said. He can tell us which rhythms express meanness, arrogance, fury, or other faults, and which should be kept for their opposites. I vaguely remember him discussing a complex Cretic rhythm, and a dactylic or heroic one, and arranging them so the rises and falls were equal, with long and short syllables alternating. I think he also mentioned iambic and trochaic rhythms, assigning long and short values to them. In some cases he seemed to evaluate the movement of the foot as much as the overall rhythm, or perhaps a combination. But these details are best left to Damon, since the analysis would take a while.
It certainly would.
But one thing we can see clearly: grace and the absence of grace are the result of good and bad rhythm.
Absolutely.

And good and bad rhythm naturally follow good and bad style. The same is true of harmony and discord — they follow the character of the words, since our principle is that rhythm and harmony are governed by the words, not the reverse.
Exactly, he said. They should follow the words.
And won't the character of the words and the style depend on the character of the soul?
Yes.
And everything else follows from the style?
Yes.

Then beauty of style, harmony, grace, and good rhythm all depend on simplicity — I mean the true simplicity of a rightly and nobly ordered mind and character, not the 'simplicity' that's just a polite word for foolishness?
Very true, he said.
And if our young people are to fulfill their purpose in life, must they not pursue these qualities of grace and harmony constantly?
They must.

And every creative art is full of these qualities — painting, weaving, embroidery, architecture, every kind of craftsmanship. Nature too, in both animals and plants, shows grace or its absence. Ugliness, discord, and clumsy movement are closely related to bad language and bad character, just as grace and harmony are twin sisters of goodness and virtue, bearing their likeness.
Absolutely true, he said.

So should our supervision extend only to poets, requiring them to express the image of goodness in their work or face expulsion? Or should the same control apply to all other artists too, forbidding them from depicting vice, excess, meanness, and indecency in sculpture, building, or any other creative art? Anyone who can't follow this rule must be prevented from practicing in our state. We don't want our guardians growing up surrounded by images of moral ugliness, like cattle in a poisonous pasture, grazing day by day on harmful influences until they've unknowingly accumulated a festering corruption in their own souls. Instead, our artists should be those gifted at discerning the true nature of beauty and grace. Then our young people will live in a land of health, surrounded by beautiful sights and sounds, receiving goodness from every direction. Beauty, streaming from fine works of art, will flow into their eyes and ears like a health-giving breeze from a pure region, and from their earliest years will gently draw their souls into harmony and sympathy with the beauty of reason.
There could be no finer education than that, he said.

That's why musical education is the most powerful instrument of all, Glaucon. Rhythm and harmony penetrate deep into the soul, grip it powerfully, and bring it grace — making the soul of the well-educated person graceful, and the soul of the poorly educated person graceless. The person who has received this true inner education will perceive faults and flaws in art and nature with the sharpest eye. With genuine taste, he'll praise and welcome the good, absorb it into his soul, and become noble and good himself. At the same time, he'll rightly criticize and reject the bad — even in his youth, before he can fully understand why. And when reason eventually arrives, he'll greet it as a familiar friend, recognized from the education that prepared him.
Yes, I completely agree that our youth should be trained in the arts for these reasons.

Think of it like learning to read, I said. We were satisfied when we knew the letters of the alphabet — just a few letters in all their various sizes and combinations. We didn't dismiss them as unimportant whether they appeared in a large or small space, but we were eager to recognize them everywhere. We didn't consider ourselves literate until we could spot them wherever they appeared.
True.
And we can recognize the reflections of letters in water or mirrors only when we already know the letters themselves. The same skill gives us knowledge of both.
Exactly.

In the same way, neither we nor our guardians can be truly cultivated until we recognize the essential forms of self-discipline, courage, generosity, and magnanimity — along with their opposites — in all their combinations, wherever they appear. We must be able to detect them and their reflections in both great and small matters, believing they all fall within a single field of study.
Absolutely.
And when a beautiful soul is found in harmony with a beautiful form, and the two are cast in the same mold — wouldn't that be the most beautiful sight for anyone with eyes to see?
The most beautiful indeed.
And the most beautiful is also the most lovable?
We can assume so.
And the person with a harmonious spirit will be most drawn to the most beautiful. But he won't love someone whose soul is disharmonious?
True, he said — not if the disharmony is in the soul. But if it's just a physical imperfection, he'll be patient with it and love the person all the same.
I see, I said, that you speak from experience, and I agree. But let me ask: does excessive pleasure have any connection with self-discipline?
How could it? he said. Pleasure robs a person of their faculties just as much as pain does.
Or any connection with virtue in general?
None at all.
Any connection with indulgence and excess?
The strongest possible connection.
And is there any greater or more intense pleasure than sexual love?
None — and none more irrational.
But true love is a love of beauty and order — temperate and harmonious?
Exactly, he said.
Then nothing excessive or irrational should come near true love?
Certainly not.
So wild, uncontrolled pleasure must never come near the lover and the beloved. If their love is genuine, neither should have any part in it?
Absolutely not, Socrates.

Then in our city, I take it, you'd establish a law that a lover's intimacy with his beloved should go no further than a father's affection for his son, and only for a noble purpose, and only with the other's consent. This rule would govern all his interactions, and going beyond it would be considered crude and tasteless.
I completely agree, he said.
So that concludes our discussion of the arts, which ends, fittingly, with the love of beauty. For what else should the arts ultimately lead to, if not the love of beauty?
I agree, he said.
After the arts comes physical training, which our young people must undertake next.
Certainly.

Physical training, like the arts, should begin early and continue throughout life. Now, here's what I believe — and I'd like to hear your thoughts on it: I don't think it's the body that improves the soul through physical excellence. Rather, the good soul improves the body through its own excellence, as far as that's possible. What do you say?
Yes, I agree.
Then once we've properly educated the mind, we can hand over the details of physical care to it. To avoid going on too long, we'll just sketch the general principles.
Very good.
We've already noted that guardians must avoid intoxication. A guardian would be the last person who should get drunk and not know where he is.
Yes, he said. It would be absurd for a guardian to need another guardian to look after him.
Now, what about their diet? These men are in training for the ultimate contest, aren't they?
Yes, he said.
Would the habits of ordinary athletes suit them?
Why not?

Because, I'm afraid, the athlete's typical physical condition is a drowsy, precarious thing. Athletes sleep their lives away and are liable to serious illness if they stray even slightly from their routine.
Yes, I've noticed that.

We need a more refined kind of training for our warrior-athletes, I said. They need to be like alert watchdogs — sharp-eyed and sharp-eared. On campaign, they'll face constant changes in water, food, summer heat, and winter cold, and they can't afford to break down.
That's my view too.
The truly excellent physical training is the twin sister of the simple music we were just describing.
How so?
There's a kind of physical training that, like our music, is simple and good — especially military training.
What do you mean?

We can learn from Homer. He feeds his heroes on campaign with soldiers' rations. They don't eat fish, even though they're camping by the sea, and they're only allowed roasted meat, not boiled — it's the most practical food for soldiers, since they only need a fire and don't have to carry pots and pans around.
True.
And I don't think Homer ever mentions fancy sauces. In fact, all professional athletes know that if you want to stay in peak condition, you avoid that kind of thing.
Yes, he said. They know it and they're right to avoid it.
So you wouldn't approve of lavish Syracusan dinners or the refinements of Sicilian cooking?
I think not.
And for a man who needs to stay in shape, you wouldn't recommend a Corinthian girlfriend?
Certainly not.
Or the famous Athenian pastries?
Certainly not.
We could compare all that elaborate eating and living to those complex, multi-mode musical compositions with every kind of rhythm.
Exactly.
In music, complexity bred indiscipline. In diet, it breeds disease. But simplicity in music produces self-discipline in the soul, and simplicity in physical training produces health in the body.
Absolutely true, he said.

But when indiscipline and disease spread through a state, courtrooms and hospitals spring up everywhere, and the professions of law and medicine start putting on airs, attracting keen interest not just from slaves but from free citizens.
Of course.

And isn't it a sign of a terrible education when not just common workers but people who claim to be well-educated need the help of top doctors and lawyers? Isn't it disgraceful that a person has to go to others for justice and medicine because he has none of his own — surrendering himself to men he makes his masters and judges?
Absolutely disgraceful, he said.

But there's something even more disgraceful, I said. What about the person who spends his entire life in court, either as plaintiff or defendant, and actually takes pride in his litigiousness? He imagines he's a master of dirty tricks, able to wriggle through every loophole and dodge justice at every turn — all for trivial stakes. He doesn't realize that ordering one's life so as not to need a judge at all is far nobler. Isn't that even worse?
Yes, he said, that's even more disgraceful.

And isn't it equally shameful to need medical help not because of a wound or seasonal illness, but because a lazy, self-indulgent lifestyle has filled your body with toxins like a swamp, forcing the brilliant doctors to invent fancy new names for diseases like 'gas' and 'inflammation'?
Yes, he said. Those are certainly strange, newfangled names for diseases.

The kind that didn't exist in Asclepius's day, I said. I base this on the fact that when the hero Eurypylus was wounded at Troy, Homer describes him drinking a concoction of strong wine mixed with barley meal and grated cheese — definitely not what a doctor would recommend. Yet the sons of Asclepius who were there didn't criticize the woman who served it or scold Patroclus for the treatment.
That's certainly an unusual drink for someone in his condition, he said.

Not if you consider, I said, that before Herodicus, the medical profession didn't practice the elaborate health management we see today. Herodicus was a physical trainer with a weak constitution who invented a method of prolonged medical self-care that tortured first himself and then the rest of the world.
How so? he said.

By inventing a drawn-out death, I said. He had a fatal illness that he endlessly managed, and since recovery was impossible, he spent his entire life as a chronic invalid. He couldn't do anything except tend to himself, and he was in constant anxiety whenever he deviated even slightly from his routine. So by the power of medical science, he dragged himself to old age while dying the whole time.
What a wonderful reward for his skill!

Yes — exactly the reward you'd expect for someone who didn't understand that Asclepius chose not to teach his descendants this kind of medicine. The reason wasn't ignorance. It was because Asclepius knew that in a well-organized society, everyone has a job to do and no one has the leisure to spend their life being ill. We see this clearly with working people, but absurdly, we don't apply the same logic to the wealthy.
How do you mean? he said.

When a carpenter gets sick, I said, he asks his doctor for a quick, rough cure — a purge, an emetic, surgery, cauterization. If someone prescribes a lengthy regime of special diets and head-wrapping and that sort of thing, he says he has no time to be sick and sees no point in a life spent nursing an illness instead of doing his work. He thanks the doctor, goes back to his usual routine, and either recovers and gets on with his life, or, if his body can't handle it, dies and is done with his troubles.
Yes, he said, that's the right approach to medicine for a working man.
Doesn't he have work to do? And wouldn't his life be worthless if he couldn't do it?
Exactly, he said.
But the rich man is different. We don't say he has any particular work that would make life unbearable without it.
People generally assume he has nothing to do.
Haven't you heard Phocylides' saying that once a man has enough to live on, he should practice virtue?
I think he should start even sooner than that, he said.

Let's not argue with Phocylides about that, I said. Let's ask ourselves: is the practice of virtue required of the rich man? Can he live without it? If it's required, then does this obsessive health management — which gets in the way of a carpenter's work — not also get in the way of following Phocylides' advice?
Without a doubt, he said. This kind of excessive body-care is deeply hostile to the practice of virtue.

Exactly, I said. And it's equally incompatible with managing a household, an army, or a government office. Most importantly, it's irreconcilable with any kind of study, thought, or self-reflection. You're always suspecting that your headache or dizziness must be caused by intellectual effort, which effectively stops any attempt at higher virtue. You're perpetually worried about your health.
That's very likely.

So we can assume that Asclepius intended his art only for people who were naturally healthy and lived well but happened to contract a specific illness. He cured them with purges and surgery and told them to carry on as usual, keeping the state's interests in mind. But bodies that were thoroughly diseased, he wouldn't have tried to cure with drawn-out treatments. He didn't want to prolong worthless lives or have sickly parents producing even sicklier children. If a person couldn't live a normal life, there was no point in treating him, since such a cure would benefit neither the patient nor the state.
You're making Asclepius sound like a statesman, he said.

That's clearly what he was. And his character is further shown by his sons. They were heroes at Troy who practiced the kind of medicine I'm describing. Remember how they treated Menelaus when Pandarus wounded him? They
'Sucked the blood from the wound and applied soothing remedies,'

but they never prescribed what the patient should eat or drink afterward. The remedies were enough, they thought, for a man who was healthy and disciplined before being wounded — even if he happened to drink a strong wine mixture. But they wanted nothing to do with unhealthy, undisciplined people whose lives were of no use to themselves or anyone else. The art of medicine wasn't designed for them, and even if they'd been as rich as Midas, the sons of Asclepius would have refused to treat them.
Very shrewd people, those sons of Asclepius.

Naturally, I said. Yet the tragedians and Pindar go against our principles. They acknowledge that Asclepius was Apollo's son but claim he was bribed to heal a rich man at the point of death, and for that he was struck by lightning. But according to our established principle, we won't accept both claims together. If he was a god's son, he wasn't greedy. If he was greedy, he wasn't a god's son.

All of that is excellent, Socrates. But let me ask you something: shouldn't a state have good doctors? And aren't the best doctors those who have treated the greatest number of different conditions, both healthy and sick? Similarly, aren't the best judges those who have experience with all kinds of moral character?
Yes, I said, I want good doctors and good judges too. But do you know what I mean by 'good'?
Tell me.
I will, but let me point out that your question combines two things that aren't really the same.
How so? he said.

Well, the best doctors are those who, from their youth, have combined knowledge of their art with the widest experience of disease. Ideally they should not be perfectly healthy themselves, and should have suffered from all sorts of illnesses. After all, they don't cure the body with their body — if so, they'd need to always be healthy. They cure the body with their mind, and a sick mind can cure nothing.
Very true, he said.

But with judges it's different. The judge governs mind with mind, so he should not have been raised among corrupt people or gained experience of every crime through personal involvement. A young person with an honorable character who is to form sound judgments should have had no contact with evil in youth. That's why good people in their youth often seem naive and are easily deceived by the dishonest — they have no corresponding evil within themselves to serve as a reference.
Yes, he said, they're much too easily taken in.

That's why, I said, a judge should not be young. He should have learned to recognize evil not through his own experience but through long observation of evil in others. Knowledge, not personal vice, should be his guide.
Yes, that would be the ideal judge.

And that man will be good — which answers your question. A person is good who has a good soul. The cunning, suspicious person we spoke of — the one who's committed many crimes and thinks himself a master of wickedness — seems clever enough when dealing with people like himself, because he judges them by his own standards. But when he encounters truly virtuous people with the wisdom of experience, he looks like a fool. His suspicions are misplaced because he has no model of honesty within himself. However, since he meets more bad people than good, he seems to himself and others to be rather wise.
Very true, he said.

Then the good and wise judge we're looking for isn't this kind of person, but the other. Vice can never understand virtue, but a virtuous nature, educated over time, will come to understand both virtue and vice. The virtuous person, not the vicious one, becomes truly wise — in my opinion.
And in mine, he said.

This is the kind of medicine and the kind of law you'll establish in your state. They'll serve better natures, providing health to both soul and body. But those whose bodies are incurably diseased will be allowed to die, and those whose souls are incurably corrupt will be put to death.
That's clearly best for both the patients and the state.
And our young people, educated in the simple music that inspires self-discipline, will be reluctant to go to court.
Clearly.
And the person trained in this music who also practices simple physical training will have no need for medicine except in extreme cases.
I'm sure of it.
His exercises and physical work are meant to strengthen the spirited element of his nature, not just to build muscle like an ordinary athlete.
Exactly right, he said.
And the arts and physical training are not actually designed, as people commonly think, one for training the soul and the other for training the body.
Then what are they really for? he asked.
I believe, I said, that both are primarily aimed at improving the soul.
How can that be? he said.
Haven't you noticed, I said, the effect on the mind of exclusive devotion to physical training versus exclusive devotion to the arts?
What effects do you mean? he said.
Exclusive physical training produces hardness and brutality. Exclusive devotion to the arts produces softness and weakness.
Yes, he said. I'm well aware that pure athletes become too savage, and pure musicians become too soft.
The fierceness comes from spirit, which, properly educated, produces courage. But when pushed too far, it naturally becomes hard and brutal.
I think so too.
And the gentleness comes from the philosophical side of our nature. When properly educated, it produces moderation. But when over-indulged, it becomes excessive softness.
True.
And we said our guardians should have both qualities?
Yes.
And the two should be in harmony?
Absolutely.
And the harmonious soul is both self-disciplined and courageous?
Yes.
And the disharmonious soul is cowardly and crude?
Very true.

When a person lets music pour into his soul through his ears — those sweet, soft, melancholy tunes we were talking about — and spends his whole life warbling and reveling in song, at first the process tempers the spirit in him like iron, making it useful instead of brittle. But if he keeps going with the softening process, he starts to melt and dissolve, until he's completely wasted away his spirit and cut the sinews of his soul. He becomes a feeble warrior.
Very true.

If his spirit was naturally weak to begin with, this happens quickly. But if he has a strong spirit, music gradually weakens it until he becomes hypersensitive. At the slightest provocation, he flares up and is just as quickly extinguished. Instead of being spirited, he becomes irritable, volatile, and impossible to deal with.
Exactly.

And in physical training: if someone trains intensely and eats heavily while completely neglecting the arts and philosophy, at first his excellent physical condition fills him with pride and energy, and he feels twice the man he was.
Certainly.

But what happens next? If he does nothing else — never engages with learning, inquiry, thought, or any cultivation of the mind — whatever intelligence he has grows weak, dull, and blind. His mind never wakes up or receives nourishment, and his senses are never cleansed of their fog.
True, he said.

He ends up hating learning and civilized life. He never uses persuasion, only force. He lives like a wild beast — all violence and aggression — in ignorance and crudeness, with no sense of grace or proportion.
That's exactly right, he said.

Since there are two elements of human nature — the spirited and the philosophical — it seems as if some god gave humanity two arts to correspond to them (and only indirectly to the body and soul): the arts and physical training. The purpose is to tune these two elements, like the strings of an instrument, tightening or relaxing each until they're in proper harmony.
That seems to be the intention.

And the person who blends the arts and physical training in the finest proportions, tempering them most skillfully in the soul, can rightly be called the true musician and harmonist — far more than someone who merely tunes instrument strings.
You're quite right, Socrates.
Our state will always need someone like this as its director, if the government is to last.
Absolutely necessary.

Those, then, are our principles of education. Why go into further detail about dances, hunting, athletic contests, and horse racing? They all follow from the general principle, and once we have that, the details aren't hard to work out.
I imagine they won't be, he said.
Good. So what's the next question? Isn't it: who shall rule and who shall be ruled?
Certainly.
Obviously the older should rule the younger.
Obviously.
And the best among the older should rule.
That too is clear.
And aren't the best farmers those most devoted to farming?
Yes.
And since we want the best guardians for our city, shouldn't they be those with the most guardian-like character?
Yes.
They need to be wise, capable, and genuinely concerned for the state?
True.
And a person is most likely to care about what he loves?
Of course.
And he's most likely to love what he believes shares his own interests — what he thinks will prosper when he prospers and suffer when he suffers?
Very true, he said.
Then from among our guardians, we must select those who show, throughout their entire lives, the greatest devotion to doing what benefits the state and the strongest refusal to act against it.
Those are the right people.
And they must be tested at every stage of life to see whether they hold firm to this conviction and never, through force or trickery, forget or abandon their sense of duty to the state.
Abandon it how? he asked.

Let me explain, I said. A conviction can leave someone's mind either willingly or unwillingly. Willingly, when someone lets go of a false belief and learns the truth. Unwillingly, when someone is robbed of a true belief.
I understand the willing kind, he said, but I still need to learn about the unwilling.

Don't you see, I said, that people are unwillingly deprived of good things and willingly deprived of bad ones? Losing the truth is a bad thing, and having the truth is good. And to understand things as they are is to have the truth?
Yes, he said. I agree that people are deprived of truth against their will.
And isn't this involuntary loss caused by theft, force, or enchantment?
I still don't follow, he said.
