I must be speaking like a playwright — too obscurely. By 'theft,' I just mean that some people are gradually argued out of their beliefs without realizing it, and others simply forget over time. Do you see what I mean now?
Yes.
By 'force,' I mean people who are compelled to change their minds by pain or suffering.
I understand, he said. You're right.
And by 'enchantment,' I mean people who change their beliefs either through the seduction of pleasure or the pressure of fear.
Yes, he said. Everything that deceives is a kind of enchantment.

So, as I was saying, we need to find out which guardians are the best at holding firm to their conviction that the state's interest should guide their lives. We must test them from youth onward, putting them in situations where they're most likely to forget or be tricked out of this belief. Those who remember and resist deception make the cut; those who fail are rejected. Right?
Yes.
And they should also face hardships, pains, and competitions that test the same qualities.
Very right, he said.

Then we need a third kind of test: enchantment. Just as people test young horses by exposing them to noise and commotion to see if they're timid, we must lead our young people through terrors and pleasures, testing them more thoroughly than gold in a furnace. We want to see if they're proof against all enchantments and maintain their noble bearing throughout — if they're good guardians of themselves and of the education they've received, preserving their rhythm and harmony under all circumstances. The person who comes through every test — as boy, youth, and adult — victorious and uncorrupted, that person shall be appointed ruler and guardian of the state. He'll be honored in life and in death, receiving the highest memorials we can bestow. But whoever fails the test, we must reject. I believe that's roughly how our rulers and guardians should be chosen, though I'm speaking in general terms rather than with exact precision.
Speaking generally, I agree, he said.

And perhaps the word 'guardian' in its fullest sense should apply only to this higher class, who protect us from foreign enemies and keep peace among our own citizens — preventing the ones from wanting to harm us and the others from having the power to. The younger people we previously called guardians would be more properly termed 'auxiliaries' — supporters who carry out the rulers' decisions.
I agree, he said.
Now, how might we devise one of those useful falsehoods we talked about earlier — a single noble lie that might persuade even the rulers themselves, or at least the rest of the citizens?
What kind of lie? he said.

Nothing new, I said — just an old Phoenician tale about something that's supposedly happened in many places before, or so the poets say and have made the world believe. It hasn't happened in our time, and I'm not sure it could be made believable today.
You seem very hesitant to say it!
You'll understand my hesitation when you hear it, I said.
Just say it, he said. Don't be afraid.

All right, here goes — though I honestly don't know how to say this with a straight face, or what words to use for such an audacious fiction. I plan to introduce it gradually, first to the rulers, then to the soldiers, and finally to the general public. They'll be told that their youth and education were a kind of dream. In reality, they were being formed and nourished in the womb of the earth, along with their weapons and equipment. When they were fully made, the earth — their mother — sent them up to the surface. So they must think of their country as their mother and nurse, defend her against attack, and regard their fellow citizens as brothers born from the same earth.
I can see why you were embarrassed to tell that lie, he said.

With good reason. But there's more. 'Citizens,' we'll tell them in our story, 'you are all brothers, but God made you differently. Some of you have the power to lead, and into these he mixed gold — they deserve the highest honor. Others he made of silver, to serve as auxiliaries. Others still — the farmers and craftsmen — he made of bronze and iron. Generally, children will be the same metal as their parents. But since all come from the same stock, a golden parent may sometimes have a silver child, and a silver parent a golden one. God's first and most important command to the rulers is this: nothing matters more than watching what mixture runs in their children's nature. If a ruler's child has bronze or iron in him, they must not show pity but demote him to the rank of craftsman or farmer. Likewise, if a craftsman's child shows gold or silver, that child must be raised to guardian or auxiliary status. For there is an oracle that says: when a man of bronze or iron stands guard over the state, it will be destroyed.' Is there any chance we could get our citizens to believe this?
Not the current generation, he said. But their children might believe it, and their grandchildren, and generations after them.

I see the difficulty, I said. But even so, fostering this belief would make people care more about the city and about each other. But enough about the fiction — let it spread on the wings of rumor. Meanwhile, let's arm our earth-born heroes and lead them out under their rulers' command. Let them survey the land and choose the best spot for a camp — a position from which they can suppress any internal rebellion and also defend against external enemies who might descend like wolves on the fold. Once they've set up camp, let them offer sacrifices to the proper gods and prepare their quarters.
Just so, he said.
And their quarters must protect them from winter cold and summer heat.
You mean houses, I assume, he said.
Yes, but soldiers' houses — not shopkeepers' houses.
What's the difference? he said.

I'll try to explain, I said. It would be monstrous and shameful for a shepherd to keep watchdogs that, from lack of discipline or hunger or bad habits, turned on the sheep and attacked them — acting like wolves instead of dogs.
Truly monstrous, he said.
So every precaution must be taken to prevent our auxiliaries, who are stronger than the citizens, from turning into savage tyrants instead of friendly allies.
Yes, great care is needed.
And wouldn't a genuinely good education be the best safeguard?
But they're already well-educated, he said.

I'm not so sure about that, Glaucon. But I am certain that they need to be, and that true education — whatever it turns out to be — will do the most to civilize them in their treatment of each other and of those they protect.
Very true, he said.

And beyond their education, their living conditions and possessions should be arranged so as not to undermine their virtue as guardians or tempt them to prey on the other citizens. Any reasonable person would agree with this.
They would.

Then let's consider how they should live to achieve our aims. First, none of them should own any private property beyond what's strictly necessary. They shouldn't have private houses or storerooms that anyone can't enter. Their provisions should be only what trained warriors of courage and discipline need — nothing more. They should agree to receive a fixed salary from the citizens, enough for the year's expenses and no more, and they should eat together in common messes, like soldiers in camp. As for gold and silver, we'll tell them they already carry a divine metal within their souls and have no need of the human kind. They must not contaminate the sacred with the profane, because that common metal has been the source of countless crimes. Their own gold is pure. They alone among all citizens may never touch, handle, or be under the same roof with gold and silver, nor wear it, nor drink from vessels made of it. This will be their salvation, and they will save the state. But the moment they acquire private homes, land, or money of their own, they'll become property managers and farmers instead of guardians — enemies and tyrants instead of allies of the other citizens. They'll spend their lives in hatred and plots, in far greater terror of internal enemies than external ones. And the hour of ruin for both themselves and the entire state will be at hand. For all these reasons, shouldn't we say that this is how our state should be organized, and these should be the rules for our guardians regarding their houses and everything else?
Yes, said Glaucon.

chapters.title: Book IV
paragraphs: At this point Adeimantus broke in with a question: How would you respond, Socrates, if someone said you're making these guardians miserable — and that it's their own fault? The city essentially belongs to them, but they get nothing out of it. Other people acquire land, build fine houses, furnish them beautifully, make their own sacrifices to the gods, and entertain guests. They have gold and silver and everything that supposedly makes people happy. But our guardians are no better than hired soldiers stationed in the city who do nothing but stand guard.

Yes, I said, and you could add that they only receive food, not wages on top of it. So they can't travel for pleasure, keep a mistress, or spend money on any of those luxuries that supposedly constitute happiness. You could pile on many more accusations of that kind.
Right, said he. Let's take all of that as part of the charge.
You want to know how we'd answer? I said.
Yes.

If we stick to our original path, I think we'll find the answer. We'd say that even as things stand, our guardians may well be the happiest people alive. But that wasn't our goal in founding the state. Our aim wasn't the exceptional happiness of any one class, but the greatest happiness of the whole. We thought we'd be most likely to find justice in a state organized for the good of all, and injustice in one that's poorly organized. Once we find both, we can decide which produces greater happiness. Right now, we're building the happy state as a whole, not trying to make a select few happy. Imagine we were painting a statue and someone walked up and said, 'Why aren't you using the most beautiful colors on the most beautiful parts? The eyes should be purple, but you've made them black.' We could fairly reply, 'Sir, you wouldn't want us to beautify the eyes so much that they stop looking like eyes. Consider whether, by giving each feature its proper proportions, we make the whole beautiful.' The same applies here: don't force us to give the guardians a kind of happiness that would make them anything but guardians. We could just as easily dress our farmers in royal robes, crown them with gold, and tell them to farm whenever they feel like it. We could let our potters recline on couches by the fire, drinking wine, with their wheel conveniently nearby, working only when the mood strikes. We could make every class 'happy' that way — and then, as you imagine, the whole state would be happy. But don't put that idea in our heads. If we follow it, farmers won't be farmers, potters won't be potters, and no one will truly be anything at all. This doesn't matter much when it's limited to cobblers. But when the guardians of law and government are merely pretending to be guardians, they'll destroy the entire state. Only they have the power to create order and genuine happiness. We mean for our guardians to be true protectors, not destroyers. Your critic is imagining farmers at a festival, not citizens doing their duty. We're talking about different things — his idea isn't really a state at all. So the question is whether, in appointing guardians, we should aim at their individual happiness, or at the happiness of the state as a whole. If it's the whole, then guardians, auxiliaries, and everyone else must do their own work in the best way possible. Then the entire state will develop in good order, and each class will receive whatever share of happiness nature assigns to it.
I think you're absolutely right.
I wonder if you'll agree with another observation of mine.
What is it?
There seem to be two things that corrupt the crafts.
What are they?
Wealth and poverty.
How do they work?
Think about it: when a potter gets rich, will he still put the same effort into his work?
Certainly not.
He'll get lazier and more careless?
Very true.
And the result is that he becomes a worse potter?
Yes, much worse.
On the other hand, if he's too poor to afford proper tools and materials, his work will suffer just as much, and he won't be able to train his apprentices properly either.
Certainly not.
So whether it's wealth or poverty, both workers and their work suffer?
That's clear.
Here, then, are new evils for our guardians to watch out for, or they'll creep into the city unnoticed.
What evils?
Wealth and poverty. One breeds luxury and laziness, the other breeds meanness and bad character. Both breed discontent.
Very true, he said. But Socrates, how will our city fight a war, especially against a rich and powerful enemy, when it has no financial resources?
Fighting a single such enemy would be difficult, I admitted. But against two, it wouldn't be.
How do you mean? he said.
First, I said, if we have to fight, our side will be trained warriors fighting against an army of rich men.
True, he said.
Adeimantus, don't you think a single expert boxer could easily handle two well-fed gentlemen who don't know how to box?
Maybe not if they both attacked at once.
Not even if he could retreat and then turn to strike whoever came at him first? And if he kept doing this under a scorching sun, couldn't a trained fighter take down quite a few overweight opponents?
Certainly, he said. That wouldn't be surprising at all.
And rich men probably have an even bigger advantage in boxing skill compared to their military skill.
Probably.
So we can assume our warriors could handle opponents two or three times their number?
I agree — I think you're right.

And suppose that before the battle, we sent an embassy to one of the two enemy cities, telling the truth: 'We have no gold or silver and aren't allowed to have any. But you do. So join us in the war and take the other city's wealth.' Who, hearing this, would choose to fight against lean, tough dogs rather than join the dogs against fat, tender sheep?
That doesn't seem likely. But there might be a danger if many states' wealth were concentrated in one.
How naive of you to call any of those places a 'state'!
Why?

You should use the plural. None of them is really one city — each is many cities, as they say in the game. Every city, however small, is really divided into two: the city of the rich and the city of the poor. These are at war with each other, and within each there are many smaller factions. If you treat them all as a single state, you're completely off the mark. But if you treat them as many and offer the wealth, power, or people of one faction to the others, you'll always have many allies and few enemies. Our state, as long as its wise order is maintained, will be the greatest of all — not in reputation or appearance, but in actual power, even if it has only a thousand defenders. You'll hardly find another state equal to it, among Greeks or non-Greeks, though many will seem as great or many times greater.
That's very true, he said.
So what should be the upper limit on our state's size and territory? At what point should the rulers say: enough?
What limit would you suggest?
The state should grow only as far as it can while remaining unified. That's the proper limit.
Good answer, he said.
So here's another directive for our guardians: keep the city neither too large nor too small, but unified and self-sufficient.
That's not too demanding, he said.

And there's an even easier one that we mentioned before: the duty of demoting guardians' children who prove inferior and promoting lower-class children who prove superior. The idea is that each person in the city should be assigned to the role nature designed them for. Each person does one thing, becoming one person rather than many. And so the whole city becomes one rather than many.
Yes, that's not difficult, he said.
These regulations we're establishing, Adeimantus, aren't really a lot of grand principles. They're all minor details, provided we take care of one great thing — or rather, one sufficient thing.
What is it? he asked.

Education and upbringing. If our citizens are well-educated and grow into sensible people, they'll easily figure out everything else on their own — including matters I'm leaving out, like marriage, having children, and the principle that friends share everything in common, as the saying goes.
That will be the best approach.

And once a state gets off to a good start, it gains momentum like a wheel. Good education produces good character, and good character taking root in good education improves even further — and this improvement carries forward through generations, just as in animal breeding.
Very likely, he said.

So to sum up: this is the point our rulers must focus on above all else — that the arts and physical training be preserved in their original form, with no innovations allowed. When someone quotes the line about people always wanting
'The newest song the singers have to sing,'

the rulers should be careful that the poet isn't praising new types of music, which absolutely must not be allowed. Any innovation in the musical arts endangers the entire state and should be prohibited. As Damon says, and I completely believe him, when the modes of music change, the fundamental laws of the state always change with them.
You can add my vote to Damon's and yours, said Adeimantus.
Then our guardians must build their fortress on the foundation of the arts?
Yes, he said. The lawlessness you describe sneaks in too easily.
Right — it comes in disguised as harmless amusement.

Yes, and it seems harmless enough at first. But gradually this spirit of license finds a home and seeps into people's habits and customs. From there, with growing force, it invades business contracts. From contracts, it moves into laws and the constitution itself, with complete recklessness, until finally, Socrates, it overturns all rights, public and private.
Is that really how it happens? I said.
That's what I believe, he said.
Then, as I was saying, our young people must be trained strictly from the start. If their amusements become lawless and they become lawless themselves, they can never grow into virtuous citizens.
Very true, he said.

But when children make a good start in play and develop habits of order through the arts, this orderliness — so different from the disorder of the others — will follow them through everything and become a force for growth. And if the state's standards ever slip, this habit will restore them.
Very true, he said.
Young people raised this way will discover for themselves the minor rules that their predecessors entirely neglected.
What kind of rules?

Things like: when young people should be silent in the presence of elders; how to show respect by standing and offering seats; what honor is due to parents; how to dress and wear their hair; general deportment and manners. Do you agree?
Yes.
But I don't think there's much point in legislating about such things. Written laws on these matters are unlikely to be either effective or lasting.
Impossible.
It seems, Adeimantus, that the direction education takes in childhood determines a person's entire future life. Like attracts like.
Of course.
Until it reaches some grand result, which may be good or may be the opposite.
That can't be denied.
And for that reason, I won't try to legislate further about these things.
Naturally enough.

And what about marketplace regulations, business contracts, disputes between individuals, legal actions, jury selection, market and harbor taxes, and all the various rules governing markets, police, and harbors? Good heavens — should we really bother legislating about all these details?
I don't think so, he said. Good people won't need laws imposed on them for these things. They'll figure out whatever regulations are needed soon enough on their own.
Yes, my friend — as long as God preserves the laws we've already given them.
Without divine help, said Adeimantus, they'll spend forever endlessly making and amending their laws and their lives, always hoping to achieve perfection.
Like those chronic invalids, I said, who have no self-control and refuse to change their bad habits?
Exactly.
What a delightful life they lead! Always treating and complicating their conditions, always imagining they'll be cured by whatever remedy someone recommends.
That's very common with that sort of patient, he said.

And the charming thing is that they consider anyone who tells them the truth their worst enemy — namely, that unless they stop overeating, overdrinking, womanizing, and being lazy, no drug or surgery or spell or charm will help them.
Charming indeed! he said. I see nothing charming about getting angry at someone who tells you what you need to hear.
You're not a fan of these people, I take it.
Not at all.

Then you wouldn't praise states that behave the same way? Aren't there badly governed states where citizens are forbidden on pain of death from changing the constitution, yet whoever most skillfully flatters the people living under that system, caters to their whims, and anticipates their desires is considered a great statesman? Don't these states resemble the invalids I was just describing?
They do, he said — these states are just as bad as those individuals, and I'm far from praising them.
But don't you admire the nerve and skill of these eager servants of political corruption?
I do, he said — though not all of them. Some have been so deluded by popular applause that they actually believe they're real statesmen. Those aren't very admirable.
What do you mean? Have some sympathy for them. When a man can't measure and a crowd of equally incapable people declare he's four cubits tall, can he help believing them?
I suppose not.

Then don't be too angry with them. Aren't they quite entertaining, really? They keep tinkering with petty reforms of the kind I was describing, always imagining they can legislate away fraud and cheating, not realizing they're cutting off the heads of a hydra?
Yes, that's exactly what they're doing.

I believe, I said, that a true legislator won't bother with this kind of legislation, whether in a well-ordered or a badly ordered state. In the one, it's useless; in the other, it's unnecessary. The important regulations will follow naturally from what we've already established.
Then what work of legislation remains for us? he asked.
Nothing for us, I said. But for Apollo, the god of Delphi, the greatest, noblest, and most important matters remain.
What are those?

The founding of temples and sacrifices, and the whole service of gods, demigods, and heroes. Also the arrangements for the dead, and the rites required to honor those in the world below. We don't know about these things ourselves, and as founders of a city, we'd be foolish to trust any authority other than our ancestral god. He sits at the center, at the navel of the earth, and interprets religion for all of humanity.
You're right — that's what we'll do.

So then, son of Ariston: where in all of this is justice? Now that our city has been built, light a candle and search. Get your brother, Polemarchus, and the rest of our friends to help. Let's find where justice and injustice are, how they differ, and which one a person who wants to be happy should choose — whether or not gods and humans are watching.
That's absurd, said Glaucon. You promised to do the searching yourself, saying it would be impious not to come to justice's defense.
You're right, and I did promise. I'll keep my word. But you have to help.
We will, he said.
Here's how I think we can find it: I'll start from the assumption that our state, if properly organized, is perfect.
That's a safe assumption.
And being perfect, it must be wise, brave, self-disciplined, and just.
Clearly.
And whichever of these qualities we identify, the remaining ones will be whatever we haven't yet found.
Right.
If we were looking for one of four things, we might recognize it immediately. Or we might identify the other three first, and the fourth would be whatever's left.
Very true, he said.
The same method should work for the virtues, since there are also four.
Obviously.
The first virtue I see in our state is wisdom, and there's something peculiar about it.
What's that?
Our state is said to be wise because it has good judgment?
Very true.
And good judgment is clearly a kind of knowledge. People don't make good decisions through ignorance but through knowledge.
Obviously.
But there are many kinds of knowledge in a state.
Of course.
Take carpentry. Is that the kind of knowledge that makes a city wise and sound in judgment?
Certainly not. That would only give the city a reputation for good woodwork.
So a city isn't called wise for its expertise in building wooden things?
Certainly not.
Or for its knowledge of metalworking, or any similar specialized skill?
None of those.
Or for its knowledge of agriculture? That would make it a good farming city.
Yes.

So here's the key question: is there any knowledge in our newly founded state, held by any group of citizens, that deals not with some particular aspect of the state, but with the state as a whole — considering how it can best manage its internal affairs and its relations with other states?
There certainly is.
What is this knowledge, and who has it?
It's the knowledge of the guardians, he said — those we described as the true, complete guardians.
And what does the city derive from possessing this knowledge?
The reputation of being sound in judgment and truly wise.
And will our city have more of these true guardians, or more blacksmiths?
Far more blacksmiths, he said.
In fact, won't the guardians be the smallest class of all those defined by some professional knowledge?
By far the smallest.

So it's through its smallest part — the ruling and guiding element — and the knowledge residing in that part, that the whole state, constituted according to nature, will be wise. And this class, which nature ordains should be the smallest, possesses the only knowledge worthy of the name wisdom.
Absolutely true.
So we've discovered one of our four virtues and where it lives in the state — more or less satisfactorily, I'd say.
Very satisfactorily, in my humble opinion.
Now courage isn't hard to identify either — or which part of the state gives it the name 'courageous.'
How do you mean?
When we call a state courageous or cowardly, we're obviously thinking of the part that goes to war on the state's behalf.
Obviously, he said.
Whether the rest of the citizens are personally courageous or cowardly doesn't determine whether the city itself is brave or not.
Certainly not.

A city is courageous because of that portion of itself which preserves, under all circumstances, the correct belief about what should and should not be feared — the belief our lawgiver instilled through education. That's what I'm calling courage.
Could you say that again? I don't think I fully understood.
Courage is a kind of preservation.
Preservation of what?

Of the belief, instilled by law through education, about what is and isn't truly dangerous. By 'under all circumstances,' I mean that the person holds onto this belief through pleasure and pain, through desire and fear, without losing it. Want an analogy?
Please.

You know that when dyers want to produce true sea-purple, they start by selecting white wool. They prepare and treat it with great care so that the white ground absorbs the purple perfectly. Whatever is dyed this way becomes colorfast — no amount of washing with soap or without can fade the color. But when the wool hasn't been properly prepared, the result looks washed-out and ridiculous, whether it's purple or any other color.
Yes, he said, I know those dyes look washed-out and pathetic.

That's exactly what we were doing when we selected our soldiers and educated them in the arts and physical training. We were contriving influences that would prepare them to absorb the dye of our laws perfectly, so their beliefs about what's dangerous and what's not would be permanently fixed by their upbringing — immune to those powerful solvents: pleasure (the most potent of all), sorrow, fear, and desire. This universal preserving power — the ability to maintain the correct, law-given belief about real and false dangers through everything — that's what I call courage. Unless you disagree.

I don't disagree at all, he said. I assume you mean to distinguish this from the mindless bravery of an untrained person or an animal — that kind of 'courage' isn't what the law prescribes and should have a different name.
Absolutely.
Then I accept your account of courage?

Yes, I said — accept it as the courage of a citizen, and you won't be far wrong. We can examine it more precisely later, but for now we're looking for justice, not courage, and this is sufficient for our purposes.
You're right, he said.
Two virtues remain to be found in the state: self-discipline first, then justice, which is the goal of our whole search.
Exactly.
Can we find justice without dealing with self-discipline?
I don't know how, he said, and I'd rather not find justice at the cost of overlooking self-discipline. Please examine self-discipline first.
Of course — I wouldn't refuse that request.
Then let's examine it, he said.
All right, I said. As far as I can see, self-discipline is more like a kind of harmony or agreement than the previous virtues.
How so? he asked.

Self-discipline, I said, is the ordering and control of certain pleasures and desires. That's oddly captured in the expression 'being master of yourself,' and you can find traces of the same idea throughout our language.
Certainly, he said.
But isn't 'master of himself' a strange expression? The master would also be the slave, and the slave the master — both refer to the same person.
Of course.

What the expression really means, I think, is that within the human soul there's a better element and a worse one. When the better element controls the worse, we say the person is 'master of himself' — and this is praise. But when the better element, which is also smaller, is overwhelmed by the greater mass of the worse — through bad education or bad company — the person is called a 'slave to himself' and unprincipled.
That makes sense.
Now look at our new state. You'd agree it can rightly be called 'master of itself,' if 'self-discipline' and 'self-mastery' mean the rule of the better part over the worse.
Yes, he said. I see that what you say is true.
Let me also note that the many complex pleasures, desires, and pains are generally found in children, women, servants, and the lower, more numerous class of free citizens.
Certainly, he said.
Whereas the simple, moderate desires that follow reason and are guided by good judgment are found in only a few — the best born and best educated.
Very true.
Both groups exist in our state, and the base desires of the many are controlled by the virtuous desires and wisdom of the few.
I see that, he said.
So if any city can be called master of its own pleasures and desires, ours can?
Certainly, he said.
And it can also be called self-disciplined, for the same reasons?
Yes.
And if there's any state where rulers and subjects agree on who should rule, that would be ours?
Without a doubt.
And with this agreement, in which class does self-discipline reside — in the rulers or the subjects?
In both, I'd say, he replied.
Do you see that we weren't far off when we guessed that self-discipline is a kind of harmony?
Why?

Because self-discipline, unlike courage and wisdom, doesn't reside in just one part. It extends through the whole — running through all the notes of the scale, creating harmony between the weaker and the stronger and the middle, whether you measure strength by wisdom, power, numbers, wealth, or anything else. We can rightly say that self-discipline is the agreement of the naturally superior and inferior about which should rule, in both states and individuals.
I completely agree.
Good. So three of the four virtues have been found in our state. The remaining one — the one that completes the state's excellence — must be justice. If only we knew what it was.
Obviously.

Now it's time, Glaucon! Like hunters, we must surround the thicket and make sure justice doesn't escape. She's definitely in here somewhere. Keep your eyes sharp, and if you spot her first, point her out to me.
I wish I could! But you'd be better off treating me as a follower with just enough vision to see what you show me.
Then join me in a prayer and follow.
Lead the way.
The path is unclear, I said, and the forest is dark and confusing. But we must press on.
Let's go.
Wait — I think I see something! I'm picking up a trail. I don't think our quarry will escape.
Good news! he said.
We've really been quite foolish.
Why?

Because justice has been lying at our feet from the very beginning, and we never saw it! We're like people searching everywhere for something they're holding in their hands. We've been gazing into the distance instead of looking at what was right in front of us.
What do you mean?
I mean we've been talking about justice this whole time without recognizing it.
You're taking a long time to get to the point.
Fine, then tell me: do you remember the original principle we kept insisting on when we founded the state? That each person should do the one thing he's naturally best suited for?
Yes, we said that repeatedly.
And we also said that justice means doing your own work and not meddling in other people's business. We said it many times, and others have said the same.
Yes, we did.
So doing your own work, in a certain sense, is justice. Can you tell me how I arrive at this conclusion?
I can't, but I'd like to hear.

Because I think this is the only virtue left in the state after we've identified self-discipline, courage, and wisdom. And it's also the ultimate cause and condition of their existence. While present alongside them, it preserves them all. We said that once we found three of the four, justice would be whatever remained.
That necessarily follows.

But here's the test: if we had to decide which of these four contributes most to the state's excellence — the agreement between rulers and subjects, the soldiers' preservation of correct beliefs about dangers, the wisdom and vigilance of the rulers, or this other quality I'm describing, found in everyone from children to rulers — the quality of each person doing their own work and not meddling in others' — it would be hard to say which matters most.
It certainly would be difficult, he said.
So the power of each person doing their own work seems to compete with the other political virtues: wisdom, self-discipline, and courage.
Yes, he said.
And the virtue that competes with them is justice?
Exactly.
Let's approach this from another angle. When the rulers judge legal cases, what's the basic principle they apply?
Certainly.
Isn't it that no one should take what belongs to another, or be deprived of what belongs to them?
Yes, that's the principle.
And that's a just principle?
Yes.
So from this angle too, justice means having and doing what is properly your own.
Very true.

Now think about this: if a carpenter started doing a cobbler's work, or a cobbler did a carpenter's, or they swapped tools and duties, or the same person tried to do both — would any great harm come to the state?
Not much.

But when a cobbler or trader, puffed up by wealth, power, popularity, or some other advantage, tries to force his way into the warrior class, or a warrior into the ruling class, without being qualified — when they swap tools and duties, or when one person tries to be trader, soldier, and ruler all at once — I think you'd agree that this kind of interchange and meddling is the ruin of the state.
Absolutely.
So when three distinct classes meddle in each other's business, or one class tries to become another, that's the greatest harm to the state and would be rightly called the worst kind of wrongdoing?
Precisely.
And the greatest wrongdoing against one's own city is what you'd call injustice?
Certainly.
That, then, is injustice. Conversely, when traders, auxiliaries, and guardians each mind their own business — that's justice, and that's what will make the city just.
I agree completely.

Let's not be too hasty, though. If this same principle, tested in the individual, also turns out to be justice, then we can be confident. If not, we'll need a new inquiry. First, let's complete the original investigation. We started by assuming that if we could see justice in the larger model — the state — it would be easier to see it in the individual. The larger model was the state, so we built the best one we could, knowing justice would be in it. Now let's apply what we found to the individual. If the two match, we're done. If they differ, we'll go back and test the theory again. Rubbing the two together might strike a spark that lights up justice, and once we see it clearly, we'll fix that vision in our minds.
Good method. Let's do it.
When two things, one large and one small, share the same name, are they alike or unlike in what that name refers to?
Alike, he said.
So the just person, considered purely in terms of justice, will be like the just state?
He will.
And we determined that a state is just when its three classes each do their own work. It's also wise, brave, and self-disciplined because of certain other qualities of those same classes?
True, he said.
So if the individual has the same three principles in his soul as the state, shouldn't he be described in the same terms for the same reasons?
Necessarily, he said.
Here we are again, my friend, stumbling onto an easy question: does the soul have these three elements or not?
Easy? Hardly, Socrates! The proverb is right: the good is hard.

So it seems. And honestly, I don't think our current method is rigorous enough to answer this precisely. The truly accurate method would be much longer. But we can reach a conclusion that's at least as good as what we've established so far.
That would satisfy me under the circumstances, he said.
And me too, I said.
Then don't give up, he said.

We have to agree, I said, that the same principles and characteristics found in the state also exist in each of us individually. Where else would they come from? Take spiritedness — it would be absurd to say a state possesses it without getting it from the individuals who make it up. The same goes for other qualities: the Thracians and Scythians and northern peoples are noted for their spiritedness; Greeks are known for their love of knowledge; and Phoenicians and Egyptians are associated with the love of money.
Exactly, he said.
That's not hard to see.
Not at all.

But the harder question is this: do we do everything with our whole soul, or are there three distinct parts — one that reasons, one that gets angry, and one that desires? Do we learn with one part, feel spirited with another, and experience appetite with a third? Or does the whole soul engage in each activity? That's the real difficulty.
Yes, he said, that is the difficulty.
Let's try to determine whether these are the same or different.
How? he asked.

The same thing obviously cannot do or undergo opposite things at the same time, in the same respect, and in relation to the same object. So whenever we find this happening in something, we'll know we're dealing with more than one thing.
Good.
For example, can the same thing be at rest and in motion at the same time, in the same respect?
Impossible.

Let me be more precise, to avoid confusion later. Imagine someone standing still but moving his hands and head. You wouldn't say the same person is both at rest and in motion — you'd say one part is in motion while another is at rest.
Very true.

And if someone cleverly objected that a spinning top is both at rest and in motion simultaneously — since the whole thing spins while its peg stays fixed — we wouldn't accept that. The axis and the circumference aren't the same thing. The axis is at rest while the circumference moves. But if the axis itself tilts in any direction, then nothing about it is at rest.
That's the correct description, he said.
So no such objection will confuse us or make us believe the same thing can simultaneously do or undergo opposites in the same part, in the same respect, and in relation to the same object.
It certainly won't confuse me, he said.
Still, rather than examining every possible objection, let's just assume our principle is correct and agree that if it later turns out to be wrong, we'll withdraw everything that follows from it.
Yes, that's the best approach.
Good. Now, would you agree that assent and dissent, desire and aversion, attraction and repulsion are all opposites, whether we consider them active or passive?
Yes, they're opposites.

And hunger, thirst, and desires in general, as well as wishing and wanting — wouldn't you place all of these in the category of seeking or attraction? When someone desires something, doesn't their soul reach toward it, draw it to itself? When they want something given to them, they mentally nod 'yes,' as if answering a question?
Very true.
And unwillingness, reluctance, and the absence of desire — wouldn't those fall in the opposite category of rejection and repulsion?
Certainly.
Given this, let's take a specific class of desires — hunger and thirst, the most obvious examples.
All right, he said.
The object of one is food, and of the other, drink?
Yes.

Now here's the critical point: is thirst simply the desire for drink and nothing more? Not for hot or cold drink, much or little drink, or any particular kind of drink — just drink? If you're also hot, you'll want cold drink. If also cold, warm drink. If the thirst is extreme, you'll want a lot. If mild, a little. But thirst in itself is simply the desire for drink in itself, just as hunger in itself is the desire for food in itself?
Yes, he said. Each simple desire is for its simple object, and a qualified desire is for a qualified object.

But we need to guard against a potential confusion. Someone might object that nobody desires just 'drink' — they desire good drink. And nobody desires just 'food' — they desire good food. Since good is the universal object of desire, thirst must really be thirst for good drink, and likewise for every other desire.
That objection might seem to have some force, he said.
But I'd maintain that among relative terms, some are qualified and their correlatives are qualified too, while others are simple and have simple correlatives.
I don't understand what you mean.
Well, you know that 'greater' is relative to 'less'?
Of course.
And 'much greater' is relative to 'much less'?
Yes.
And 'sometimes greater' to 'sometimes less,' and 'future greater' to 'future less'?
Certainly, he said.
The same holds for 'more' and 'less,' 'double' and 'half,' 'heavier' and 'lighter,' 'faster' and 'slower,' 'hot' and 'cold,' and all similar relative terms?
Yes.

Doesn't the same principle apply to forms of knowledge? Knowledge in general has its general object. But a specific kind of knowledge has a specific kind of object. Take architecture: it's a kind of knowledge distinguished from other kinds, which is why it has its own name.
Certainly.
Because it has a specific quality that no other kind has?
Yes.
And it has that quality because it has a specific kind of object. The same is true of all other arts and sciences?
Yes.

So now you understand what I was saying about relative terms. When the relation is unqualified, the correlative is unqualified. When the relation is qualified, the correlative is qualified. I'm not saying that relatives must share the same quality — that the science of health is itself healthy, or the science of disease is diseased. I'm saying that when 'science' stops being used in the abstract and takes on a specific object — like the nature of health and disease — it becomes specific, and we call it not just 'science' but 'medical science.'
I fully understand, and I agree.
Now, wouldn't you say thirst is one of those relative terms with a clear correlative —
Yes — thirst is relative to drink.

And a specific kind of thirst is relative to a specific kind of drink. But thirst in itself is for neither much nor little, neither good nor bad, nor any particular kind of drink — just drink in itself?
Absolutely.
So the thirsty soul, insofar as it's thirsty, wants nothing but drink. That's what it yearns for and tries to get.
Clearly.

So if something pulls a thirsty soul away from drink, that 'something' must be a different element from the thirsty part. As we established, the same thing can't simultaneously act in opposite ways toward the same object in the same respect.
Impossible.
Just as you wouldn't say the archer's hands are simultaneously pushing and pulling the bow. One hand pushes while the other pulls.
Exactly, he said.
Now, can someone be thirsty and yet not want to drink?
Yes, he said, that happens all the time.
Then what do we say? Isn't there something in the soul urging the person to drink, and something else holding them back — something different from and stronger than the urge to drink?
I'd say so.
And the restraining element comes from reason, while the driving and attracting element comes from bodily states and conditions?
Clearly.

Then we can reasonably assume these are two distinct elements: the part we reason with, which we'll call the rational element, and the part that craves, hungers, thirsts, and feels the pull of all desires, which we'll call the irrational or appetitive element — the companion of various pleasures and satisfactions.
Yes, it's reasonable to regard them as different, he said.
Good — so we've established two elements in the soul. But what about spirit, or passion? Is it a third element, or is it the same as one of the other two?
I'd be inclined to say it's a kind of desire.

Well, let me tell you a story I once heard and believe. Leontius, son of Aglaion, was coming up from the Piraeus along the outside of the north wall when he noticed some corpses lying at the place of execution. He felt a desire to look at them but also felt disgust and tried to turn away. For a while he struggled and covered his eyes. But finally the desire overpowered him, and he forced his eyes open and ran toward the bodies, saying: 'There — look, you wretches! Take your fill of this lovely sight!'
I've heard that story too, he said.
The point is that anger can go to war against desire, showing they're two distinct things.
Yes, that's the meaning, he said.

And don't we often see that when a person's desires overpower their reason, they get angry at themselves? In this internal struggle — like a civil war — spirit takes the side of reason. But spirit siding with desires against reason's judgment? I don't think you've ever observed that in yourself or in anyone else.
Certainly not.

And consider this: when a person believes he's wronged someone, the nobler he is, the less he can bring himself to resent whatever suffering the wronged person inflicts on him — hunger, cold, or any other hardship. He considers such punishment just, and his spirit refuses to be stirred up against it.
True, he said.

But when a person believes he's the one being wronged, then he boils and rages, siding with what he believes is just. No matter how much hunger, cold, or other suffering he endures, he perseveres and fights on until he either wins or dies — or until reason, like a shepherd calling back his dog, tells his spirit to stand down.
That's a perfect analogy, he said. And in our state, we said the auxiliaries would be like dogs obeying the rulers, who are their shepherds.
Yes, you understand me perfectly. But there's one more point to consider.
What's that?
Remember how spirit initially seemed to be a kind of desire? But now we see the opposite: in a conflict within the soul, spirit fights on the side of reason.
Absolutely.

But is spirit different from reason too, or just a form of reason? If it's the latter, the soul has only two elements — rational and appetitive — rather than three. Or, just as the state had three classes (traders, auxiliaries, and rulers), might there be a third element in the soul — spirit — that naturally supports reason when it hasn't been corrupted by bad upbringing?
Yes, there must be a third, he said.
There must — provided spirit turns out to be different from reason as well as from appetite.
And that's easy to prove. You can see it even in young children: they're full of spirit almost from birth, but some never seem to develop reason at all, and most develop it rather late.
Excellent point, I said. And you can see spirit in animals too, which is further evidence. And we can also cite Homer's line that we've already quoted:
'He struck his chest and rebuked his heart.'
In this verse, Homer clearly treats the part that reasons about better and worse as different from the unreasoning anger that it rebukes.
Very true, he said.
So after much effort, we've finally reached solid ground: the same three principles that exist in the state also exist in the individual soul.
Exactly.
Doesn't it follow that the individual is wise in the same way and by the same quality that makes the state wise?
Certainly.
And the same quality that makes the state brave makes the individual brave, and the same relationship between the individual and every other virtue holds true?
Absolutely.
And the individual will be just in the same way the state is just?
That follows necessarily.
We can't have forgotten that the state's justice consisted in each of the three classes doing its own work?
I don't think we've forgotten.
And we must remember that the individual is just when each element of their nature does its own work?
Yes, we must remember that too.
Shouldn't the rational element rule, since it's wise and responsible for the whole soul? And shouldn't the spirited element be its ally and subject?
Certainly.

And as we said, the combined influence of the arts and physical training will bring them into harmony — strengthening reason with noble ideas and education, while moderating and civilizing the wildness of spirit through rhythm and harmony?
Exactly, he said.

These two, properly educated and trained in their true functions, will then govern the appetitive element — which is the largest part of the soul and naturally the most insatiable. They'll keep watch over it, preventing it from gorging itself on physical pleasures, growing too strong, and trying to enslave and dominate the parts that aren't its natural subjects — which would overturn a person's entire life.
Very true, he said.

Together, these two will be the best defenders of the whole soul and body against external threats — one providing counsel, the other fighting under the leader's direction and bravely carrying out his commands.
True.
We call a person brave when their spirited element preserves, through pleasure and pain, reason's commands about what should and shouldn't be feared?
Right, he said.
And we call a person wise when that small ruling element possesses the knowledge of what benefits each of the three parts and the whole?
Certainly.

And a person is self-disciplined when all three elements are in friendly harmony — when the ruling principle of reason and the two subordinate principles of spirit and appetite all agree that reason should rule, without rebellion?
Certainly, he said. That's the true account of self-discipline in both the state and the individual.
And we've explained again and again how and why a person will be just.
Yes, we certainly have.
Does justice look any different in the individual than in the state? Or is it the same?
There's no difference, in my opinion.
If any doubt remains, a few ordinary examples should settle it.
What kind of examples?
Would the just person — or someone raised in our just state — be likely to steal gold or silver deposited with him for safekeeping? Would anyone deny this?
No one, he said.
Would the just person ever commit sacrilege, theft, or betrayal of friends or country?
Never.
Would he ever break his oaths or agreements?
Impossible.
Would anyone be less likely to commit adultery, dishonor their parents, or neglect their religious duties?
No one.
And the reason is that each part of his soul is doing its own work, whether ruling or being ruled?
Exactly.
Are you satisfied that this quality — what makes both states and people like this — is justice? Or do you hope to discover something else?
No, I'm satisfied.
Then our dream has come true! Remember the suspicion we had at the very start, that some divine power must have guided us to a basic form of justice?
Yes, certainly.
And the principle of specialization — the carpenter doing carpentry, the shoemaker making shoes, and so on — was a shadow of justice, which is why it was useful?
Clearly.

But in reality, justice isn't about external actions but about the inner self — the true person. The just person doesn't let the different elements within him interfere with each other or do each other's work. He organizes his inner life, becoming his own master, his own law, at peace with himself. When he's harmonized the three principles — like the high, low, and middle notes of a scale, with all the intervals between — when he's no longer many but has become one, perfectly balanced and attuned, then he acts. Whether in business, physical matters, politics, or private affairs, he always considers what preserves and serves this harmonious condition to be just and good, and the knowledge governing it to be wisdom. Whatever damages this harmony, he calls unjust, and the ignorance behind it, he calls foolishness.
Socrates, you've spoken the exact truth.
Good. And if we claimed to have discovered the just person, the just state, and the nature of justice in each, we wouldn't be lying?
Certainly not.
Can we say so, then?
Let's say so.
Now we need to consider injustice.
Clearly.

Injustice must be a conflict among the three elements — meddling, interference, and rebellion of one part against the whole. It's the attempt by a subordinate part to seize unlawful authority, like a subject revolting against a rightful ruler. This confusion and disorder is injustice, and also intemperance, cowardice, ignorance — every form of vice.
Exactly.
And now that we know what justice and injustice are, the meaning of acting justly or unjustly should be perfectly clear?
What do you mean? he said.
They're like health and disease — but in the soul instead of the body.
How? he said.
What's healthy causes health; what's unhealthy causes disease.
Yes.
And just actions produce justice; unjust actions produce injustice?
Certainly.
Health is the establishment of a natural order and hierarchy among the body's parts. Disease is a disruption of that natural order.
True.
And justice is the establishment of a natural order and hierarchy among the soul's parts, while injustice is a disruption of that natural order?
Exactly, he said.
So virtue is the soul's health, beauty, and well-being, and vice is its disease, ugliness, and weakness?
True.
And good practices lead to virtue, bad practices to vice?
Certainly.

But we still haven't answered our original question about the comparative benefit of justice versus injustice. Which is more profitable: to be just and act justly, whether or not gods and men are watching? Or to be unjust and act unjustly, as long as you escape punishment and reform?

Socrates, the question has become absurd at this point. We know that when the body's constitution breaks down, life is unbearable even with every luxury and all the power in the world. And shall we be told that life is still worth living when the soul's vital principle is corrupted and destroyed — as long as the person can do whatever they want, except acquire justice and virtue, or escape injustice and vice? Given what we've shown these to be?
Yes, I said, the question is absurd. But since we're so close to seeing the truth with perfect clarity, we shouldn't quit now.
Absolutely not, he said.
Come up here then, I said, and look down at the many forms of vice — at least the ones worth examining.
Lead the way, he said.
From the height we've reached in this argument, as from a watchtower, I said, we can see that virtue is one, but vice takes countless forms. Four of them especially deserve our attention.
What do you mean? he said.
There appear to be as many types of soul as there are types of government.
How many?
Five types of government and five corresponding types of soul, I said.
What are they?
The first, I said, is the form we've been describing. It can be called either monarchy or aristocracy, depending on whether one exceptional person rules or several.
True, he said.
But I consider these as one form, whether one person or many govern. If the rulers have been trained the way we've described, the fundamental laws will be the same.
That's true, he said.

chapters.title: Book V
paragraphs: So that's the good and true state, and the good and true person follows the same pattern. If this form is right, every other is wrong. And the corruption takes four forms, affecting both the organization of the state and the character of the individual soul.
What are they? he said.

I was about to describe the order in which these four corrupt forms seemed to follow one another, when Polemarchus, who was sitting a little beyond Adeimantus, reached out and grabbed him by the shoulder, pulling him closer and whispering something in his ear. I only caught the words: 'Shall we let him off, or what?'
Certainly not, said Adeimantus, raising his voice.
Who won't you let off? I asked.
You, he said.
Why me in particular?

Because we think you're being lazy and trying to cheat us out of a whole major section of the argument. You think you can slip past us with that casual remark that 'in the matter of women and children, friends share everything in common' — as if that were self-evident!
And wasn't I right, Adeimantus?

Yes, he said, but like everything else, 'right' still needs to be explained. There are many kinds of sharing. Please tell us what kind you mean. We've been waiting for you to explain how your citizens will handle family life — how they'll have and raise children, and what exactly this community of women and children involves. We believe the management of these matters will have an enormous impact on the state, for good or ill. And now, since you're moving on to another topic without addressing it, we've resolved — as you heard — not to let you go until you give a full account.
Count me in on that resolution, said Glaucon.
And you can consider us all equally agreed, said Thrasymachus.

You have no idea what you're doing by ambushing me like this! I said. What a huge question you're raising! I thought I was finished and was only too happy that you'd accepted what I said. Now you're dragging me back to the very foundations, not realizing what a hornet's nest of arguments you're stirring up. I saw this trouble coming and deliberately avoided it.
What do you think we came here for? said Thrasymachus. To prospect for gold, or to hear ideas?
Ideas, yes — but ideas should have a limit.

Socrates, said Glaucon, a whole lifetime is the only limit that wise people set on listening to discussions like these. Don't worry about us — just take heart and answer the question your own way. What kind of community of women and children will there be among our guardians? How will the period from birth to education be managed — since that seems to need the most care? Tell us how you'd handle it.

Yes, my friend, but the answer is far from easy. Many more doubts arise here than about anything we've discussed before. People will question whether what I'm describing is even possible, and even if possible, whether it's actually desirable. So I'm reluctant to tackle the subject — I'm afraid my ideas will turn out to be nothing more than wishful thinking.
Don't be afraid, he said. Your audience won't be hard on you. They're not skeptical or hostile.
I take it you're trying to encourage me with those words, my friend.
Yes, he said.

Well, you're having the exact opposite effect. If I were confident in my knowledge, your encouragement would make sense. Speaking truthfully among wise friends who care about you is nothing to fear. But conducting an argument when you're unsure of yourself, which is my position, is dangerous and slippery. Not because I might be laughed at — that would be childish — but because I might miss the truth precisely where I most need to be accurate, and drag my friends down with me. I pray to Nemesis not to punish me for what I'm about to say. I truly believe that being an accidental killer is a lesser crime than being a deceiver about beauty, goodness, or justice in the realm of laws. That's a risk I'd rather take among enemies than friends — so your encouragement is well-meant but ill-timed.
Glaucon laughed and said: Well then, Socrates, if your argument does us any harm, we'll acquit you in advance of intellectual homicide and clear you of deception. Speak with confidence.
Fair enough, I said. The law says that once acquitted, a person is free from guilt. And what holds in law may hold in argument.
Then why hesitate?

All right, I said. I suppose I need to go back and say what I should have said earlier. We've finished with the men's part; now it's the women's turn. And I'm the more willing since you've invited me.

For people born and educated like our citizens, I think the only way to settle the question of women and children is to follow the path we started on, when we said the men were to be guardians and watchdogs of the community.
True.
Let's apply the same or similar rules to the women's birth and education, and see if the result fits our plan.
What do you mean?

Let me put it as a question: among dogs, do we divide them into males and females? Do both share equally in hunting, guarding, and other duties? Or do we keep the females at home because bearing and nursing puppies is work enough for them, while giving all the outdoor duties exclusively to the males?
No, he said — they share alike. The only difference is that males are stronger and females weaker.
But can you use different animals for the same purpose unless they're bred and raised the same way?
You can't.
So if women are to have the same duties as men, they must have the same education?
Yes.
The education we assigned to men was the arts and physical training.
Yes.
Then women must also learn the arts, physical training, and the art of war, and must practice them alongside men?
That seems to follow.
I expect, I said, that many of our proposals will seem ridiculous if they're actually carried out.
No doubt.

And the most ridiculous sight of all will be women exercising naked in the training grounds alongside men, especially the older women. They certainly won't be a pretty picture — any more than those enthusiastic old men who keep coming to the gym despite their wrinkles and sagging bodies.
Yes indeed, he said. That would look pretty ridiculous by today's standards.

But since we've committed to speaking our minds, we mustn't be afraid of the jokes that wits will aim at this kind of innovation — all the comedy about women learning the arts and physical training, and especially about them wearing armor and riding horses!
Very true.

Still, having begun, we must push forward through the rough terrain. Let's ask these comedians to be serious for once. Not long ago, Greeks considered it shameful and ridiculous for men to be seen naked — as many non-Greek peoples still do today. When the Cretans and then the Spartans first introduced public nudity, the wits of the time no doubt mocked it just as much.
No doubt.

But when experience showed that exercising unclothed was far better than exercising clothed, the apparent absurdity vanished before the rational principle. People realized that anyone who ridicules anything other than what's genuinely foolish or wrong is himself the fool. And anyone who judges beauty by any standard other than goodness is making a serious mistake.
Very true.

So first, whether we're joking or serious, let's settle the fundamental question: is it in women's nature to share in all the activities of men, or in none, or in some but not others? And specifically, is warfare one of those activities they can share in? This will give us the best starting point and lead to the fairest conclusion.
That's the best approach.
Shall we start by arguing against ourselves, to make sure the opposing position gets a fair hearing?
Why not? he said.

Then let's imagine what our opponents would say: 'Socrates and Glaucon, no one else needs to refute you — you refuted yourselves when you first founded your state. You admitted the principle that each person should do the work that suits their nature.' We did indeed make that admission. 'And don't men and women have very different natures?' Of course they do. 'Then shouldn't different natures be assigned different tasks — tasks suited to their respective natures?' Certainly. 'But then haven't you fallen into a serious contradiction by now saying that men and women, with their completely different natures, should do the same things?' How would you defend us against that objection, my friend?
That's a tough question to answer on the spot. I'd beg you to make the case for our side.
These are the objections I foresaw long ago, Glaucon, and they made me afraid to tackle the question of women and children.
I can see why, he said. This problem is anything but easy.
True, I said. But the fact is, whether you've fallen into a swimming pool or the middle of the ocean, you still have to swim.
Very true.
So we'd better swim and try to reach shore. Maybe a dolphin will save us, like the one that saved Arion.
I suppose so, he said.

All right, let's look for a way out. We agreed that different natures should have different occupations, and that men's and women's natures are different. Now we're saying different natures should have the same occupations. That's the inconsistency we're charged with.
Precisely.
The art of verbal contradiction is truly powerful, Glaucon!
Why do you say that?

Because many people fall into it without meaning to. They think they're reasoning when they're really just arguing — because they can't properly define and distinguish what they're talking about. They pursue verbal disputes in a spirit of competition rather than genuine inquiry.
Yes, that happens a lot. But what does that have to do with us?
A great deal. We're in danger of falling into exactly this kind of verbal dispute.
How so?

We've been bravely insisting on the verbal truth that different natures should have different occupations. But we never stopped to ask what we actually meant by 'sameness' or 'difference' of nature, or what kinds of difference are relevant to assigning different occupations.
No, he said, we never considered that.
So by way of illustration, I said: suppose we agreed that bald people and people with hair have 'different natures.' If bald people are cobblers, should we forbid hairy people from cobbling?
That would be absurd, he said.

Absurd — and for a good reason. When we founded the state, we never meant that every difference in nature should determine different occupations. We only meant differences relevant to the occupation in question. A doctor and someone with a doctor's mind have the same nature in the relevant sense.
True.
While a doctor and a carpenter have different natures?
Certainly.

So if men and women turn out to differ in their aptitude for a specific art or occupation, then we should assign that occupation to one sex or the other. But if the only difference is that women bear children and men beget them, that doesn't prove women are different from men in any way relevant to education. We should continue to maintain that our guardians and their wives should share the same occupations.
Very true, he said.
Next, we'll challenge our opponent to name any civic art or occupation in which a woman's nature differs from a man's.
That's fair.
And perhaps, like you, he'll reply that giving an immediate answer is hard, but with some thought it's not difficult.
Perhaps.
Then let's invite him to join our argument, and we'll try to show him that there's nothing in women's constitution that disqualifies them from governing the state.
By all means.

Let's put it to him this way: when we said someone was 'naturally gifted' or 'naturally ungifted' for something, we meant that one person picks it up quickly while another struggles; one needs little training to go far, while the other forgets even after much study; one's body works with their mind, while the other's body works against it. These are the differences that distinguish natural talent from its absence, right?
No one would deny that.

And can you name any human activity in which men don't outperform women in all these respects? I won't waste time mentioning cooking, weaving, and baking, where women do seem to excel and where it would be truly ridiculous for a man to outdo them.
You're right, he said, that men are generally superior. Though many individual women are better than many individual men at many things, your overall point holds.

So there's no civic function that belongs to women because they're women, or to men because they're men. Natural abilities are distributed equally between both sexes. Women can share in all occupations, and so can men, though in all of them women are generally somewhat weaker.
Very true.
Then shall we impose all our rules on men and none on women?
That would be absurd.
One woman has a gift for healing, another doesn't. One is naturally musical, another isn't.
Very true.
And one woman has an aptitude for athletics and military service, while another is unwarlike and hates exercise?
Certainly.
And one woman is philosophical, another is hostile to philosophy. One is spirited, another lacks spirit?
That's true too.
So one woman will have the guardian temperament and another won't. Wasn't it qualities like these that determined which men we selected as guardians?
Yes.
Men and women alike possess the qualities that make a guardian. They differ only in degree of strength.
Obviously.
So women with these qualities should be selected as companions and colleagues of men with the same qualities, since they're alike in capacity and character?
Very true.
And shouldn't the same natures have the same occupations?
They should.
Then we've come full circle: there's nothing unnatural about assigning the arts and physical training to the guardians' wives.
Certainly not.
The law we established was in harmony with nature and therefore not impossible or utopian. The current practice, which contradicts it, is what actually violates nature.
That seems to be true.
We needed to establish two things: first, that our proposals are possible; second, that they're beneficial.
Yes.
And the possibility has been established?
Yes.
Now we need to show the great benefit?
Exactly.
You'd agree that the same education that makes a man a good guardian will also make a woman a good guardian, since their fundamental nature is the same?
Yes.
Let me ask you something.
What?
Would you say all people are equally excellent, or that some are better than others?
Some are better.
And in our state, who would be more excellent — the guardians raised on our educational system, or the cobblers whose education consisted of cobbling?
What a ridiculous question!
You've answered it, I said. So may we also say that our guardians are the best citizens?
By far.
And their wives will be the best women?
Yes, by far.
And can anything be better for a state than having the best possible men and women?
Nothing.
And that's what education in the arts and physical training, as we've described it, will accomplish?
Certainly.
So our proposal is not only possible but maximally beneficial to the state?
True.

Then let the guardians' wives strip for exercise — their virtue will be their clothing — and share in warfare and the defense of the state. We'll assign lighter tasks to women, since they're the physically weaker sex, but otherwise their duties will be the same as men's. And anyone who laughs at the sight of women exercising for the noblest reasons is plucking
'An unripe fruit of wisdom,'
and doesn't understand what he's laughing at. For the truest saying is and always will be: what is useful is beautiful, and what is harmful is ugly.
Very true.
So we've survived the first wave without drowning! Our law that guardian men and women should share all activities in common has been justified as both useful and possible.
A mighty wave indeed, and you've made it through, he said.
You won't think it was so mighty when you see the next one, I said.
Let me see it.

The next law, which follows from everything before it, is this: the guardians' wives shall be held in common, and their children shall be raised in common. No parent shall know their own child, nor any child their parent.
That's a much bigger wave, he said. The possibility and the usefulness of such a law are both much more questionable.
I don't think the usefulness can be seriously disputed, I said. Having wives and children in common would bring enormous benefits. The real question is whether it's possible.
I think serious doubts can be raised about both, he said.
So you're making me defend on two fronts at once, I said. I was hoping you'd grant me the usefulness so I'd only have to deal with possibility.
Your escape attempt has been detected. You'll have to defend both.

All right, I submit. But grant me one favor: let me indulge in a bit of daydreaming, the way people do when they're walking alone. They don't bother figuring out how to get what they want — they skip straight to imagining what they'd do if they had it. They know it's just a fantasy, but it's pleasant. Let me do the same. I'll set aside the question of possibility for now and assume our plan is in place. Then I'll explore how the rulers would implement it and show why it would bring the greatest benefit to the state and guardians. If you agree, we'll come back to the question of possibility afterward.
I have no objection. Proceed.

First, I think that if our rulers and auxiliaries deserve their titles, the auxiliaries must be willing to obey and the rulers must have the power to command. The rulers must follow the laws themselves and embody their spirit in whatever details they oversee.
That's right, he said.

As their legislator, you who selected the men will now select the women. Choose women as similar in nature to the men as possible. They'll live in common houses, eat at common meals. None will have anything private. They'll be together and exercise together. And the natural consequence of all this togetherness will be that they'll be drawn to each other. 'Necessity' isn't too strong a word, I think?
Not mathematical necessity, he said, but the other kind — the necessity of attraction, which lovers understand. That kind of necessity is far more persuasive for most people.
True, I said. But this, Glaucon, like everything else, must proceed in an orderly way. In a city of the blessed, unregulated sexual relations would be unholy, and the rulers will forbid them.
Yes, and rightly so, he said.
Then clearly, the next step is to make marriages as beneficial as possible. And marriages will be deemed sacred?
Exactly.
But what makes marriages most beneficial? Let me ask you something — I notice you keep hunting dogs and fine birds at home. Have you ever paid attention to their breeding?
In what way?
Well, even though they're all good stock, aren't some better than others?
True.
And do you breed from all of them indiscriminately, or do you select only the best?
Only the best.
And do you breed from the very youngest or the very oldest, or only those in their prime?
Only those in their prime.
And if you didn't breed carefully, your dogs and birds would deteriorate badly?
Certainly.
The same goes for horses and other animals?
Undoubtedly.
Good heavens, my friend! I said. What extraordinary skill our rulers will need if the same principle applies to humans!
It certainly does apply. But why does it require extraordinary skill?

Because, I said, our rulers will often need to use medicines on the body politic. When patients only need a change of diet, an ordinary doctor will do. But when actual medicine is required, you need a bolder practitioner.
That's true, but what are you getting at?
I mean that our rulers will need to employ a good deal of deception and manipulation for the benefit of their subjects. We said earlier that such tools, used as medicines, could be beneficial.
And we were right.
And this 'medicine' will be especially necessary in regulating marriages and births.
How so?

We've already established that the best should mate with the best as often as possible, and the worst with the worst as seldom as possible. The offspring of the first pairing should be raised, while the offspring of the second should not, if we want to keep the flock in top condition. All of this must be kept secret from everyone except the rulers, or our guardian 'herd' will break into rebellion.
Very true.

So we should establish festivals where we bring brides and grooms together, with sacrifices and wedding songs composed by our poets. The number of marriages will be left to the rulers' discretion, since they'll need to maintain a stable population size while accounting for wars, diseases, and other factors.
Certainly, he said.
We'll need to devise some ingenious lottery system so that the less worthy can blame their bad luck rather than the rulers when pairings are made.
Of course, he said.

And our bravest and best young men, in addition to other honors and rewards, should have more opportunities to be with women. Their courage gives them the right, and such fathers should produce as many children as possible.
True.
The proper officials — whether male, female, or both, since women can hold offices too —
Yes —

will take the children of good parents to a special nursery with designated nurses in a separate quarter. But the children of inferior parents, or of superior parents who happen to be born defective, will be quietly disposed of in some secret place.
Yes, he said. That must be done if the guardian breed is to remain pure.

These officials will oversee the nursing. They'll bring the mothers to the nursery when they're full of milk, taking every precaution to prevent any mother from recognizing her own child. If more nurses are needed, they'll hire wet-nurses. They'll make sure nursing doesn't go on too long, and they'll assign all the nighttime care and hard work to nurses and attendants.
You're giving the guardians' wives an easy time when it comes to childbearing, he said.
As they should, I said. But let's continue with our plan. We said the parents should be in the prime of life?
Very true.
And what is 'the prime of life'? For women, roughly twenty years; for men, roughly thirty?
Which years exactly?
A woman should bear children for the state from age twenty to forty. A man should begin at twenty-five, when life's energy peaks, and continue until fifty-five.
Certainly, he said. Both physically and mentally, those are the prime years for both sexes.

Anyone outside these age ranges who participates in public breeding will be declared guilty of an unholy and impious act.
