Any child resulting from such a union — if one slips into existence — will have been conceived not under the auspices of the sacred ceremonies and prayers that priests, priestesses, and the whole city will offer at each wedding festival, asking that each new generation improve upon the last, but under the shadow of darkness and undisciplined desire.
Very true, he said.

The same law applies to anyone within the approved age range who has relations with a woman of childbearing age without the rulers' authorization. We'll declare that he's giving the state an illegitimate, uncertified, unconsecrated child.
Very true, he said.

Once men and women pass the age of childbearing, we'll set them free to be with whomever they wish — except that a man may not be with his daughter or granddaughter, or his mother or grandmother, and women may not be with their sons or fathers, or their grandsons or grandfathers. We'll grant this freedom along with strict instructions to prevent any pregnancies from coming to term. And if a child is somehow born despite these precautions, the parents must understand that such an offspring cannot be maintained.
That's reasonable, he said. But how will they know who their fathers and daughters are?

They won't. Here's how it works: counting from the day of the wedding, any male children born in the seventh to tenth month afterward will be called the groom's sons, and any female children his daughters. They'll call him father, and he'll call their children his grandchildren. All children born during the same period as one's own children will be called brothers and sisters. As I said, these 'siblings' won't be allowed to marry. However, if the lottery happens to pair them and the oracle at Delphi approves, the law will permit it.
Exactly right, he said.

So that's the plan, Glaucon, for how our guardians will share wives and children. Now we need to confirm that this arrangement is consistent with the rest of our political system and is in fact the best arrangement. Shall we?
Yes, certainly.

Let's start by asking ourselves: what should be the legislator's chief aim? What is the greatest good for a state, and what is the greatest evil? Then we can check whether our plan bears the stamp of good or evil.
By all means.
Can there be any greater evil than discord and division where there should be unity? Or any greater good than the bond of unity?
There cannot.
And unity exists where people share pleasures and pains — where all citizens rejoice or grieve at the same things?
No doubt.
But where there's only private feeling, not shared feeling, the state falls apart — with one half celebrating and the other mourning over the same events?
Certainly.
And these divisions typically originate in disputes about 'mine' and 'not mine,' 'his' and 'not his'?
Exactly.
And isn't the best-ordered state the one where the most people apply the words 'mine' and 'not mine' to the same things?
Absolutely.

The state that most resembles a single organism — like a body, where if a finger is hurt, the whole structure, organized around the soul as its center, feels the pain together. We say 'the person has a pain in their finger,' and the whole body shares in the suffering and relief. The best-ordered state has the closest approach to this kind of shared feeling.
Very true, he said. And I agree that in the best-ordered state, this common feeling comes closest to being realized.
So when any citizen experiences good or ill fortune, the whole state will treat it as their own, and will rejoice or grieve together?
That's how it must be in a well-ordered state, he said.
It's time for us to return to our state and see whether it embodies these principles better than any other.
Very good.
Like every other state, ours has rulers and subjects?
True.
And all will call each other 'citizens'?
Of course.
But what else do people in other states call their rulers, besides 'citizens'?
Usually 'masters.' In democracies, they just call them 'rulers.'
And in our state, what do the people call the rulers besides 'citizens'?
Saviors and helpers, he said.
And what do the rulers call the people?
Their providers and supporters.
And what do rulers in other states call the people?
Slaves.
And what do rulers call each other in other states?
Fellow-rulers.
And in ours?
Fellow-guardians.
In other states, have you ever heard a ruler call one colleague 'a friend' and another 'a stranger'?
Yes, very often.
He considers the 'friend' as someone in whom he has a personal stake, and the 'stranger' as someone he doesn't?
Exactly.
But would any of our guardians think of another guardian as a stranger?
Certainly not. Everyone they meet will be regarded as a brother, sister, father, mother, son, or daughter — or as the child or parent of such.

Excellent. But let me push further: will these just be empty titles, or will people actually live by them? Will they show the real respect, care, and obedience that the words 'father,' 'mother,' 'brother,' and 'sister' imply? Will anyone who violates these family duties be considered impious and likely to suffer at the hands of both gods and humans? Will these be the lessons that ring in children's ears from all the citizens about the people they're told are their relatives?
These and no others, he said. It would be ridiculous to mouth family titles without acting in their spirit.

Then in our city, more than any other, when anything happens to a citizen, everyone will say together: 'What happens to you, happens to me.' As I described before, when one citizen does well or poorly, the whole city will share that experience.
Very true.
And consistent with this way of thinking, didn't we say they'll share pleasures and pains in common?
Yes, and rightly so.
And they'll have a shared interest in what they each call 'my own' — and this shared interest will produce shared feelings of pleasure and pain?
Yes, far more than in other states.
And the reason for this, beyond the general constitution of the state, is the community of women and children among the guardians?
That will be the chief reason.
And we agreed that this unity of feeling is the greatest good — comparing a well-ordered state to a body whose parts share sensations of pleasure and pain?
We did, and rightly.
Then the community of wives and children among the guardians is clearly the source of the state's greatest good?
Certainly.

And this is consistent with our earlier principle that guardians should have no houses, land, or private property. Their pay was to be food from the other citizens, with no private expenses — to preserve their true character as guardians.
Right, he said.

Both the sharing of property and the sharing of families will make them more truly guardians. They won't tear the city apart by arguing over 'mine' and 'not mine' — each person dragging acquisitions into their private house, where they have a private wife and children and private pleasures and pains. Instead, all will be affected by the same pleasures and pains because they agree about what is near and dear to them, and they'll all work toward a common goal.
Certainly, he said.

And since they have nothing they can call their own except their own persons, there will be no lawsuits or complaints among them. All those quarrels that arise from money, children, or family relations will simply disappear.
Of course they will.
There won't even be assault or insult charges among them. We'll establish that equals should defend themselves against equals — making self-defense a matter of duty.
Good, he said.
Yes, and there's another benefit to this law: if someone has a grievance against another, he'll settle it on the spot rather than letting it escalate into something dangerous.
Certainly.
Older people will be charged with supervising and disciplining younger ones.
Obviously.

And the younger ones would never dare to strike or disrespect an elder, unless the authorities commanded it. There are two powerful deterrents: shame and fear. Shame prevents them from laying hands on those who are like parents to them. Fear of being immediately surrounded by others who are their brothers, sons, and fathers.
True, he said.
So in every way, these laws will keep the citizens at peace with each other?
Yes, very much so.
And since the guardians won't quarrel among themselves, there's no danger of the rest of the city dividing against them or against each other.
None whatever.

I hardly want to mention the petty troubles they'll be free from — they're beneath notice. Things like poor people flattering the rich, all the anxiety and stress of raising a family, borrowing money, scraping together household expenses, handing money to wives and slaves to manage — all the many familiar, obvious miseries of this sort.
Yes, he said. You don't need eyes to see those.
They'll be free from all of this, and their lives will be more blessed than even Olympic victors'.
How so?

Olympic victors are considered happy for winning only a fraction of what our guardians have won. Our guardians' victory is nobler — they've won the salvation of the entire state. The crown they and their children receive is a life fully supplied with everything they need. They receive honors from their country while alive, and after death they receive an honorable burial.
Yes, glorious rewards indeed, he said.

Do you remember, I said, how earlier someone — I won't name names — criticized us for making our guardians unhappy, since they had nothing while they could have had everything? We replied that if the occasion arose, we might revisit the question, but for now we were focused on making them true guardians and shaping the state for the happiness of the whole, not of any one class.
Yes, I remember.
And now that the guardians' life turns out to be far nobler and better than even Olympic victors' — can it really be compared to the life of shoemakers or any other workers?
Certainly not.

But I should repeat what I said before: if any guardian tries to achieve happiness in a way that stops him from being a guardian, if he's not content with this safe and harmonious life — which is, in my judgment, the best of all lives — but is seduced by some foolish, youthful notion of happiness into seizing the whole state for himself, then he'll learn how wise Hesiod was when he said: 'the half is more than the whole.'
If he asked my advice, I'd tell him to stay exactly where he is.

Then you agree, I said, that men and women should share a common way of life, as we've described — common education, common children. They'll guard the citizens together, whether staying in the city or going to war. They'll keep watch together and hunt together like dogs. In all things and in every way possible, women will share with men. In doing this, they'll be doing what's best and won't be violating but preserving the natural relationship between the sexes.
I agree, he said.
We still need to determine, I said, whether this kind of community is actually possible among humans, as it is among animals, and if so, how.
You've anticipated the very question I was about to ask.
There's no difficulty in seeing how they'll wage war, I said.
How?

They'll go on campaigns together and bring along any children old enough to observe, so they can watch the work they'll eventually do themselves — just as craftsmen's children watch and help before they practice the craft. Besides observing, the children will serve as helpers and attendants in war. Haven't you noticed how potters' children watch and assist long before they touch the wheel themselves?
Yes, I have.
And should potters be more careful about educating their children and giving them practical experience than our guardians?
That would be ridiculous, he said.
There's also the effect on the parents. Having their children present will be the greatest incentive to bravery, as it is for all animals.
True, Socrates. But there's a serious risk: if they lose the battle — which happens often in war — the children will be lost along with the parents, and the state will never recover.
True, I said. But would you never allow them to face any risk?
I'm not saying that.
Well, if they're ever going to face risks, shouldn't it be on occasions where surviving will make them better for it?
Obviously.
Whether future soldiers see war in their youth is extremely important — important enough to justify some risk.
Yes, very important.
So our first step is to bring children to observe war, while also ensuring their safety. Then everything will be fine.
True.
Their parents will presumably know, as far as human foresight allows, which expeditions are safe and which are dangerous?
We can assume so.
They'll take the children on the safe ones and be cautious about the dangerous ones?
True.
And they'll put the children under the command of experienced veterans who'll serve as their guides and teachers?
Very appropriate.
Still, the dangers of war can't always be predicted. There's always an element of chance.
True.
Then we must give the children wings from the start, so they can escape when necessary.
What do you mean? he said.

We must put them on horseback from their earliest youth. After they've learned to ride, we'll take them to observe battles. The horses should be gentle and fast rather than warlike — that way the children will get an excellent view of what they'll one day do, and if danger arises, they can follow their leaders and escape quickly.
I think you're right, he said.

Now, what about the treatment of enemies? What should the rules be for our soldiers among themselves and toward their opponents? First, any soldier who deserts his post or throws away his weapons or commits any other act of cowardice should be demoted to the rank of a craftsman or farmer. What do you think?
Absolutely.
And anyone who lets himself be taken prisoner might as well be handed over to the enemy as a gift. They can do whatever they want with him.
Certainly.
But the hero who distinguishes himself — what should happen to him? First, he'll be honored on the spot by all his young comrades, each crowning him in turn. Agreed?
Agreed.
And they'll shake his hand?
Agreed to that too.
But my next proposal you might not accept.
What is it?
That he should be kissed by them.

I'd go even further, he said. While the campaign lasts, no one he wants to kiss should be allowed to refuse. That way, if anyone has a lover in the army, man or woman, they'll be all the more eager to win the prize of valor.
Excellent, I said. And we've already established that the brave man gets more marriage opportunities than others and gets first pick, so he'll father as many children as possible.
Agreed.

And there are other ways to honor brave young warriors, as Homer describes. Ajax, after distinguishing himself in battle, was rewarded with extra cuts of meat — a fitting tribute for a hero in his prime, being both an honor and a source of strength.
Very true, he said.

We'll follow Homer's example on this point, I said. At sacrifices and similar occasions, we'll honor the brave according to their valor, whether men or women, with hymns and the other distinctions we mentioned, plus
'Seats of honor, and meats, and overflowing cups.'
And by honoring them this way, we'll also be training them.
Excellent, he said.
And when someone dies gloriously in war, shall we say first that he belongs to the golden race?
Certainly.
And we have Hesiod's authority for saying that when such people die,
'They become holy spirits on earth, guardians of good, protectors against evil, watchers over mortal humanity'?
Yes, we accept his authority.
We'll consult the oracle about how to bury these divine and heroic figures, and what special honors to give them, and then follow its instructions?
By all means.

And for all time, we'll revere their graves and worship at their tombs as heroes. The same honors will extend to anyone judged exceptionally good, whether they die in battle, of old age, or any other way.
Very right, he said.
Now, how should our soldiers treat their enemies?
In what respect?
First, slavery. Should Greeks enslave other Greeks, or should they prevent it as far as possible, keeping in mind that the entire Greek race might one day fall under barbarian domination?
Sparing them is infinitely better.
Then no Greek should be enslaved by our citizens, and they should advise other Greeks to do the same.
Certainly, he said. That way Greeks will be united against the barbarians and keep their hands off each other.

And what about the slain? Should the victors strip their bodies of anything besides armor? Doesn't the habit of looting the dead give cowards an excuse to avoid the actual fighting? Many armies have been lost because soldiers were busy plundering instead of fighting.
Very true.

And isn't there something petty, greedy, and almost cowardly about making an enemy of a dead body? The real enemy has fled, leaving behind only his equipment. It's like a dog that can't reach the person who threw a stone, so it bites the stone instead.
Very like a dog, he said.
Then we must forbid stripping corpses and preventing their burial?
Yes, we absolutely must.

And we won't display captured weapons in temples, especially Greek weapons — not if we want to maintain good relations with other Greeks. In fact, we should be concerned that dedicating spoils taken from fellow Greeks might be sacrilege, unless the god himself commands it.
Very true.
And what about devastating Greek territory or burning houses?
I'd like to hear your opinion, he said.
Both should be forbidden, in my view. We should take only the year's harvest and nothing more. Shall I explain why?
Please.

Because there's a meaningful difference between 'discord' and 'war,' and I believe their natures are also different. Discord is internal and domestic; war is external and foreign. The first we call discord; only the second deserves the name war.
That's a very proper distinction, he said.
And isn't it equally proper to say that the Greek race is united by blood and friendship, and that barbarians are alien and foreign to them?
Very good, he said.

So when Greeks fight barbarians, or barbarians fight Greeks, we'll call it war — they're natural enemies. But when Greeks fight Greeks, we'll say Greece is in a state of civil disorder and discord — since they're natural friends. Such conflict should be called discord, not war.
I agree.

Consider then: when discord occurs and a city is divided, if both sides destroy each other's lands and burn each other's houses, the conflict seems wicked and unpatriotic. No true patriot would destroy his own motherland. There might be reason for the victors to take the losers' harvest, but both sides should aim at eventual peace, not perpetual war.
Yes, he said, that's a much better attitude.
And the city we're founding will be a Greek city?
It should be, he said.
Then its citizens will be good and civilized?
Very much so.
And as Greeks, they'll love their fellow Greeks and think of Greece as their own land, sharing in common religious life?
Most certainly.
So any conflict among Greeks will be seen as discord — a quarrel among friends, not a war?
Certainly not a war.
And they'll quarrel as people who expect to reconcile eventually?
Certainly.
They'll correct each other as friends, not enslave or destroy — acting as correctors, not enemies.
Exactly.

Being Greeks themselves, they won't devastate Greek land, burn houses, or treat an entire city's population — men, women, and children — as their enemies. They know that the guilt of war belongs only to a few, while the many are their friends. For all these reasons, they won't waste the land or destroy homes. Their hostility will last only until the innocent majority forces the guilty few to make amends.
I agree, he said, that our citizens should treat Greek enemies this way — and treat barbarians the way Greeks currently treat each other.
Then let's add this law for our guardians: they shall neither devastate Greek land nor burn Greek houses.
Agreed. And we can agree that these rules, like all our previous ones, are very good.

But honestly, Socrates, if we let you keep going like this, you'll completely forget the question you pushed aside at the beginning: is such a state actually possible, and how? I'm ready to admit that if it could exist, it would bring every benefit you've described. I'll even add benefits you haven't mentioned — our warriors would be the bravest, since they'd all know each other and call each other father, brother, son. And if women fought alongside them, whether in the same ranks or in reserve, they'd be absolutely invincible. I also see all the domestic advantages and fully acknowledge them. But since I admit all this, we don't need to discuss benefits any further. Let's assume the state exists and focus on the question of possibility.

You've staged a sudden raid on my argument! I said. Just when I thought I'd escaped the first two waves! And you seem unaware that you're now sending the third and greatest wave crashing over me. Once you see and hear this one, I think you'll be more forgiving about my reluctance to tackle such an extraordinary proposal.
The more you protest, he said, the more determined we are. Tell us how such a state is possible. Speak!
Let me start by reminding you that we arrived here while searching for justice and injustice.
True, he said. But what of it?

I just want to ask: if we find what justice is, will we demand that the just person be a perfect embodiment of it? Or will we be satisfied with an approximation — with them coming closer to justice than anyone else?
The approximation will be enough.

Good. We were investigating the nature of perfect justice and perfect injustice, and their perfectly just and unjust representatives, as ideals. We wanted to use them as standards for judging our own happiness, not to prove they could literally exist.
True, he said.
Would a painter be any less skilled because, after creating an ideal portrait of a perfectly beautiful person, he couldn't prove such a person actually exists?
He'd be no less skilled.
Well, weren't we creating an ideal of a perfect state?
Of course.
And is our theory any worse because we can't prove such a city could actually be built exactly as described?
Not at all, he said.
That's the truth. But if you want me to try to show how and under what conditions the possibility is greatest, you'll need to grant me the same assumptions as before.
What assumptions?
Can ideals ever be perfectly realized in practice? Doesn't the actual always fall short of the ideal? Whatever anyone may think, isn't that in the nature of things? Do you agree?
I do.

Then don't insist that the actual state match the ideal in every detail. If we can discover how a city might be governed very nearly as we've described, you'll have to admit we've found the possibility you're asking for. Would that satisfy you? It would satisfy me.
Me too.

Next, let me try to identify the one defect in existing states that causes all their problems, and the smallest possible change that would transform a state into our ideal — one change if possible, or if not, two. The fewer changes, the better.
Certainly, he said.
I think one single change could do it, I said — though it's neither small nor easy. But it is possible.
What is it?
Now I face the wave I said was the greatest. But I'll say it, even if it crashes over me in a flood of mockery. Listen carefully.
Go on.

Unless philosophers become kings, or those who are now called kings and rulers come to be genuinely and thoroughly inspired by philosophy — unless political power and philosophical wisdom are united in the same persons, while those who currently pursue one without the other are compelled to step aside — there will be no end to the troubles of states, nor of the human race itself. Only then will this state we've been describing have any chance of coming to life and seeing the light of day. This is what I've been afraid to say, because I knew how utterly paradoxical it would sound. It's hard for people to accept that no other arrangement can bring happiness, whether in public or private life.

Socrates, do you realize what you've just said? Picture a crowd of very respectable people figuratively ripping off their jackets, grabbing whatever weapon is at hand, and charging at you full speed, ready to do who knows what. Unless you can mount a defense and get out of their way, they'll tear you to shreds with their sharp wit.
And you got me into this, I said.

True, and I was right to. But I'll do everything I can to get you out — I'll give you my goodwill, my encouragement, and perhaps I can answer your questions better than someone else. With this kind of support, do your best to show the skeptics you're right.

I'd better try, I said, since you're offering such powerful help. If we're going to escape, we need to explain to these skeptics whom we mean when we say philosophers should rule. Once we've made that clear, we can defend the claim by showing that certain people are naturally suited to pursue philosophy and lead the state, while others should leave philosophy alone and follow the leaders.
Time for a definition, he said.
Follow me, I said, and maybe I can give a satisfactory explanation.
Go on.
You'll remember — so I needn't remind you — that a true lover loves the whole of what he loves, not just a part.
Actually, I don't quite follow. Please remind me.

Someone else might get away with that, I said, but a man of your amorous experience should know that anyone in the bloom of youth stirs something in a passionate lover's heart. Isn't that your way with beautiful people? One has a turned-up nose, and you call it charming. Another has a hooked nose — you say it's 'regal.' A straight nose has 'perfect proportions.' Dark complexions are 'manly,' pale ones are 'divine.' The term 'honey-pale' itself was surely invented by a lover who revels in diminutives and doesn't mind a bit of pallor on youth's cheek. In short, you'll make any excuse and say anything rather than reject a single flower of youth's spring.
If you want to make me an authority on love for the sake of the argument, I'll accept.
And don't wine-lovers do the same? They'll seize any excuse to drink any wine.
Very true.
And ambitious people? If they can't command an army, they'll command a squadron. If they can't be honored by important people, they'll take honor from nobodies. But honor of some kind they must have.
Exactly.
Then answer me this: when someone desires something, do they desire the whole class or only part of it?
The whole.
Then the philosopher — the lover of wisdom — desires not just part of wisdom, but all of it?
Yes, all of it.

And someone who dislikes learning — especially when young and unable to distinguish good from bad — is not a philosopher or a lover of knowledge. Just as someone who refuses food isn't hungry — they have a bad appetite, not a good one.
Very true, he said.
But someone who has a taste for every kind of knowledge, who's curious to learn and is never satisfied — that person can rightly be called a philosopher, don't you think?

Glaucon said: If curiosity makes a philosopher, you'll end up with some strange philosophers. All the lovers of spectacles delight in learning and would qualify. And music enthusiasts are a peculiar addition to the ranks of philosophy — they're the last people you'd find at a philosophical discussion, but they'll run all over the country to hear every chorus perform at every festival, as if they'd rented out their ears. Are we going to call all these people philosophers, along with people who study trivial arts?
Certainly not, I said. They're only imitations of philosophers.
Then who are the true philosophers? he asked.
Those who love the vision of truth, I said.
That sounds right, he said, but what do you mean exactly?
It would be hard to explain to anyone else, I said, but I'm sure you'll grant me this.
Grant you what?
That since beauty is the opposite of ugliness, they are two distinct things?
Of course.
And since they're two, each is one?
True.

The same applies to just and unjust, good and evil, and every other form: each is one in itself. But through their various combinations with actions, objects, and each other, each appears in many different guises and seems to be many.
Very true.
This is the distinction I draw between the sight-lovers and art-lovers on one hand, and those who alone deserve the name 'philosopher' on the other.
How do you distinguish them? he said.
The lovers of sights and sounds, I said, enjoy fine tones, colors, shapes, and everything made from them. But their minds can't perceive or love absolute beauty itself.
True, he said.
And very few can attain the vision of beauty itself.
Very true.

Now consider someone who has a sense for beautiful things but no sense of beauty itself — someone who, even if guided toward that knowledge, can't follow. Is that person awake or dreaming? Think about it: isn't the dreamer, whether asleep or awake, the person who mistakes the copy for the real thing?
I'd certainly say such a person is dreaming.

But take the person who recognizes the existence of beauty itself and can distinguish the ideal from the things that participate in it, never confusing the one with the other. Is that person dreaming or awake?
Fully awake.
And can we say that the mind of the one who knows has knowledge, while the mind of the one who merely believes has opinion?
Certainly.
But if the person with mere opinion disputes our claim, can we calm them down without revealing that something is seriously wrong with their understanding?
We should certainly try, he said.

Then let's think of how to address them. We'll start by reassuring them that we welcome whatever knowledge they have, and we're glad they have it. But we'd like to ask a question: does the person who knows, know something or nothing? (You'll answer for him.)
I answer that he knows something.
Something that exists, or something that doesn't?
Something that exists. How could something nonexistent be known?
So we can be confident, from every angle we've examined, that what fully exists can be fully known, and what doesn't exist at all can't be known at all?
Absolutely certain.
Good. But if there's something that both exists and doesn't exist, it would occupy a middle ground between pure existence and pure nonexistence?
Yes, between them.
And since knowledge corresponds to existence and ignorance to nonexistence, there must be something corresponding to this middle ground — something between knowledge and ignorance?
Certainly.
Do we acknowledge that opinion exists?
Of course.
Is opinion the same faculty as knowledge, or a different one?
A different one.
So opinion and knowledge deal with different subjects, corresponding to their difference as faculties?
Yes.
Knowledge is related to what exists and aims to know what exists. But before going further, let me make a distinction.
What distinction?
Let me place faculties in their own category. They are powers in us — and in everything else — by which we do what we do. Sight and hearing, for instance, are faculties. Is my meaning clear?
Yes, I understand perfectly.

Here's how I think about them: I can't see faculties, so I can't distinguish them by color, shape, or any visible feature. I identify a faculty only by its domain and its result. If two faculties have the same domain and produce the same result, I call them the same. If they differ in either domain or result, I call them different. Would you agree with that approach?
Yes.
Good. Now tell me: is knowledge a faculty? And if so, which one?
Knowledge is certainly a faculty — the mightiest of all.
And is opinion also a faculty?
Of course. Opinion is the power by which we form opinions.
But didn't you agree just now that knowledge and opinion are not the same?
How could any thinking person identify what's infallible with what makes mistakes?
Excellent — that proves we clearly recognize them as distinct.
Yes.
So if knowledge and opinion are distinct faculties, they must have distinct domains?
That's certain.
The domain of knowledge is what exists — knowledge aims to know the nature of what is?
Yes.
And the function of opinion is to opine?
Yes.
Does opinion deal with the same subject as knowledge? Can the same thing be both known and merely opined?
No, he said. That's already been ruled out. If different faculties have different domains, and knowledge and opinion are different faculties, then they can't have the same domain.
So if the domain of knowledge is what exists, the domain of opinion must be something else?
Yes, something else.

Is nonexistence the domain of opinion? Or rather — how can you have an opinion about something that doesn't exist at all? When you form an opinion, isn't it always about something? Can you have an opinion about nothing?
Impossible.
Someone who has an opinion has an opinion about some one thing?
Yes.
But nonexistence isn't 'some one thing' — it's properly nothing?
True.
We assigned ignorance to nonexistence, and knowledge to existence?
True, he said.
So opinion is concerned neither with existence nor with nonexistence?
Neither.
And therefore opinion is neither knowledge nor ignorance?
It seems not.
Then is opinion beyond both of them — clearer than knowledge or darker than ignorance?
Neither.
So opinion strikes you as darker than knowledge but lighter than ignorance?
Yes, and by a significant margin.
And it falls between them?
Yes.
Then opinion is intermediate?
No question.

But didn't we say earlier that if something turned out to both exist and not exist simultaneously, it would lie in the interval between pure existence and pure nonexistence — and that the corresponding faculty would be neither knowledge nor ignorance but something between them?
True.
And something has now been found in that interval, which we call opinion?
Yes.

Then we still need to find the object that partakes of both existence and nonexistence, that can't properly be called either one — the thing that, once discovered, we can rightfully call the subject of opinion. We'll assign the extremes to the extreme faculties and the middle to the middle faculty.
True.

With this established, I'd like to ask the person who denies the existence of any absolute, unchanging form of beauty — the one who believes only in the many beautiful things, the lover of sights who can't stand being told that beauty is one, or that justice is one, or that anything has a single nature. Let me ask him: among all these many beautiful things, is there one that won't also appear ugly? Among all the just things, one that won't also seem unjust? Among all the holy things, one that won't also seem unholy?
No, he said. Everything beautiful will in some respect be found ugly, and the same goes for the rest.
And can't the many things that are 'doubles' also be 'halves' — doubles of one thing and halves of another?
Quite true.
And things called great, small, heavy, or light — can't they equally well be described by the opposite term?
True. Each will always have a claim to both descriptions.
Can any one of these many things be said to definitively be what it's called, rather than not be it?

They're like the riddles people tell at dinner parties, he said, or like the children's puzzle about the eunuch throwing something at the bat sitting on something. These things are riddles too — you can't pin them down as definitively being or not being, or both, or neither.

Then where should we place them? I asked. Can they have a better home than somewhere between pure existence and pure nonexistence? They're clearly not darker than nonexistence or more real than full existence.
That's exactly right, he said.
So it seems we've discovered that the many conventional ideas most people have about beauty and everything else are tossing about in a region halfway between pure existence and pure nonexistence.
We have.
And we agreed earlier that anything of this sort would be the subject of opinion, not of knowledge — this flux between existence and nonexistence caught by the intermediate faculty.
Exactly.

Then those who perceive many beautiful things but can't see beauty itself, and can't follow anyone who points the way to it — those who perceive many just things but not justice itself, and so on — such people have opinion but not knowledge?
That's certain.
But those who see the absolute, eternal, and unchangeable — they have knowledge, not mere opinion?
That can't be denied either.

The first group loves and embraces the objects of opinion; the second, the objects of knowledge. The first group, remember, are the ones who enjoyed beautiful sounds and sights but couldn't tolerate the existence of absolute beauty.
Yes, I remember.
Then would we be wrong to call them 'lovers of opinion' rather than 'lovers of wisdom'? And will they be very angry at us for saying so?
I'd tell them not to be angry. No one should be angry at the truth.
But those who love the truth in each thing are to be called lovers of wisdom — philosophers — not lovers of opinion.
Absolutely.

chapters.title: Book VI
paragraphs: So there you have it, Glaucon. After a long and exhausting argument, the true philosophers and the false ones have finally come into view.
I don't think the road could have been any shorter, he said.

I suppose not, I said. And yet I think we'd have gotten a clearer picture of both if we could have stuck to just this one question, without all the other issues still waiting for us — issues anyone must face who wants to understand how the life of the just really differs from the life of the unjust.
So what's the next question? he asked.

The obvious one, I said. Since only philosophers can grasp what is eternal and unchanging, while those who wander among shifting particulars are not philosophers — which of these two groups should rule our State?
How should we decide that?
Whichever group is better at guarding the laws and institutions of the State — let them be the guardians.
Very good.
And surely, I said, there's no question that the person who's meant to guard something should have eyes rather than be blind?
No question at all.

Now consider those who lack real knowledge of each thing as it truly is, who have no clear model in their souls, and who can't look — like a painter looks at his subject — toward what is absolutely true, referring back to it constantly as their standard when they establish laws about beauty, goodness, and justice, or guard and preserve the laws that already exist. Aren't such people essentially blind?
They really are in that condition, he replied.
Then should we make them our guardians, when there are others who match them in experience and fall short in no virtue, and who also know the truth of each thing?
There'd be no reason to reject people with this greatest of qualities, he said, unless they fail in some other way.
So let's work out, I said, how these same people can have both this knowledge and those other excellences.
By all means.

First, as we said at the start, we need to understand the philosopher's nature. And once we do, I think we'll agree that the same person can have all these qualities, and that only such people should rule the State.
What do you mean?
Let's take it as given that philosophical minds always love the kind of knowledge that reveals eternal reality — reality that doesn't shift with generation and decay.
Agreed.
And further, I said, let's agree that they love all of reality, every part of it, and won't willingly give up any portion — just as we said about the lover and the ambitious man.
True.
And if they're to be what we described, isn't there another quality they need?
What quality?
Truthfulness. They'll never willingly let falsehood into their minds. They hate it, and they love the truth.
Yes, that's certainly true of them.
Not just 'certainly true,' my friend — necessarily true. Anyone who is passionate about something can't help loving everything related to the object of that passion.
Right, he said.
And is there anything more closely related to wisdom than truth?
How could there be?
Can the same person love both wisdom and falsehood?
Never.
So the true lover of learning must, from his earliest years, pursue truth in every form?
Absolutely.
But we also know from experience that when someone's desires run strongly in one direction, they run more weakly in others — like a stream diverted into another channel.
True.

So the person whose desires are channeled toward knowledge in every form will be absorbed in the pleasures of the soul and will barely feel bodily pleasure — if he's a genuine philosopher and not a pretender.
That's absolutely certain.
A person like that will naturally be moderate and free from greed. The motives that drive other people to chase and spend money simply don't exist in his character.
Very true.
There's another mark of the philosophical nature we should consider.
What's that?
There must be no hidden corner of small-mindedness. Nothing is more opposed to a soul that constantly reaches for the wholeness of things, both divine and human, than pettiness.
Absolutely true, he replied.
And someone who possesses greatness of mind and contemplates all of time and all of existence — can such a person think human life is anything very important?
He can't.
So he won't consider death something to be feared?
No indeed.
Then a cowardly and small-natured person has no place in true philosophy?
Certainly not.
And someone who is well-balanced, neither greedy nor petty, neither boastful nor cowardly — can that person ever be unjust or harsh in his dealings?
Impossible.
So when you're trying to spot the philosophical nature in someone young, you'll look for whether he's just and gentle, or rude and antisocial. Those are the telltale signs.
True.
There's another point to note.
What's that?
Whether he takes pleasure in learning. No one will love something that causes him pain and in which he makes little progress despite great effort.
Certainly not.
And if he's forgetful and retains nothing of what he learns — won't he be like an empty vessel?
Of course.
Working hard for nothing, he'll end up hating himself and his fruitless activity.
A soul that can't retain knowledge doesn't belong among genuine philosophical natures. We have to insist that the philosopher has a good memory.
Certainly.
And an unharmonious, graceless nature can only tend toward disproportion?
Undoubtedly.
Do you think truth is more akin to proportion or to disproportion?
To proportion.
Then, besides the other qualities, we should look for a naturally well-proportioned and graceful mind, one that moves instinctively toward the true nature of everything.
Certainly.
So don't all these qualities we've been listing go together? Aren't they all necessary for a soul that is to have a full and complete grasp of reality?
They're absolutely necessary, he replied.
And isn't this a pursuit beyond criticism — one that only a person with a good memory, a quick mind, nobility, grace, and a kinship with truth, justice, courage, and temperance can follow?
Not even the god of jealousy could find fault with such a pursuit, he said.
And to people like this, I said — once perfected by years and education — and to them alone, you would entrust the State.

Here Adeimantus broke in and said: No one can actually argue against what you're saying, Socrates. But here's the thing — whenever you talk like this, your listeners get a strange feeling. They think they're being led astray step by step, each concession seeming small, until the little steps pile up and by the end they find their original position has been completely overturned. Like amateur players of checkers who get boxed in by more skilled opponents and can't make a move — your listeners feel trapped. They have nothing to say in this game where words are the pieces, yet they remain convinced they're right. The point I'm making is this: anyone listening could say that while he can't counter you at each step of the argument, what he actually sees is that people who take up philosophy and stick with it beyond their schooling years — most of them turn into complete eccentrics, if not outright rogues. Even the best of them are made useless to society by the very pursuit you praise so highly.
And do you think those who say that are wrong?
I can't say, he replied; but I'd like to know what you think.
My answer is that they're quite right.
Then how can you justify saying that cities won't be free of evil until philosophers rule them, when we've just agreed that philosophers are useless to cities?
That's a question, I said, that can only be answered with a parable.
Right, Socrates — and parables are something you're clearly not at all used to, he said with a smile.

I see you're enjoying watching me flounder in this impossible discussion, I said. But hear the parable, and then you can enjoy the clumsiness of my metaphor even more. The way the best philosophers are treated in their own states is so appalling that nothing else on earth compares, which is why I have to piece together an image from several different things. Imagine a ship, then, whose captain is taller and stronger than any of the crew, but somewhat deaf, somewhat shortsighted, and whose knowledge of navigation isn't much better. The sailors are all quarreling about who should steer. Each one thinks he has the right, though none of them has ever learned navigation and none can name his teacher or say when he studied it. In fact, they insist navigation can't be taught, and they're ready to tear apart anyone who says otherwise. They crowd around the captain, begging and pleading for control of the helm. When they don't get their way, they kill or throw overboard whoever does. Then they drug the worthy captain with drink or something stronger, seize the ship, help themselves to the stores, and sail along eating and drinking exactly as you'd expect such people to sail. What's more, the man who's best at helping them overthrow the captain — whether through force or cunning — they call a true sailor, a real pilot, a man who knows ships. Anyone else they dismiss as useless. They have no conception that the true pilot must study the seasons, the sky, the stars, and the winds — that he must understand these things if he's actually going to command a ship, regardless of whether anyone else wants him to. They've never even considered that such knowledge could be combined with the art of steering. Now, on a ship run by mutineers — how will the true pilot be regarded? Won't they call him a stargazer, a useless babbler, a good-for-nothing?
Of course, said Adeimantus.
I don't think you need me to spell out the parable, I said. You can see that it describes the true philosopher's relationship to the State.
Certainly.
So take this parable to whoever is surprised that philosophers get no respect in their cities. Explain it to him and try to convince him that it would be far more surprising if they did get respect.
I will.

Tell him this: he's right that the best philosophers are useless to the world. But tell him to blame their uselessness on the people who refuse to use them, not on the philosophers themselves. It's not natural for the pilot to beg the sailors to accept his command. That's not how it works. And the clever saying that 'the wise go knocking at rich men's doors' — the author of that was lying. The truth is this: when you're sick, you go to the doctor, whether you're rich or poor. And when you need to be governed, you go to the person who can govern. It makes no sense for the ruler to beg his subjects to be ruled. You'd be right to compare our present rulers to the mutinous sailors, and the true philosophers to the pilots they dismiss as useless stargazers.
Exactly, he said.

For these reasons, and among people like these, philosophy — the noblest of all pursuits — is unlikely to be valued by those on the other side. But the worst damage to philosophy isn't done by its opponents. It's done by its own supposed followers — the very people your accuser was talking about when he said that most of them are total rogues and the best are useless. And I agreed with him.
Yes.
And we've now explained why the good ones are useless?
True.
Shall we go on to show why the majority inevitably become corrupt — and that this too shouldn't be blamed on philosophy?
By all means.

Let's work through this step by step. Remember, we started by describing the nature of the philosopher. He follows truth as his leader in everything. If he falls short of that, he's a fraud and has no genuine connection to philosophy.
Yes, that was what we said.
Isn't this one quality alone sharply at odds with what people currently think about philosophers?
It certainly is, he said.

And haven't we a right to defend the philosopher by saying this: the true lover of knowledge always strives toward being — that's his nature? He won't rest in the world of shifting appearances. He'll press on — his desire won't fade and his edge won't be dulled — until he grasps the true nature of each thing with the part of his soul that's fit to grasp it. And when he approaches true reality, mingles with it, and generates understanding and truth, then at last he knows, truly lives, and is nourished. Then, and only then, does his labor end.
Nothing could be more accurate, he said.
And will the love of falsehood be any part of his nature? Won't he utterly hate it?
He will.
And when truth leads the way, we can't suspect any evil in the company that follows?
Impossible.
Justice and a sound mind will be in that company, with temperance right alongside?
True, he replied.

And there's really no need for me to parade the philosopher's virtues again. You'll remember we said courage, greatness of mind, quick comprehension, and memory were his natural gifts. And you objected that while no one could deny these claims in the abstract, when you look at actual philosophers, most of them are clearly useless and the majority are thoroughly bad. We were investigating the reasons for this accusation, and that's brought us back to examining what corrupts the philosophical nature and why so many are ruined.
Exactly.

We now need to consider the corruptions of the philosophic nature — why so many are spoiled and so few survive. I mean those we called useless rather than wicked. After that, we'll look at the imitators who set themselves up as philosophers without deserving the title, and who, through their inconsistencies, bring down the universal contempt that people heap on philosophy and all philosophers.
What corruptions are you talking about? he said.
I'll try to explain. Everyone would agree that a nature with all the qualities we required in a philosopher is a rare thing — seldom found among human beings.
Rare indeed.
And think how many powerful forces conspire to destroy these rare natures!
What forces?

First — and this is the strangest part — their own virtues. Their courage, their temperance, every one of the qualities we praised: these very things corrupt and pull away from philosophy the soul that possesses them.
That is strange, he replied.
Then there are all the ordinary advantages people value — beauty, wealth, physical strength, powerful family connections. You know the kind of thing. These also corrupt and distract.
I understand the general idea, but I'd like you to be more precise.
Grasp the principle as a whole, I said, and the earlier points won't seem strange anymore. They'll make complete sense.
How should I do that? he asked.

Think of it this way, I said. We know that any seed or young growth — plant or animal — when it doesn't get the right nourishment, climate, or soil, suffers more the stronger it is. Bad conditions are a worse enemy to what's excellent than to what's mediocre.
Very true.
So it makes sense that the finest natures, placed in hostile conditions, take more damage than inferior ones. The greater the nature, the greater the contrast with its surroundings.
Certainly.

So, Adeimantus, isn't it the case that the most gifted minds, when badly educated, become the worst criminals? Don't great evils and pure wickedness spring from powerful natures that have been ruined, rather than from weak ones? A weak nature is never responsible for anything very great — whether good or evil.
I think you're right there.

The same goes for our philosopher. He's like a plant that must grow into every virtue if properly nurtured, but that becomes the most poisonous of weeds if sown in alien soil — unless some divine power preserves him. Now, do you really believe what people commonly say — that young people are corrupted by individual Sophists who teach them privately? Does that actually matter much? Aren't the people who say these things the greatest Sophists of all? Don't they themselves educate young and old, men and women, and shape everyone to their liking?
When does this happen? he said.

Whenever the crowd gathers — in an assembly, a courtroom, a theater, an army camp, or any other public gathering — and there's a huge uproar. They cheer some things that are said or done, they jeer at others, always exaggerating wildly, shouting and clapping while the echo of the space doubles the noise. In that moment, what young person's heart isn't going to pound? What private education could hold firm against that flood of popular opinion? Won't he be swept along with the current? Won't he end up calling good and evil whatever the crowd calls good and evil — doing what they do, becoming what they are?
Inevitably, Socrates. He'd have no choice.
And yet, I said, there's an even greater pressure we haven't mentioned.
What's that?
The not-so-gentle force of property seizure, imprisonment, or death — which these great educators, the public, apply when their words aren't enough to persuade.
They certainly do — and they mean it.
So what individual Sophist, what private teacher, could possibly hold out against such overwhelming force?
None, he replied.

None at all, I said. Even to try is sheer folly. There has never been — there is not now — there never will be a character shaped by any teaching that runs counter to the education imposed by the public. I'm speaking of human virtue only, my friend. Divine virtue, as the saying goes, is a different matter. You can be sure that if anything is saved and turns out well under our present corrupt governments, it is saved by the power of God.
I quite agree, he replied.
Then let me ask you to agree on one more point.
What are you going to say?

Consider this: all those hired teachers whom the public calls Sophists and treats as rivals are really teaching nothing but the public's own opinions — the views that emerge from their assemblies. And these teachers call that wisdom. It's as if someone were studying a large and powerful animal he had to tend — learning when it gets angry and when it calms down, what sounds soothe it and what sounds provoke it, how to approach and handle it — and after mastering all this through long experience, he called this knowledge wisdom, organized it into a system, and started teaching it. But he'd have no real understanding of which of the creature's desires and opinions are noble or shameful, good or evil, just or unjust. He'd simply use those labels according to the beast's reactions — calling good whatever pleases it and evil whatever annoys it — with no other basis for these distinctions at all. He'd call the necessary things just and noble, never having understood how fundamentally different necessity and goodness really are. Wouldn't that be a remarkable educator?
Remarkable indeed.

Now, is there any difference between that person and the one who thinks wisdom consists in understanding the moods and tastes of the masses — whether in painting, music, or politics? Whenever anyone mingles with the crowd and makes them his judges — beyond what's strictly necessary — the so-called 'compulsion of Diomedes' will force him to produce whatever they praise. But has anyone ever offered a reason for calling these popular tastes genuinely good or beautiful that wasn't utterly absurd?
No, and I don't expect to.

So you see the truth of what I've been saying? Now consider this: can the masses ever be brought to believe in the existence of absolute beauty as opposed to the many beautiful things, or in the absolute form of anything as opposed to its many instances?
Certainly not.
Then the masses can never be philosophers?
Impossible.
And so philosophers must inevitably face the masses' disapproval?
They must.
And the disapproval of individuals who associate with the mob and try to please them?
That's obvious.

Given all this, do you see any way for the philosophical nature to be preserved and to stay true to its calling? Remember what we said: he was supposed to have quickness, memory, courage, and greatness of mind.
Yes.
Won't such a person excel at everything from childhood, especially if his physical gifts match his mental ones?
Certainly, he said.
And his friends and fellow citizens will want to use him for their own purposes as he gets older?
No question.
They'll fall at his feet, showering him with flattery and honors, because they want to secure in advance the power he'll someday hold.
That often happens, he said.

So what will such a man probably do — especially if he's a citizen of a great city, rich, well-born, and tall and handsome to boot? Won't he be swollen with limitless ambition, convinced he's fit to manage the affairs of Greeks and foreigners alike, puffing himself up with vain pride and empty grandeur?
He certainly will.

And if, while he's in this state of mind, someone approaches him gently and tells him the truth — that he's actually foolish and needs to acquire real understanding, which can only be gotten through hard work — do you think he'll be eager to listen, given all these influences working against it?
Not at all.

And even if someone, through natural goodness or sound judgment, does have his eyes opened a little and is humbled and drawn toward philosophy — how will his friends react when they see themselves losing the advantage they expected from his company? Won't they do and say anything to prevent him from yielding to his better nature? They'll work against his teacher too — through private schemes and public prosecutions if necessary.
No doubt about it.
Then how can someone in these circumstances ever become a philosopher?
It's impossible.

So were we not right in saying that the very qualities which make a person philosophical can, if he's poorly educated, pull him away from philosophy? And that wealth, status, and the rest of life's supposed advantages do the same?
We were quite right.

And that, my friend, is how the ruin comes about — the ruin of natures best suited for the best of all pursuits. These natures are rare to begin with. And from this same type come both the greatest benefactors of humanity and the greatest destroyers — depending on which way the current carries them. A small nature never does anything truly great, either for individuals or for states.
That is absolutely true, he said.

And so philosophy is left abandoned, her marriage incomplete. Her true partners have deserted her and gone off to live false, unworthy lives. Meanwhile, others who don't deserve her — seeing she has no family to protect her — move in, abuse her, and heap on her the very reproaches you mentioned: that her followers are either worthless or, in most cases, thoroughly bad.
That's certainly what people say.

And what else would you expect? I said. Think of all the petty characters who see this territory open — a field rich with impressive titles and grand appearances — and leap into philosophy from their trades, like prisoners escaping into a sanctuary. They're probably the cleverest at their own miserable crafts. But even in its degraded state, philosophy retains a dignity that the other arts lack. And that dignity attracts many whose natures are flawed and whose souls are warped by their occupations, just as their bodies are warped by their trades. Isn't this inevitable?
Yes.

They're exactly like a bald little tinker who's just gotten out of prison and come into money. He takes a bath, puts on a new suit, and dresses himself up as a bridegroom — about to marry his master's daughter, who's been left poor and alone.
A perfect parallel.
What kind of offspring will come from such a marriage? Won't they be base and illegitimate?
Absolutely.

And when people who are unworthy of education attach themselves to philosophy — which is above their station — what kind of ideas and opinions will they produce? Won't they be mere sophisms that may sound impressive but contain nothing genuine, nothing truly worthy of wisdom?
No doubt, he said.

So, Adeimantus, only a very small remnant of worthy followers of philosophy will survive. Perhaps someone of noble character detained in exile and kept free from corrupting influences remains devoted to her. Or a great soul born in a small city whose politics he rightly despises and ignores. A gifted few may come from other professions that they justly look down on. And perhaps some are held back by Theages' bridle — everything in Theages' life was pushing him toward politics, but his poor health kept him from it. My own case — the inner sign that guides me — is barely worth mentioning; it's been given to almost no one else. Those who belong to this small group have tasted how sweet and blessed philosophy truly is. They've also seen clearly enough the madness of the masses. They know that no one in politics is honest, and that there's no ally with whom they could fight for justice and survive. Such a person is like someone who's fallen in among wild animals: he won't join in their savagery, but he can't fight them all alone. He'd be killed before he could do the world any good. So he holds his peace and goes his own way — like someone who steps under the shelter of a wall during a storm of dust and driving rain. Watching the rest of humanity drenched in wickedness, he's content if he can somehow keep himself clean from injustice and impiety, and depart this life at peace, with good will and bright hope.
Well, he said, that's no small achievement before he goes.
No small achievement — but not the greatest either, unless he finds a State that suits him. In the right State, he would grow even greater and become the savior of his country as well as of himself.
I think we've now explained well enough why philosophy has such a bad reputation. The charges against her are unjust — have I covered that sufficiently, or would you like to add anything?
Nothing more on that subject, he replied. But which of the existing governments do you think is suited to philosophy?

Not one of them, I said. And that's exactly my complaint against them — none of our existing states is worthy of the philosophical nature. That's why it gets twisted and corrupted. It's like an exotic seed planted in foreign soil: it loses its character and is overpowered by its surroundings. But if philosophy ever finds a state as perfect as she herself is, then it will be clear that she is truly divine, and that everything else — human natures and institutions alike — is merely mortal. And now I know you're going to ask: what is that state?
Actually, no, he said — you're wrong about that. I was going to ask whether it's the state we've been founding in this conversation, or some other one.

Ours, in most respects, I replied. But you may remember that we said there would always need to be some living authority in the State who holds the same understanding of the constitution that guided you, as legislator, when you were laying down the laws.
That was said, he replied.
Yes, but not satisfactorily. You frightened us with your objections, which made clear that the discussion would be long and difficult. And what still remains to discuss is anything but easy.
What remains?
The question of how the study of philosophy can be organized so that it doesn't destroy the State. All great undertakings carry risk. As they say, what's good is hard.
Still, he said, let's clear this up. That will make the inquiry complete.

If anything stops me, I said, it won't be lack of desire but lack of ability. You can see how eager I am. And notice how boldly and even recklessly I'm about to declare that the State should pursue philosophy in a completely different way than it does now.
What way?

As things stand now, I said, students of philosophy are far too young. They pick it up barely past childhood, dabbling in it during whatever time they can spare from money-making and housekeeping. Even the ones who are considered the most philosophically inclined give up when they hit the real difficulty — I mean dialectic. Later in life, if someone invites them, they might attend the occasional lecture, and they make a big deal out of that — but they don't treat philosophy as their real business. And by old age, most of them are snuffed out more thoroughly than the sun of Heraclitus — because unlike his sun, they never rekindle.
What should they do instead?

The exact opposite. In childhood and youth, their studies and their philosophy should be suited to their age. During their growing years, the main focus should be on developing their bodies, so they have strong bodies to serve them later when philosophy demands their full attention. As they mature and their minds begin to ripen, increase the exercise of the soul. And when their physical strength fades and they're past the age for civic and military duties — then let them roam freely in the pastures of philosophy, devoting themselves to nothing else, if they're meant to live happily here and crown this life with equal happiness in the next.
You really are in earnest, Socrates! he said. I can see that. But most of your listeners, I think, will resist you even more earnestly and never be convinced. Thrasymachus least of all.

Don't stir up trouble between Thrasymachus and me, I said. We've only just become friends — not that we were ever really enemies. I'll keep trying until I either convert him and everyone else, or at least do them some good for the day when they live again in another existence and encounter arguments like these.
You're talking about a time rather far off.

Not far at all, I replied, compared to eternity. But I'm not surprised that most people refuse to believe what we're saying. They've never seen it realized. What they've seen are artificial combinations of words that try to sound philosophical — not words like ours that grow naturally from the argument. They've never seen a real human being molded as perfectly as possible into the image of virtue, living in a city worthy of him — not one, let alone many. Have they?
Never.

And they've rarely if ever heard truly free and noble speech — the kind uttered by people who are genuinely seeking truth for its own sake, who care nothing for the clever disputations that end in nothing but opinion and quarrel, whether in courts or in social gatherings.
They're strangers to such talk, he said.

And this is exactly what we foresaw. This is why truth compelled us to say — reluctantly, and with some fear — that neither states nor individuals will ever reach perfection until that small class of philosophers we called useless but not corrupt are somehow compelled to take charge of the State, or until kings, or the sons of kings, are genuinely inspired with a true love of true philosophy. I see no reason to declare either possibility impossible. If they were, we could fairly be dismissed as dreamers. Isn't that right?
Quite right.

If, then, in the countless ages of the past, or right now in some distant land beyond our knowledge, the perfect philosopher has been or is being compelled by fate to take charge of a state — then we're ready to insist that our constitution has existed, does exist, and will exist whenever Philosophy is queen. It's not impossible. We admit it's difficult.
That's my view as well, he said.
But you'd say the majority disagrees?
I'd imagine so, he replied.

My friend, I said, don't attack the majority. They'll change their minds if you approach them not aggressively but gently, soothing their hostility toward education, showing them what real philosophers are actually like — describing their character and calling as you were just doing. When people see philosophers in this light, they'll surely revise their opinions. Who would remain hostile to someone who bears them no malice? Who would be jealous of someone free from jealousy? Let me answer for you: a few might hold onto their bitterness, but the majority of people won't.
I quite agree, he said.

And don't you think, as I do, that the hostility most people feel toward philosophy comes from the pretenders — people who barge in uninvited, constantly complaining and attacking each other, turning philosophy into a contest between personalities instead of a search for truth? Nothing could be less worthy of philosophy.
Nothing could be less worthy.

For the person whose mind is fixed on true reality, Adeimantus, has no time to look down at the petty affairs of men, or to fill himself with envy and hostility by fighting against them. His gaze is always directed upward, toward things that are fixed, unchanging, and orderly — things that neither harm nor are harmed by one another but exist in perfect rational harmony. He imitates these things and makes himself as much like them as he can. Don't you think a person becomes like whatever he spends his time admiring?
That's inevitable.
So the philosopher, holding communion with what is divine and orderly, becomes orderly and divine himself — as far as human nature allows. Though he'll still face plenty of slander, of course.
Of course.

And if he's called upon to shape not only himself but human nature in general — in states and in individuals — molding it according to the pattern he sees in that higher realm, will he be a clumsy craftsman of justice, temperance, and every civic virtue?
Anything but clumsy.

And if people realize that what we're saying about him is true, will they be angry at philosophy? Will they refuse to believe us when we say that no state can be happy unless its constitution is designed by artists who work from the divine pattern?
They won't be angry if they understand, he said. But how would these artists go about their work?

They'd begin by taking the State and human character as a kind of canvas, and they'd wipe it clean. That's no easy task. But this is what distinguishes them from every other reformer — they won't touch either individuals or institutions until they've either found or created a clean surface.
They'd be quite right, he said.
Having done that, they'd start sketching the outline of a constitution.
No doubt.

And as they fill in the picture, I imagine they'd constantly look back and forth — first at absolute justice, beauty, and temperance, then at the human version they're creating. They'd mix and blend the various elements of life into the image of a true human being, guided by that quality which Homer calls, when it appears among men, the form and likeness of God.
Very true, he said.
They'd erase one feature and paint in another, over and over, until they'd made human character as close as possible to the divine pattern.
Indeed, he said, they couldn't produce a finer picture than that.

So are we starting to win over those opponents you described — the ones who were charging at us with full force? Are they getting any calmer now that we've shown them what kind of artist designs constitutions — the very person they were so furious about when we put the State in his hands?
Much calmer, if they have any sense.
Where can they still find grounds for objection? Will they deny that the philosopher is a lover of truth and reality?
That would be unreasonable.
Or that his nature, as we've described it, is akin to the highest good?
They can't deny that either.
Will they insist that such a nature, given favorable conditions, won't become perfectly good and wise? Would they prefer the people we rejected?
Surely not.
Then will they still be angry at our saying that until philosophers rule, neither states nor individuals will have any rest from evil, and our ideal state will never be realized?
I think they'll be less angry.
Shall we say they're not just less angry but actually quite gentle — that they've been won over and, if only out of embarrassment, can't refuse to agree?
By all means, he said.
Good, let's take that as settled. Now, will anyone deny that sons of kings or princes might be born with philosophical natures?
No one could deny that, he said.
And once they exist, is there any reason they must inevitably be corrupted? We admit they're hard to save — but will anyone claim that across all of time, not a single one could survive?
Who could say that!
But one is enough, I said. Let one man like this gain a city that's willing to obey him, and he could bring the ideal state into being — the one the world finds so incredible.
Yes, one is enough.
If the ruler established the laws and institutions we've described, and the citizens were willing to obey — that's at least possible?
Certainly.
And that other people might approve of what we approve — that's no miracle or impossibility?
I think not.
And we've already shown at length that all this, if possible, is certainly for the best.
We have.
So our conclusion is: not only would these laws be best if enacted, but their enactment, while difficult, is not impossible.
Very good.

Well then — painfully and with great effort we've finished that topic. What remains is to discuss how and through what studies the saviors of our constitution will be produced, and at what ages they should take up each study.
Certainly.

I was too clever earlier when I skipped over the thorny questions about women, procreation, and the appointment of rulers — I knew these would provoke jealousy and be hard to work out. But that cleverness didn't help much: I had to deal with them anyway. The women and children are now settled, but the question of rulers needs to be examined from scratch. We said, you'll recall, that they must love their country, must be tested by pleasures and pains, and must never, in hardship or danger or any crisis, lose their patriotism. Whoever failed the test was rejected; whoever came through pure, like gold in the refiner's fire, was to be made ruler and given honors in life and after death. That was the gist of it, but the argument averted its eyes and hurried past, afraid to stir up the difficulty we now face.
I remember perfectly, he said.
Yes, my friend, and at the time I shrank from saying what I'm about to say. But now let me say it boldly: the perfect guardian must be a philosopher.
Yes, let that be affirmed, he said.
And don't expect there to be many of them. The qualities we said were essential rarely come together in one person. They're usually found in fragments.
What do you mean? he said.

Think about it, I replied. Quick intelligence, memory, shrewdness, cleverness, and similar qualities don't often coexist with high spirits and greatness of mind. People who have these intellectual gifts tend not to live steady, orderly lives — they're pulled this way and that by their impulses, and all their stability drains away.
Very true, he said.

On the other hand, the steady, dependable types — the ones who are like rocks in battle, immovable in the face of fear — tend to be equally immovable when it comes to learning. They're sluggish, always yawning, always drowsy whenever anything intellectual is required of them.
Quite true.
But we said both kinds of qualities are needed in anyone who's to receive the highest education and hold any position of authority.
We certainly did, he said.
And this combination is rare?
Very rare.

So candidates must be tested not only through the hardships, dangers, and pleasures we mentioned earlier, but also through many kinds of study — to see whether their soul can handle the highest knowledge or whether it will break under the strain, just as bodies break under physical exertion.
That's the right way to test them, he said. But what do you mean by the highest knowledge?
You remember, I said, that we divided the soul into three parts and identified the natures of justice, temperance, courage, and wisdom?
If I'd forgotten that, he said, I wouldn't deserve to hear the rest.
And do you remember the qualification we added before discussing those virtues?
What qualification?

We said that to see them in their true perfection, we'd need to take a longer road. By that route, they would become fully clear. But we could also sketch them roughly at the level of our earlier discussion. You all said that would be good enough, and so we continued — but the result, it seemed to me, was far from precise. Whether you were satisfied is for you to say.
I thought — and the others agreed — that you gave us a reasonable account of them.

But my friend, I said, any account that falls short of the whole truth is not a reasonable measure. Nothing incomplete is the measure of anything, though people are too ready to settle for less and think they don't need to search further.
That's a common tendency in people who are lazy.
Yes, I said. And it's the very worst tendency in a guardian of the State and its laws.
True.

Then the guardian, I said, must take the longer road and work just as hard at learning as at physical training. Otherwise he'll never reach the highest knowledge — the one that most truly belongs to him, as we were just saying.
Wait, he said — is there something even higher than justice and the other virtues?

Yes, I said. And even for the virtues themselves, we can't settle for a rough sketch — we need the finished painting. Isn't it absurd to labor over trivial things until they're perfectly clear, but then not demand the highest precision for the highest truths?
Absolutely, he said. But do you think we'll let you off without asking what this highest knowledge is?

Ask away, I said. But I'm sure you've heard the answer many times. Either you've forgotten or you're being deliberately difficult. I suspect the latter. You've heard me say often enough that the Form of the Good is the highest knowledge, and that everything else — justice, beauty, all of it — only becomes useful and beneficial through its relationship to the Good. You must realize that if we don't know the Good, then knowing everything else is worthless. It's like possessing everything but lacking the one thing that gives everything else its value.
Of course not.
You also know that most people say pleasure is the good, while the more refined say it's knowledge?
Yes.
And you know that those who say knowledge can't explain what knowledge they mean, and end up having to say 'knowledge of the good'?
How absurd!
Absurd indeed, I said — to reproach us for not knowing the good and then to define it as 'knowledge of the good,' as if we understood them when they use the word 'good.'
Exactly right, he said.
And those who define the good as pleasure are in the same muddle — they're forced to admit that there are bad pleasures as well as good ones.
Certainly.
Which means they're admitting that the same things are both good and bad?
True.
So clearly this question is full of difficulties.
Full of them.

And here's another thing we can see: when it comes to justice and beauty, many people are content with appearances — they'll do, have, or seem to have what appears just or beautiful, even if it isn't real. But with the good? No one is satisfied with what merely appears good. Everyone wants the real thing. When it comes to the good, appearances are scorned by everyone.
Very true, he said.
