This, then — this thing that every soul pursues, making it the goal of all its actions, sensing that it exists but unable to grasp its nature, unable to achieve the same certainty about it as about other things, and therefore missing whatever value those other things might have — should the best men in our State, to whom everything is entrusted, remain in the dark about something this important?
Certainly not, he said.

I don't think anyone who doesn't understand how beauty and justice are connected to the good will make a very good guardian of them. And I suspect that without knowledge of the good, no one can truly know anything else.
That's a shrewd suspicion, he said.
And if our guardian has this knowledge, our State will be in perfect order?
Necessarily, he replied. But tell me, Socrates — do you think the good is knowledge, or pleasure, or something different from both?
There it is, I said. I knew all along that a demanding fellow like you wouldn't be satisfied with what other people think about these things.
Well, Socrates, he said, it doesn't seem right that someone who's spent his entire life studying philosophy should only be able to repeat other people's opinions without ever stating his own.
But does anyone have the right to speak with authority about what he doesn't know?
Not with the authority of certainty, he said. But he can share what he thinks, as an opinion.

Haven't you noticed, I said, that opinions without knowledge are poor, ugly things? The best of them are blind. People who hold a true opinion without understanding are no better than blind travelers who happen to be on the right road.
Very true.
So you'd rather see what's blind and crooked and base, when others can show you brightness and beauty?

Please, Socrates, said Glaucon, don't stop now, right when you're approaching the goal! If you give us even the kind of explanation you gave for justice, temperance, and the other virtues, we'll be satisfied.

So will I, my friend — more than satisfied. But I'm afraid I'll fail and make a fool of myself with my clumsy efforts. No, let's not try to define the good itself right now — that's too ambitious for the present moment. But I can tell you about the child of the good, the thing most like it. Would you like to hear about that? If not, we'll drop it.
By all means, he said. Tell us about the child, and you can owe us the parent.
I wish I could pay in full, I replied, instead of just giving you the interest. But take this account of the offspring as payment on account, and watch carefully that I don't accidentally cheat you.
We'll watch carefully. Go ahead.
First, I said, I need to establish common ground and remind you of something we've discussed before, and many other times.
What?
The familiar distinction: there are many beautiful things and many good things, and so on for every category — and we apply the word 'many' to all of them.
True, he said.
And then there is absolute beauty and absolute good — a single Form for each of those things we call 'many.' Each group of many things can be brought under one idea, which is the essence of each.
Very true.
The many things are seen but not known; the Forms are known but not seen.
Exactly.
And what is the organ by which we see visible things?
Sight, he said.
And we hear with hearing, I said, and perceive other things with the other senses?
True.
But have you ever noticed that sight is by far the most elaborate and expensive piece of engineering among the senses?
No, I hadn't thought about that, he said.
Then think about this: does hearing need anything beyond the ear and the sound — any third element — for hearing to take place?
Nothing at all.
And the same holds for most or all of the other senses — they don't need any additional element. Agreed?
Certainly.
But have you noticed that sight and visibility do require something extra?
What do you mean?

Sight resides in the eyes, and the person who has eyes wants to see. Color is present in the things to be seen. But unless there's a third element, specifically suited for this purpose, the eyes will see nothing and the colors will remain invisible.
What element are you talking about?
The one you call light, I replied.
True, he said.
So the bond between sight and visibility is a noble one — far nobler than the bonds connecting the other senses to their objects. And light itself is no ordinary thing.
Far from ordinary, he said.
And among the gods of heaven, which one is the lord of this element? Whose light is it that enables the eye to see and the visible to appear?
The sun, obviously — as you and everyone else would say.
Now, may I describe the relationship between sight and the sun in this way?
How?
Neither sight nor the eye that contains it is the sun.
No.
Yet of all the sense organs, the eye is the most sun-like?
By far.
And the power that the eye possesses is a kind of gift dispensed by the sun?
Exactly.
So the sun is not sight itself, but the cause of sight — recognized by sight?
True, he said.

This, then, is what I call the child of the good. The good produced the sun in its own likeness. What the good is in the realm of thought — in relation to mind and the objects of thought — the sun is in the visible world — in relation to sight and the objects of sight.
Can you spell that out a bit more? he said.
You know, I said, that when you look at things in the dark — lit only by moonlight or starlight — your eyes see dimly and seem almost blind, as if they had no clear vision at all.
Very true.
But when you look at things illuminated by the sun, you see them clearly?
Certainly.

Well, the soul works the same way. When it's directed toward what is illuminated by truth and reality, it perceives, understands, and seems full of intelligence. But when it turns toward the dim realm of becoming and perishing, it gropes around with mere opinions, shifting from one view to another, and seems to have no intelligence at all.
Just so.

Now, this thing that gives truth to the objects of knowledge and the power of knowing to the knower — I want you to call that the Form of the Good. It's the cause of knowledge and truth, insofar as truth is known. Beautiful as both knowledge and truth are, you'll be right to think of the Good itself as something even more beautiful. Just as light and sight can be called sun-like but are not the sun, so knowledge and truth can be called good-like but are not the Good. The Good holds an even higher place of honor.
What incredible beauty, he said — if it's the source of knowledge and truth and yet surpasses them in beauty! Surely you don't mean that the good is pleasure?
Don't even suggest it, I replied. But consider the image from another angle.
Which angle?
The sun, you'd agree, not only makes things visible but also gives them generation, nourishment, and growth — though the sun itself is not generation?
Certainly.
In the same way, the good not only makes things knowable but gives them their very being and essence — yet the good itself is not essence. It surpasses essence in dignity and power.
By the light of heaven! said Glaucon, with mock solemnity. What an extraordinary idea!
Blame yourself, I said. You're the one who forced me to share my thoughts.
Don't stop now. At the very least, finish the comparison with the sun, if there's anything left.
Oh, there's a great deal left, I said.
Then don't leave anything out, however small.
I'll try not to, I said. But I suspect quite a lot will have to be left out.
I hope not, he said.

Now picture this, I said. There are two ruling powers: one presides over the intellectual realm, the other over the visible realm. (I won't say 'heaven,' in case you think I'm playing word games.) Do you have this distinction — visible and intelligible — clearly in mind?
I do.

Now imagine a line divided into two unequal segments. Divide each segment again in the same ratio. The two main segments represent the visible and the intelligible. Now compare the subdivisions. In the visible realm, the first subdivision consists of images — by which I mean shadows, reflections in water, reflections on smooth polished surfaces, and things of that kind. Do you follow?
Yes, I follow.
The second subdivision of the visible includes the actual things of which those images are copies — the animals we see, the plants, and everything made by human hands.
Very good.
Would you say that these two subdivisions differ in their degree of truth — that copies stand to originals as the realm of opinion stands to the realm of knowledge?
Absolutely.
Now consider how the intelligible realm should be divided.
How?

Like this: in the lower subdivision, the soul uses the objects from the visible realm as images. It can only proceed by hypothesis, moving downward to a conclusion rather than upward to a first principle. In the higher subdivision, the soul moves beyond hypotheses, ascending to a first principle that is not hypothetical, proceeding through Forms alone — by means of Forms, through Forms, and ending in Forms.
I don't quite follow, he said.

Let me try again. You'll understand better with some examples. You know that students of geometry and arithmetic start by assuming certain things — odd and even numbers, the three kinds of angles, various figures. They treat these as known, adopt them as hypotheses, and don't bother to justify them to themselves or anyone else. Starting from these assumptions, they work through a consistent chain of reasoning until they reach their conclusion.
Yes, I know that, he said.

And you know that although they use visible shapes and reason about them, they're not really thinking about those particular drawings. They're thinking about the perfect square, the perfect diameter — the Forms that these drawings merely resemble. The figures they draw, which themselves have shadows and reflections, are used as images. But what they're really trying to grasp are the realities that can only be seen with the mind's eye.
That's true.

This is the kind of thing I called intelligible — but in pursuing it, the soul is forced to rely on hypotheses. It can't rise above the realm of hypothesis, so it uses physical objects (which themselves have copies further down the scale) as images. Relative to those lower copies, these objects are treated as clear and valuable, but the inquiry itself remains tethered to its assumptions.
I see, he said. You're talking about geometry and its sister disciplines.

And when I talk about the higher division of the intelligible, I mean the kind of knowledge that reason itself achieves through the power of dialectic. Here, hypotheses aren't treated as starting points but as genuine hypotheses — stepping stones and launching points into a realm that lies beyond hypothesis, where reason grasps the first principle of everything. Having seized that principle, reason then follows out everything that depends on it, descending step by step back down — but using nothing from the sensible world along the way. The entire journey proceeds through Forms, by means of Forms, and ends in Forms.

I think I understand you, he replied, though not perfectly — what you're describing sounds enormously ambitious. But let me say what I take you to mean. The knowledge that dialectic deals with — the knowledge of being and reality — is clearer than what the mathematical sciences achieve. Those sciences start from hypotheses and are grasped by understanding rather than by the senses. But because they don't ascend to a first principle, they fall short of true reason, even though their objects become knowable through reason when a first principle is supplied. I take it you'd call the mathematical way of thinking 'understanding' rather than 'reason' — placing it between mere opinion and full rational knowledge.

You've grasped my meaning exactly, I said. Now, assign four mental faculties to these four divisions: reason to the highest, understanding to the second, conviction to the third, and conjecture to the lowest. Arrange them proportionally — each faculty possessing as much clarity as its objects possess truth.
I understand, he replied. I agree and accept your arrangement.

chapters.title: Book VII
paragraphs: Now, I said, let me show you an image of how far human nature is enlightened or unenlightened. Picture people living in an underground cave with a long entrance open to the daylight. They've been there since childhood, with their legs and necks chained so they can't move, forced to look only straight ahead — the chains prevent them from turning their heads. Behind and above them, a fire blazes in the distance. Between the fire and the prisoners there's a raised walkway, and along it runs a low wall — like the screen that puppet-masters put up in front of themselves, over which they show their puppets.
I see.

Now imagine people walking along behind this wall, carrying all sorts of objects — statues, figures of animals made of wood and stone and other materials — that stick up above the wall. Some of these people are talking, others are silent.
That's a strange image, and strange prisoners, he said.
They're just like us, I replied. Tell me — can they see anything of themselves or each other except the shadows cast by the fire on the wall of the cave facing them?
How could they, he said, if they've been forced to keep their heads still their whole lives?
And they'd only see shadows of the objects being carried behind them?
Yes, he said.
And if they could talk to each other, wouldn't they assume that the shadows they saw were real things — that the names they gave the shadows referred to actual objects passing before them?
Very true.
And if the cave had an echo from the far wall, whenever one of the people behind them spoke, wouldn't the prisoners think the sound came from the passing shadow?
No question, he replied.
To these prisoners, I said, the truth would be literally nothing but shadows.
That's certain.

Now think about what would happen if one of them were freed and forced to stand up, turn around, and walk toward the light. Every movement would be painful. The glare would overwhelm him, and he wouldn't be able to see the real objects whose shadows he'd been watching all his life. Imagine someone telling him that what he saw before was an illusion — that now he's closer to reality and seeing more clearly. What do you think he'd say? And if his guide pointed to each object as it passed and demanded he name it — wouldn't he be completely confused? Wouldn't he think the shadows he used to see were more real than the objects now being shown to him?
Much more real.

And if he were forced to look directly at the light of the fire, wouldn't the pain in his eyes make him turn away and retreat to the things he could see clearly — which he'd still believe were more real than what was being shown to him?
True, he said.

And if he were dragged by force up the steep, rough passage and held in the sunlight — wouldn't he be in pain and furious about it? When he faced the light, his eyes would be so dazzled that he couldn't see any of the things now called real.
Not right away, he said.

He'd need time to adjust. At first he'd see shadows most easily, then reflections of people and things in water, then the things themselves. After that he'd find it easier to look at the night sky — the moon and stars — than at the sun or sunlight during the day.
Certainly.
And last of all, he'd be able to look at the sun itself — not just its reflection in water, but the actual sun in its proper place — and contemplate it as it really is.
Certainly.

Then he'd work out that the sun is responsible for the seasons and the years, that it governs everything in the visible world, and that it is, in a way, the cause of everything he and his fellow prisoners used to see.
Clearly, he said — that's where his reasoning would lead him.
And when he remembered his old home in the cave, and the so-called wisdom of the place, and his fellow prisoners — don't you think he'd count himself lucky and feel sorry for them?
Very much so.

And if they used to award honors among themselves to whoever was quickest to spot the passing shadows, or who could best remember which shadows came first, which followed, and which appeared together, and could therefore best predict what would come next — do you think he'd want those honors? Would he envy the ones who held power and prestige down there? Wouldn't he rather say, with Homer —
'Better to be a poor man's servant above ground'
— and endure anything rather than go back to thinking and living as they do?
Yes, he said. I think he'd endure anything rather than live that way.
Now imagine him going back down into the cave. His eyes would be full of darkness, wouldn't they?
To be sure, he said.

And if he had to compete again with the prisoners who'd never left — measuring shadows while his eyes were still weak and unadjusted (and it might take quite a while to get used to the dark again) — wouldn't they ridicule him? They'd say he went up and came back with ruined eyes, and that it wasn't even worth trying to go up. And if anyone tried to free another prisoner and lead him upward, they'd kill the person who tried, if they could catch him.
No question, he said.

Now, my dear Glaucon, you can apply this whole allegory to what we've been discussing. The cave is the visible world, the fire is the sun, and the journey upward into the sunlight represents the soul's ascent into the intelligible world. That, at least, is my belief — whether it's true, only God knows. But my view is this: in the world of knowledge, the Form of the Good is the last thing to be seen, and it takes real effort to see it. But once seen, the conclusion is inescapable — it is the cause of everything right and beautiful; in the visible world it produces light and the lord of light, and in the intelligible world it is the source of truth and reason. Anyone who wants to act wisely, in public or private life, must keep his eye fixed on it.
I agree, he said, as far as I can follow you.

Then you won't be surprised, I said, that those who reach this vision are reluctant to go back to human affairs. Their souls are always straining toward the higher world where they long to dwell. And that's perfectly natural, if our allegory holds.
Yes, perfectly natural.

And is it surprising if someone who has passed from divine contemplation back into the human world stumbles and makes a fool of himself — if, while still blinking and before his eyes have adjusted to the darkness, he's forced to argue in courtrooms or other public places about shadows and images of justice, and to compete with people who have never seen the real thing?
Not surprising at all, he replied.

Anyone with sense will remember that confusion of the eyes comes in two forms and from two causes — moving from light into darkness, and moving from darkness into light. The same is true of the mind's eye. When you see someone whose vision is confused and weak, don't be too quick to laugh. First ask whether that soul has come from a brighter life and can't yet see because it's not used to the dark, or whether it has come from ignorance into the light and is dazzled by the brightness. You'd consider the first person fortunate and pity the second. And if you wanted to laugh at someone, there'd be more reason to laugh at the soul coming up from below into the light than at the one coming down from the light into the cave.
That's a very fair distinction, he said.
If that's right, I said, then certain educators are wrong when they claim they can put knowledge into a soul that didn't have it before — as if they could put sight into blind eyes.
They certainly do claim that, he replied.

But our argument shows that the power and capacity for learning already exists in the soul. Just as the eye can't turn from darkness to light without turning the whole body, so the organ of knowledge can only be turned from the world of becoming to the world of being by turning the whole soul — until it can bear to look at the brightest and best of being: that is, the Good.
Very true.

Then there must be an art of turning the soul as effectively and quickly as possible — not an art of implanting sight, since sight already exists but is pointing the wrong way. It needs to be redirected toward the truth.
Yes, he said, such an art seems likely to exist.

Now, the other so-called virtues of the soul seem to be somewhat like physical qualities — they can be developed through habit and practice even when they're not innate. But the virtue of wisdom is different. It contains something more divine, which never loses its power. Depending on which way it's turned, it becomes either useful or harmful. Haven't you noticed how sharp the vision of a clever criminal can be — how keenly his wretched little soul sees the path to its goals? His eyesight isn't defective; it's just been conscripted into the service of evil. The sharper his vision, the more damage he does.
Very true, he said.

But imagine if natures like these had been cut free in youth from the heavy pleasures — eating, drinking, and the rest — that weigh the soul down and drag its vision toward lower things. If they'd been turned in the opposite direction, those same sharp eyes would have seen truth just as keenly as they now see the things they're aimed at.
Very likely.

And here's something else that follows logically from all this: neither the uneducated who've never encountered truth, nor those who are allowed to spend their whole lives in study, are fit to govern. The first group has no single goal to guide all their actions, public and private. The second group won't act at all unless compelled — they think they've already arrived at the Islands of the Blessed.
Very true, he replied.

So our task as founders of the State, I said, is to compel the best minds to reach the highest knowledge — the knowledge of the Good — by continuing their ascent. But once they've ascended and seen enough, we must not let them do what they do now.
What do you mean?
I mean we can't let them stay in the upper world. They must go back down into the cave and share in the prisoners' labors and honors, whatever those may be worth.
But isn't that unjust? he said. Should we give them a worse life when they could have a better one?

You've forgotten again, my friend, I said. The legislator's goal isn't to make any one class in the State exceptionally happy, but to spread happiness across the whole State. He uses persuasion and necessity to bind the citizens together, making each class share its benefits with the others. He creates such citizens not to let them go their own way, but to use them as instruments for binding the whole State together.
True, he said — I had forgotten.

Consider, Glaucon, that there's no injustice in what we're asking of our philosophers. We'll explain it to them this way: In other states, philosophers grow up on their own, without the government's help. Having educated themselves, they owe nothing to a system that did nothing for them, and it's fair enough that they refuse to participate. But you — we brought you into the world to be rulers of the hive, kings of yourselves and of the other citizens. We've educated you far better and more completely than philosophers elsewhere, and you're better equipped to participate in both worlds. So each of you, when your turn comes, must go down to where the others live and get used to seeing in the dark. Once you've adjusted, you'll see ten thousand times better than the cave-dwellers. You'll know what each shadow is and what it represents, because you've seen the beautiful, the just, and the good in their true form. And so our State will be governed in waking reality, not in a dream — unlike other states where rulers fight over shadows and tear each other apart in the struggle for power, as if power were some great prize. The truth is that the best-governed state is always the one where the rulers are least eager to govern, and the worst-governed is the one where they're most eager.
Quite true, he replied.
And when our pupils hear this, will they refuse to take their turn at governing — when they're allowed to spend most of their time together in the light?
Impossible, he answered. They're just men, and the demands we place on them are just. Each one will take office as a duty — a stern necessity — not in the spirit of our current rulers.

Exactly, my friend, I said. And that's the key: you must provide your future rulers with a life better than that of a ruler, and only then will you have a well-ordered State. Only a state that can offer this will be governed by the truly rich — rich not in gold and silver, but in the virtue and wisdom that make for genuine happiness. If people go into public service poor and hungry for personal advantage, hoping to snatch some good from their position, good government is impossible. They'll fight over office, and the resulting civil wars will destroy both the rulers and the State.
Absolutely true, he replied.
Is there any life that looks down on political ambition other than the life of true philosophy? Do you know of any?
None that I know of, he said.
And the people who govern should not be lovers of power — otherwise there will be rival lovers who fight over it.
No question.

Then who should we compel to serve as guardians? It should be the people who are wisest about governing and who have the best track record of administering the State — but who also have other honors and a life better than politics.
Those are the ones, he replied, and I would choose them.
Now, shall we consider how such guardians will be produced — how they'll be brought from darkness into light, as some are said to have ascended from the underworld to the gods?
By all means, he replied.
This isn't some trivial game, I said — it's the turning of a soul from a day that's barely better than night to the true day of being. This ascent is what we call true philosophy.
Quite so.
Then we need to ask: what kind of knowledge has the power to accomplish this turn?
Certainly.
And another thought occurs to me: remember that our young men are to be warrior athletes?
Yes, we said that.
Then this knowledge must have an additional quality.
What quality?
It must be useful in war.
Yes, if possible.
Our earlier educational scheme had two parts, didn't it?
Just so.
Gymnastics dealt with the growth and decay of the body — so it belongs to the world of becoming and perishing?
True.
So that's not the knowledge we're looking for?
No.
What about music — which also played a role in our earlier program?

Music, as you'll recall, he said, was the counterpart of gymnastics. It trained the guardians through habit — harmony made them harmonious, rhythm made them rhythmical — but it gave them no real knowledge. Its words, whether fictional or factual, had elements of rhythm and harmony, but there was nothing in music that aimed at the kind of good we're now seeking.

You remember perfectly, I said. There really was nothing of that sort in music. But then, my dear Glaucon, what branch of knowledge has this power? All the practical arts we dismissed as beneath our guardians.
That's right. But if we exclude music, gymnastics, and the practical arts — what's left?

Well, I said, if there's nothing special left, we'll have to find something universal — something every art, science, and discipline uses in common, and that everyone has to learn as part of a basic education.
What would that be?
Something quite humble, I said — the ability to distinguish one, two, and three. In a word: number and calculation. Every art and science depends on them, doesn't it?
Yes.
The humble matter of distinguishing one, two, and three — in a word, number and calculation. Don't all arts and sciences necessarily make use of them?
Yes.
Including the art of war?
Obviously.

Then Palamedes, whenever he appears in tragedy, proves Agamemnon ridiculously unfit to be a general. Did you know that? He claims to have invented number and used it to count the ships and arrange the ranks at Troy — implying nobody had counted anything before, and that Agamemnon couldn't even count his own feet. What kind of general doesn't know numbers?
A very strange one, if that's true, he said.
So we'd agree that a warrior needs to know arithmetic?
Absolutely — if he's to have the slightest understanding of tactics. In fact, if he's to be human at all.
I wonder if you see this study the way I do.
What's your view?
It seems to me to be exactly the kind of study we're looking for — one that naturally draws the mind toward reflection and toward being. But it's never been properly used for that purpose.
Can you explain? he said.

I'll try, I said. Follow along with me and say yes or no as I try to distinguish which kinds of knowledge have this power of attracting the soul — so we can determine whether arithmetic is one of them, as I suspect.
Go ahead, he said.
What I mean is this: some sense perceptions don't invite further thought because the senses handle them just fine. But others are so puzzling that they force the mind to investigate.
You're obviously talking about optical illusions, he said — how things look different at a distance or in paintings with light and shadow.
No, I said, that's not what I mean at all.
Then what do you mean?

The perceptions that don't invite thought are the ones where the senses don't simultaneously present opposite impressions. The ones that do invite thought present contradictory information — near or far, the sensation of one quality arrives tangled up with its opposite. An example will make this clearer: here are three fingers — the little finger, the second finger, and the middle finger.
Very good.
Assume they're seen up close. Here's the important point.
What is it?

Each of them looks equally like a finger, whether you see it in the middle or at the edge, whether it's white or dark, thick or thin — it doesn't matter. In all these cases, most people's minds aren't compelled to ask 'What is a finger?' because sight never suggests that a finger is anything other than a finger.
True.
So there's nothing here that invites or arouses thought.
Nothing, he said.

But what about the size of the fingers — their bigness and smallness? Can sight really perceive these adequately? Does it make no difference that one finger is in the middle and another at the edge? And the same with touch — can it truly judge thickness and thinness, hardness and softness? Don't all the senses have the same problem? The sense that registers hardness is the very same sense that registers softness, and it reports to the soul that the same thing is both hard and soft.
You're quite right, he said.

And the soul must be puzzled by this: if the sense of touch tells it that the same thing is both hard and soft, what does that mean? And what about light and heavy — if what's light is also heavy, and what's heavy is also light?
Yes, he said, these messages are puzzling and demand investigation.
So naturally, I said, the soul calls on calculation and intelligence for help — to figure out whether it's dealing with one thing or two.
True.
And if they turn out to be two, each of them is one and distinct?
Certainly.
And if each is one and both together are two, the soul will think of them as divided — because if they were undivided, it could only think of them as one.
True.
Now, sight did perceive big and small, but only in a confused way — jumbled together rather than distinguished.
Yes.
But thought, wanting to bring clarity to the confusion, was forced to separate big and small and see them as distinct.
Very true.
And isn't this the starting point of asking: what is big? And what is small?
Exactly.
And this is how the distinction between the visible and the intelligible first arose.
Absolutely right.
That's what I was getting at earlier. Some impressions invite thought — the ones where opposite qualities arrive simultaneously — while others don't.
I understand now, he said, and I agree.
So which class do unity and number belong to?
I'm not sure, he replied.

Think it through using what we've just established. If unity could be perfectly grasped by sight or any other sense, it wouldn't draw the mind toward being — just as with the finger. But when you always see contradictions — when one also appears to be many — then thought is aroused. The soul gets confused and starts asking: what is unity itself? This is how the study of number has the power to turn the mind toward the contemplation of true being.
And this happens especially with the number one, he said. We see the same thing as both one and infinitely many.
Yes, I said. And what's true of one must be true of all numbers.
Certainly.
And all arithmetic and calculation deal with number?
Yes.
And they clearly lead the mind toward truth?
In a truly remarkable way.

Then this is the kind of knowledge we're looking for. It serves a double purpose — military and philosophical. The soldier needs arithmetic to arrange his troops, and the philosopher needs it to rise above the world of change and grasp true being.
That's right.
And our guardian is both soldier and philosopher?
Certainly.

Then arithmetic is the sort of study our laws should prescribe. And we must persuade the leading citizens of our State to study it — not as amateurs, but until they can see the nature of numbers with the mind alone. Not for buying and selling, like merchants and shopkeepers, but for war and for the soul's own journey from becoming to truth and being.
Excellent, he said.

And now that we've discussed arithmetic, I said, notice how elegant this science really is, and how many ways it serves our purpose — when pursued in the spirit of a philosopher rather than a shopkeeper.
How do you mean?

Arithmetic has a powerful elevating effect. It compels the soul to reason about abstract numbers and resists any attempt to bring visible or tangible objects into the argument. You know how practitioners of arithmetic scold anyone who tries to divide the unit — if you try to split it up, they just multiply, making sure that one always stays one and never dissolves into fractions.
Very true.

Now imagine someone asking them: 'What are these amazing numbers you're talking about — numbers where every unit is perfectly equal to every other, absolutely uniform, indivisible?' What would they say?
They'd say they're talking about numbers that can only exist in thought.
So you see that this branch of knowledge genuinely deserves to be called necessary — since it clearly requires the mind to use pure intelligence in pursuit of pure truth.
Yes, that's one of its defining features.

And have you noticed that people who are naturally good at calculation tend to be quick at every other subject too? Even naturally slow people become much sharper after arithmetic training, even if they gain no other benefit from it.
Very true, he said.
And I don't think you'll find many subjects harder to study, or indeed as hard.
You won't.
So for all these reasons, arithmetic should be part of the training for the best natures — and it must not be abandoned.
I agree.
Good. That's our first subject. Now, shall we look at the related science to see if it also serves our purpose?
You mean geometry?
Exactly.

Well, clearly the parts of geometry that relate to warfare matter to us, he said — setting up camp, taking positions, deploying troops, and all the various military maneuvers in battle and on the march. A general's knowledge of geometry makes all the difference.

True, I said, but for that purpose only a little geometry or arithmetic is needed. The real question is whether the more advanced parts of geometry help make it easier to perceive the Form of the Good. And as I've been saying, anything that forces the soul to turn toward the place where the fullest reality resides — that's what we need.
True, he said.
So if geometry leads us to contemplate being, it serves our purpose. If it only deals with becoming, it doesn't.
That's our position.
And yet anyone with the slightest experience of geometry will admit that the science as actually practiced flatly contradicts this view.
How so?

Geometers talk exclusively about practical operations — they're always going on about squaring, extending, and constructing, as if geometry were about making things. But the real aim of the whole science is knowledge.
Absolutely, he said.
Then we need to add this further point?
What's that?
That the knowledge geometry seeks is knowledge of what is eternal — not of anything that comes into being and passes away.
That can easily be granted — it's true.
Then geometry, my noble friend, will draw the soul toward truth and create the philosophical spirit — lifting upward what is now wrongly allowed to sink downward.
Nothing is more likely to do so.
Then we must firmly require that the citizens of your ideal city study geometry. And the science has side benefits too — not trivial ones.
What kind? he said.

The military advantages you mentioned, I said. And beyond that, in every field of knowledge, experience shows that someone who has studied geometry is immeasurably quicker to learn than someone who hasn't.
The difference is enormous, he said.
So shall we make this our second required subject for the young?
Let's do that, he replied.
And shall we make astronomy the third?
I'm strongly in favor, he said. Observing seasons, months, and years is as essential to a general as it is to a farmer or sailor.

I'm amused, I said, by your nervousness about seeming to insist on useless studies. But I do think everyone should be able to see that in every person there's an eye of the soul which, when dimmed and buried by other pursuits, can be purified and re-illuminated by these studies. And that eye is worth far more than ten thousand bodily eyes, because it alone sees truth. There are two kinds of listeners: those who'll hear this as a revelation, and those who'll find it completely meaningless and will see no profit in these studies whatsoever. So decide right now which group you're addressing. Or perhaps you'd say neither — that you're mainly arguing for your own benefit, while not begrudging others whatever they might gain.
I think I'd prefer to argue mainly for my own benefit.
Then let's step back, I said. We got the order of the sciences wrong.
What was the mistake? he said.
After studying surfaces, we jumped straight to solids in motion, instead of studying solids by themselves first. After the second dimension should come the third — cubes and depth.
You're right, Socrates. But so little seems to be known about solid geometry.

Yes, I said, for two reasons. First, no government supports the study, so there's no energy behind it, and it's inherently difficult. Second, students would need a good teacher, and there's hardly one to be found. Even if one appeared, the current students are too arrogant to listen. But if the State itself took the lead in sponsoring these studies and honored them properly, students would come forward, and sustained investigation would yield discoveries. Even now, neglected by the world and stunted, with no one able to explain their usefulness, these studies are pushing forward on the strength of their own intrinsic charm. If they had the State's support, they might truly flourish.
Yes, he said, there is a remarkable charm in them. But I don't quite follow the new order. You started with plane geometry?
Yes, I said.
Then you placed astronomy next, and now you're stepping back?
Yes — in my rush to get through everything, I skipped over solid geometry (whose pathetic neglect made me jump ahead) and went straight to astronomy, which is really the study of solids in motion.
True, he said.
So let's assume solid geometry would flourish if the State supported it, and move on to astronomy as our fourth subject.

Fair enough, he replied. And now, Socrates, since you criticized my crude praise of astronomy earlier, let me praise it on your terms instead. Surely everyone can see that astronomy forces the soul to look upward and leads us from this world to a higher one.
Everyone except me, I said. I don't see it that way at all.
Then what would you say?
I'd say that the people who try to dress astronomy up as philosophy are actually making us look downward, not upward.
What do you mean? he asked.

You seem to have a pretty generous definition of 'looking upward,' I said. If someone throws his head back and stares at patterns on the ceiling, you'd probably count that as intellectual contemplation rather than just using his eyes. Maybe you're right and I'm the fool. But here's what I think: the only knowledge that makes the soul look truly upward is knowledge of what IS — knowledge of the invisible. Whether someone gazes at the sky or squints at the ground, if he's trying to learn some fact about the sensible world, I deny that he can learn — because nothing sensible is the subject of genuine knowledge. His soul is looking downward, not up, even if he floats on his back in the ocean to do his studying.
That's a fair rebuke, he said. I deserve it. But how should astronomy be studied, then, to serve the kind of knowledge we're talking about?

Like this, I said: the visible sky is beautiful — the most beautiful and perfect of visible things. But precisely because it's visible, it must be regarded as far inferior to the true motions of absolute speed and absolute slowness, moving in relation to each other and carrying what they contain, in true number and true form. These can be grasped by reason and intelligence, but not by sight.
True, he replied.

So we should use the visible sky as a pattern pointing toward higher knowledge, the way we'd use beautifully drawn diagrams. A skilled geometer, seeing diagrams by Daedalus or some great artist, would admire the craftsmanship — but he'd never imagine he could find in them the true values of equality, or the exact truth of any mathematical proportion.
No, he replied. That would be absurd.

And the true astronomer will feel the same way when he looks at the movements of the stars. He'll think the heavens have been fashioned by their creator as beautifully as possible. But he'll never suppose that the exact ratios of night to day, or day to month, or month to year, or the precise relationships of the stars to each other — things that are material and visible — can also be perfectly eternal and free from all deviation. That would be absurd. And it would be equally absurd to spend enormous effort trying to determine their exact values.
I quite agree — though I'd never thought of it that way before.

So in astronomy, as in geometry, I said, we should work with problems and leave the visible heavens alone if we want to approach the subject properly and make the soul's natural gift of reason truly useful.
That, he said, would demand infinitely more work than current astronomers do.
Yes, I said. And there are many other areas where we'll need to take a similarly ambitious approach if our education is to be worth anything. But can you think of another suitable subject?
Not off the top of my head, he said.
Well, motion has many forms, I said — not just one. Two are fairly obvious even to us, and others might require wiser heads.
What are the two?
There's a second form that corresponds to the one we've been discussing.
What would that be?

Just as the eyes seem designed for astronomy, I said, the ears seem designed for harmonious motion — for musical harmony. These are sister sciences, as the Pythagoreans say. And we agree with them, don't we, Glaucon?
We do, he replied.

But since this is a complex field, I said, we'd better learn from the Pythagoreans — they can tell us about it and whether there are any further applications. Through it all, though, we must keep our own higher purpose in view.
What purpose?

That our students must reach a certain perfection in all their knowledge — and not fall short of it, as I was saying they currently do in astronomy. In the science of harmony, the same thing happens. The teachers of harmony compare the sounds and intervals they hear, and their labor is just as futile as the astronomers'.

Exactly! he said. And it's comical to hear them talk about their 'condensed intervals' and all that. They stick their ears right up to the strings like people trying to overhear their neighbor through a wall — one group insisting they can detect an intermediate note, claiming to have found the smallest measurable interval, while the other group insists the two notes have merged into one. Both groups set their ears above their understanding.

You mean, I said, those people who torment and rack the strings on their pegs. I could extend the metaphor and talk about the blows of the plectrum, and accuse the strings of being either too reluctant or too eager to sound — but that would be tedious. What I really mean is that these aren't the people I have in mind. I'm talking about the Pythagoreans, whom we just proposed to consult about harmony. They make the same mistake as the astronomers: they investigate the numerical relationships in the harmonies they hear, but they never rise to the level of real problems — asking why some numbers are harmonious and others aren't.
That, he said, would require more than human knowledge.
I'd call it useful knowledge, I replied — if it's pursued for the sake of the beautiful and the good. Pursued for any other reason, it's useless.
Very true, he said.

Now, when all these studies reach the point where they connect and relate to one another, and their mutual relationships become clear — then, I think, and not until then, does pursuing them have real value for our purposes. Otherwise there's no profit in them.
I suspect you're right, he said. But you're describing an enormous undertaking, Socrates.
What — the prelude? I said. Don't you realize that all of this is merely the prelude to the real subject we need to learn? You surely wouldn't mistake a skilled mathematician for a dialectician.
Certainly not, he said. I've hardly ever met a mathematician who could actually reason.
But can people who can't give and receive reasoned arguments possess the kind of knowledge we're after?
They cannot.

And so, Glaucon, we've finally arrived at the real thing — the song that dialectic sings. It belongs to the intellect alone, but the faculty of sight provides an analogy. Remember how sight, in our allegory, progressed from looking at shadows to looking at real animals and stars and finally at the sun itself? So too with dialectic: when someone sets out to discover the absolute through reason alone, without any help from the senses, and perseveres through pure intelligence until grasping the absolute Good — he arrives at the summit of the intellectual world, just as the man in our allegory arrived at the summit of the visible.
Exactly, he said.
And this progression is what you'd call dialectic?
True.

Think of it as the freeing of the prisoners from their chains — the turning from shadows to the objects that cast them, then to the light, then the ascent from underground into the sunlight. Up there, they still can't look directly at animals and plants and the sunlight, but they can see divine reflections in water — shadows of true existence, not shadows of shadows cast by firelight (which is itself just an image of the sun). This power of raising the soul's highest faculty to the contemplation of the highest reality — the power given by all the studies and arts we've described — may be compared to raising the body's faculty of sight to the brightest thing in the material world.

I agree with what you're saying, he replied. It may be hard to accept, but from another point of view it's even harder to deny. Still, this isn't something we can settle in passing — we'll have to come back to it. So for now, whether our conclusion is right or wrong, let's assume all this and move from the prelude to the main theme. Tell us: what is dialectic? What are its divisions? And what are the paths that lead there — since those paths will also lead to our final destination.

Dear Glaucon, I said, you wouldn't be able to follow me the rest of the way, though I'd try my best. What you'd see would not be a mere image of truth, but the truth itself — or at least something very close to it. Whether what I'd show you would be actual reality, I can't say for certain. But I am confident it would be something like it.
No doubt, he replied.
But I must also remind you that the power of dialectic alone can reveal this truth — and only to someone who has already mastered the studies we've been discussing.
You can be just as confident of that, he said.

And no one will argue that there's any other method for systematically grasping the true nature of each thing. All the other arts concern themselves with human desires, opinions, or practical production and preservation. And the mathematical sciences — which, as we said, do touch on true being — can only dream about it. They can never truly see it while they leave their hypotheses unexamined and can't account for them. When you don't know your own starting point, and when the conclusion and every intermediate step are built on something you don't understand — how can such a patchwork ever amount to genuine knowledge?
It can't, he said.

Then dialectic — and dialectic alone — goes straight to the first principle, doing away with hypotheses to establish itself on solid ground. The eye of the soul, literally buried in a swamp of ignorance, is gently lifted by dialectic. She uses the sciences we've been discussing as helpers in this work of conversion. We call them sciences by convention, but they really deserve a different name — something implying more clarity than opinion but less than knowledge. Earlier we called this 'understanding.' But why argue about terminology when we have such important realities to consider?
Why indeed, he said. Any name that captures the thought clearly enough will do.

So we're satisfied with our earlier scheme: four divisions — two for intellect, two for opinion. The first is knowledge proper, the second understanding, the third belief, the fourth conjecture. The first pair deals with being, the second with becoming. And the proportions hold:
As being is to becoming, so is pure intellect to opinion. As intellect is to opinion, so is knowledge to belief, and understanding to conjecture.
But let's put off the further subdivision of the objects of opinion and intellect — that inquiry would be many times longer than everything we've discussed so far.
I agree, as far as I can follow, he said.
And do you also agree that the dialectician is the one who grasps the essence of each thing? Anyone who can't do this, to the degree that he fails, also fails in intelligence?
Yes, he said. How could I deny it?

And the same applies to the Good. Unless someone can rationally define the Form of the Good, separating it from everything else; unless he can survive every objection like a soldier in battle, refuting them not by appealing to opinion but to truth, never stumbling at any point in the argument — unless he can do all this, you'd say he knows neither the Good nor any other good. He grasps only a shadow, guided by opinion rather than knowledge — dreaming his way through this life until he arrives at the next world and falls asleep forever.
I'd certainly say all of that.

And you wouldn't want the children of your ideal State — the ones you're raising and educating, assuming this ideal ever becomes real — to be like signposts with no reason in them, yet set in charge of the most important matters?
Certainly not.
Then you'll establish a law requiring them to receive the kind of education that equips them to ask and answer questions with the greatest possible skill?
Yes, he said. You and I will make that law together.
So dialectic stands as the capstone of all the sciences — nothing higher can be placed above it. The nature of knowledge goes no further.
I agree, he said.
Now we need to determine who should receive these studies and how they should be assigned.
Clearly.
You remember how the rulers were chosen earlier?
Of course, he said.

The same types of character should be chosen again — the most reliable, the bravest, and ideally the most physically impressive. But beyond noble and spirited temperaments, they must have natural gifts that suit this particular education.
What gifts?

Mental sharpness and a quick capacity for learning. The mind flags more easily from the strain of study than the body does from gymnastics — the work belongs entirely to the mind and doesn't share the burden with the body.
Very true, he replied.

A good memory is essential too, along with an unflagging work ethic and a genuine love of labor. Otherwise he'll never endure both the physical training and the intellectual demands we're placing on him.
He certainly needs natural gifts, he said.

The problem right now is that philosophy's students have no real calling for it, and that's why she's fallen into disrepute. As I said before, only her true children — not imposters — should take her hand.
What do you mean?

First, her student must not be half-hearted or inconsistent in effort — industrious in one area and lazy in another. Like someone who loves athletics and hunting and all physical pursuits but hates learning, listening, and investigating. Or the opposite kind of half-heartedness.
Very true, he said.

And regarding truth — isn't a soul equally crippled if it hates deliberate lies and is outraged when others lie, but tolerates its own involuntary ignorance? If it wallows in the muck of ignorance like a pig and feels no shame when caught?
Absolutely.

And when it comes to temperance, courage, greatness of mind, and every other virtue — we must be just as careful to distinguish the genuine article from the counterfeit. Where there's no such discernment, states and individuals unwittingly make rulers or friends of people who are lame in some dimension of virtue.
That's very true, he said.

We must be careful about all of this, I said. If the people we introduce to this demanding system of education are sound in body and mind, justice itself won't fault us, and we'll be saviors of the State. But if we admit people of the wrong sort, the opposite will happen — we'll pour an even greater flood of ridicule on philosophy than she already endures.
That would be shameful.
It certainly would, I said. Though I'm afraid I may be making myself a bit ridiculous right now too.
How so?

I forgot, I said, that we weren't being entirely serious, and I got too passionate. While I was speaking, I looked at philosophy and saw how shamefully she's being treated, and I felt a surge of indignation against those responsible — I got more heated than I should have.
Not at all — I was listening and didn't find you excessive.

Well, I who was speaking certainly felt it. But let me remind you: although we chose old men last time, we shouldn't do so now. Solon was wrong when he said a person can learn many things as he grows old. An old man can learn no better than he can run. Youth is the time for extraordinary effort.
Of course.
So arithmetic, geometry, and all the preliminary studies that prepare the way for dialectic should be introduced in childhood. But not through compulsion.
Why not?
Because a free person should never learn anything under conditions of slavery. Physical exercise done under compulsion doesn't harm the body, but knowledge forced into the mind takes no hold.
Very true.
So, my friend, I said, don't use force in educating children. Let it be a kind of play. That way you'll also be better able to discover each child's natural bent.
That makes good sense, he said.
Do you remember that we also said the children should be taken to watch battles on horseback, and brought close up — like young hounds — to get a taste of danger?
Yes, I remember.
Well, the same principle applies to their studies. Whoever excels across all these trials — labors, lessons, dangers — should be selected for a special group.
At what age?

When the compulsory gymnastics period is over. That period, whether two or three years, is useless for anything else — sleep and physical exhaustion are enemies of learning. And how they perform in gymnastics is itself an important test.
Of course, he replied.

After that, at twenty, the best will be promoted and given higher status. The studies they encountered in scattered form during childhood will now be brought together, so they can see how the sciences relate to each other and to the nature of being.
Yes, he said — that's the only kind of learning that really lasts.
And the ability to see these connections is the best test of dialectical talent. The person with a comprehensive mind is the born dialectician.
I agree, he said.

So you'll need to keep these criteria in mind. Those who show the most of this comprehensive ability, who are most steadfast in their studies and in military and civic duties — when they reach thirty, you'll select them from the best and raise them to still higher honor. Then you must test them through dialectic to find which of them can give up the use of the senses and travel, in the company of truth, toward being itself. And here, my friend, great caution is needed.
Why great caution?
Haven't you noticed, I said, what an evil dialectic has introduced?
What evil?
It fills its students with lawlessness.
It certainly does, he said.
Do you think that's surprising? Is there anything unnatural about it? Will you make some allowance for them?
Allowance for what?

Think of it this way, I said. Imagine a boy raised in great wealth by a large family, surrounded by flatterers. When he grows up, he discovers that the people he called his parents aren't his real parents — but he can't find out who his real parents are. Can you guess how he'd behave toward his flatterers and his supposed parents, first when he doesn't know the truth, and then after he discovers it? Or shall I guess?
Go ahead.

While he's in the dark, I'd say he'll honor his father and mother and supposed relations more than the flatterers. He'll be less likely to neglect them, less likely to act or speak against them, less willing to disobey them on important matters.
Naturally.

But once he discovers the truth, his respect for them would fade, and the flatterers' influence would grow. He'd start living by their rules, associating with them openly. Unless he had an unusually good disposition, he'd stop caring about his supposed parents entirely.
That's all very plausible. But how does it apply to philosophy students?
Like this: there are certain principles about justice and honor that we've been taught since childhood. We grew up obeying and respecting them, like parental authority.
True.
And there are opposing habits and pleasures that flatter and attract the soul but have no influence on people with any sense of right — who continue to obey and honor their inherited principles.
True.

Now, when the questioning spirit arrives and asks 'What is honor? What is justice?' — and argument after argument tears down the answers the young person learned from his teachers, until he's driven to believe that nothing is truly honorable or just — or the opposite — and the same for everything he once valued most — what do you think happens? Will he still honor and obey those principles?
Impossible.
And when he no longer considers them honorable or natural, and he can't discover what's truly right — what life will he pursue, if not the one that flatters his desires?
Nothing else.
So from a law-keeper he becomes a law-breaker?
Inevitably.
And all of this is perfectly natural for students of philosophy as I've described them — and, as I said, very much deserving of our sympathy.
Yes, he said — and pitiable too.
Which is precisely why great care is needed in introducing thirty-year-olds to dialectic — so as not to arouse that pity.
Certainly.

There's a real danger that they'll taste the thrill of argument too early. You know how it is with young people: once they discover the power of refutation, they use it as a game — constantly contradicting and tearing down anyone they can, like puppies who love to pull and rip at whatever comes near them.
They certainly love nothing more, he said.

And after they've demolished many opponents — and been demolished themselves — they quickly arrive at the conclusion that nothing they ever believed is true. And that's how philosophy and everything associated with it gets a bad name among ordinary people.
All too true, he said.

But an older person won't indulge in this kind of madness. He'll imitate the person who genuinely seeks truth through dialogue, not the one who argues just for the fun of contradicting. His greater maturity will bring more honor to the pursuit, not less.
Very true, he said.
And weren't we guarding against exactly this when we said that the students admitted to dialectic must be orderly and steady by nature — not, as things are now, any random person who shows up?
Exactly right.
Now suppose the study of dialectic replaces gymnastics and is pursued intensely and exclusively for twice the number of years spent on physical training. Would that be enough?
Would you say six years or four? he asked.

Make it five, I replied. After that, they must be sent back down into the cave and made to hold whatever military or civic offices are appropriate for young people. This will give them practical experience, and we'll be able to test whether they stand firm when pulled in every direction by temptation, or whether they give way.
And how long should this stage last?

Fifteen years, I answered. And when they reach fifty, those who have survived and distinguished themselves in every action and every branch of knowledge must finally reach the summit. They must raise the eye of their soul to the universal light that illuminates all things and behold the absolute Good. For that is the pattern by which they must order the State and the lives of individuals, as well as the remainder of their own lives. They'll spend most of their time in philosophy, but when their turn comes, they'll take on the work of governing — not as some heroic feat, but simply as a duty. When they've raised up a new generation like themselves to be the next guardians, they'll depart to the Islands of the Blessed. The city will honor them with public memorials and sacrifices — as demigods, if the oracle approves, or at the very least as blessed and godlike.
What a sculptor you are, Socrates! You've carved these rulers to perfection.
And the women rulers too, Glaucon. Don't think that anything I've said applies only to men and not to women, as far as their natures allow.
You're right, he said, since we've given them equal share in everything, just like the men.

Well then, I said — would you agree that what we've said about the State and its government isn't just a dream? It's difficult, certainly, but not impossible — and possible only in the way we've described: when true philosopher-kings arise in a state, one or more of them, who despise the honors of this present world as petty and worthless, who value justice above all things and regard it as the greatest necessity, whose service to justice shapes every institution — when such rulers set their own city in order?
How will they do it?

They'll send everyone over the age of ten out into the countryside and take charge of the children — raising them free from the habits of their parents, in the customs and laws we've been describing. This is the quickest and easiest way for the State and constitution we've outlined to become reality, bringing happiness to the nation and the greatest benefit to the people.
Yes, I think that's right, Socrates. You've described very well how such a state could come into being, if it ever does.
So we've said enough about the perfect State and the kind of person who embodies it. It's clear enough what he would look like.
Clear enough, he replied. And I agree that there's nothing more to be said on this point.

chapters.title: Book VIII
paragraphs: So, Glaucon, we've established that in the perfect State, wives and children are to be shared in common. Education, war, and peace are all shared activities, and the wisest philosophers and bravest warriors are to be the kings.
That has been agreed, replied Glaucon.

Yes, I said. And we further agreed that the rulers, once appointed, will take their soldiers and house them in the kind of dwellings we described — common to all, with nothing private or individual. And about their property — you remember what we decided?

Yes, I remember. No one was to have any ordinary possessions. They were to be warrior athletes and guardians, receiving only their maintenance from the other citizens instead of an annual salary. Their job was to look after themselves and the whole State.
Right, I said. Now that we've finished that part of our task, let's find where we got sidetracked so we can get back on the main path.

That's easy enough. You were implying then, as now, that you'd finished describing the State. You said it was good, and that the man who corresponded to it was also good — though as it turns out, you had even better things to say about both. You also said that if this was the true form, the others were false, and that there were four main false forms worth examining, along with the individuals who correspond to them. Once we'd seen them all and agreed who was the best and who was the worst, we were to consider whether the best was also the happiest and the worst the most miserable. I asked you what the four forms were, and then Polemarchus and Adeimantus interrupted. You started over, and here we are.
Your memory is excellent, I said.
Then like a wrestler, he replied, get back into the same position. Let me ask the same question, and give me the answer you were about to give then.
If I can, I will, I said.
I'd particularly like to hear about those four constitutions you mentioned.

That's an easy question, I said. The four governments I meant, insofar as they have distinct names, are: first, the Cretan and Spartan type, which is widely admired. Second comes oligarchy — not so highly regarded, and full of evils. Third is democracy, which naturally follows oligarchy though it's very different. And last comes tyranny, great and infamous, which differs from all the rest and is the fourth and worst disorder a state can suffer. I can't think of any other constitution with a truly distinct character. There are hereditary monarchies and purchased governments and various intermediate forms, but these are hard to classify and can be found equally among Greeks and non-Greeks.
Yes, he replied, we certainly hear of many curious forms of government like that.

Do you realize, I said, that governments are as varied as the characters of the people in them? There must be as many types of the one as there are of the other. States aren't made of wood and stone — they're made of the human natures they contain, and those natures tip the scales and drag everything else along with them.
Yes, he said. States are as the men are — they grow out of human characters.
Then if there are five types of constitution, there must be five types of individual character?
Certainly.
The man who corresponds to aristocracy — the one we rightly call just and good — we've already described.
We have.

Then let's now describe the inferior types: the contentious and ambitious, who correspond to the Spartan system; then the oligarchical, the democratic, and the tyrannical. By placing the most just alongside the most unjust, we'll be able to compare how happy or miserable each one's life is. That will complete our inquiry and tell us whether we should follow Thrasymachus's advice and pursue injustice, or whether the argument points us toward justice.
Absolutely, he replied. We must do as you say.

Shall we follow our old method of examining the State first, then the individual? Let's start with the government of honor — I don't know what else to call it besides timocracy, or perhaps timarchy. We'll compare this to the corresponding individual, then look at oligarchy and the oligarchical man, then democracy and the democratic man, and finally visit the tyrannical city and peer into the tyrant's soul, aiming for a definitive conclusion.
That's an excellent approach.

First, then, I said, let's ask how timocracy — the government of honor — arises from aristocracy — the government of the best. One thing is clear: all political revolutions originate in divisions within the ruling class. A government that's united, however small, can't be overthrown.
Very true, he said.

So how will our city be destabilized? How will the auxiliaries and rulers come to disagree? Shall we, like Homer, call on the Muses to tell us 'how discord first arose'? Shall we imagine them in playful solemnity, teasing us as if we were children, speaking in the elevated voice of tragedy while pretending to be serious?
How would they address us?

Something like this: A city built as yours can hardly be shaken. But since everything that has a beginning also has an end, even your constitution won't last forever — it will eventually dissolve. Here is how the dissolution happens: In plants and animals alike, fertility and barrenness of body and soul follow cycles. Short-lived creatures have short cycles, long-lived ones have long cycles. But the knowledge of when humans should and shouldn't reproduce will elude even your wisest rulers. The laws governing this will escape minds clouded by sensory knowledge, and they'll produce children at the wrong times. What is divinely born has a cycle expressed in a perfect number, but human birth is governed by a more complex number involving squares and cubes, three intervals and four terms, waxing and waning, all made commensurable. When your guardians fail to understand the law of births and match couples badly, the children won't be blessed. The best of these lesser children will still be appointed as rulers, but they'll prove unworthy of their fathers' positions. Once in power, they'll begin by neglecting us, the Muses — first undervaluing music, then gymnastics. The youth will grow less cultivated. The next generation of rulers will lose the ability to test the metals of your different races — Hesiod's gold, silver, bronze, and iron. Iron will mix with silver, and bronze with gold, producing inequality and irregularity, which are always and everywhere the causes of hatred and war. This, the Muses declare, is the origin of discord.
Yes, and we can assume they speak truly.
Of course they speak truly, I said. How could the Muses lie?
And what do the Muses say happens next?

When discord arose, the two races pulled in different directions. The iron and bronze types turned to acquiring money, land, houses, gold, and silver. But the gold and silver types, having no desire for wealth because true riches were in their nature, inclined toward virtue and the old order. They struggled, and finally compromised: they divided land and houses into private property, enslaved the people they'd formerly protected as free citizens, and made them subjects and servants. Then they devoted themselves to war and to guarding against these new subjects.
I think you've captured the origin of the change correctly.
And the new government that emerges — it'll be a form midway between oligarchy and aristocracy?
Exactly.

That's how the change happens. Now, after the change, how will they proceed? Since this new State sits between oligarchy and the ideal State, it'll partly follow one and partly the other, with some distinctive features of its own.
True, he said.

In honoring rulers, in keeping the warrior class away from farming and trade, in common meals, in attention to gymnastics and military training — in all these respects, this State will resemble the former one.
True.

But it'll be afraid to let philosophers into power, since the available philosophers are no longer simple and sincere but of mixed character. It will turn instead to spirited, less complicated people who are naturally suited for war rather than peace. It will value military strategy and cunning, and wage wars endlessly. In these respects, the State will be distinctive.
Yes.

Yes, I said. And men of this type will be greedy for money, like those in oligarchies. They'll nurse a fierce secret craving for gold and silver, hoarding it in hidden vaults and private treasuries — building little fortresses that are really nests for their money, where they'll lavish spending on their wives or whoever else they please.
That's exactly right, he said.

And they're stingy because they have no legitimate way to acquire the money they crave. So they spend other people's money on their pleasures, enjoying them in secret, running from the law like children from their father. They've been educated by force rather than persuasion, because they neglected the true Muse — the companion of reason and philosophy — and honored gymnastics over music.
No question, he said. The government you're describing is a mixture of good and evil.
A mixture, yes, I said. But one thing dominates: the spirit of rivalry and ambition, which comes from the spirited element holding sway.
Without a doubt, he said.

That's the origin and character of this State — described in outline only, since a sketch is enough to show the types of the most just and most unjust. Going through every state and every character in full detail would be an endless task.
Very true, he replied.
Now, what kind of man corresponds to this government? How did he come into being, and what is he like?
I think, said Adeimantus, that in his competitiveness he's not unlike our friend Glaucon.
Perhaps in that one respect, I said. But in many others he's quite different.
In what ways?

He should be more assertive and less refined, though still a friend of culture. He's a good listener but no speaker. He tends to be harsh with servants — unlike the truly educated man, who is too dignified for that — but courteous to free citizens and remarkably obedient to authority. He loves power and honor, claiming the right to rule not on the basis of eloquence or any such quality, but because he's a soldier and has proven himself in arms. He's also devoted to athletics and hunting.
Yes, that's the character that matches timocracy.

Such a person will scorn wealth when he's young. But as he ages, he'll be drawn to money more and more, because there's an avaricious streak in him. He's not single-mindedly devoted to virtue, having lost his best guardian.
Who was that? said Adeimantus.
Philosophy, I said — tempered with music, the only thing that can take up residence in a person's soul and preserve his virtue throughout life.
Good, he said.
Such, I said, is the timocratic youth, and he resembles the timocratic State.
Exactly.

His origin goes like this: he's often the young son of a brave father who lives in a poorly governed city. The father refuses its honors and offices, avoids the courts, and doesn't exert himself in public — he's willing to give up his rights just to avoid trouble.
And how does the son turn out?

The son's character starts to develop when he hears his mother complaining that her husband holds no position in the government, which means she gets no standing among other women. She sees him indifferent to money, refusing to fight in the courts or the assembly, taking whatever happens to him calmly. She notices that his thoughts are always turned inward and that he treats her with considerable neglect. So she tells the son that his father is only half a man, far too passive — adding all the other complaints about her own mistreatment that women love to rehearse.
Yes, said Adeimantus. Women certainly give us plenty of those complaints, and the complaints are just like them.

And you know, I said, that the old family servants also talk privately to the son in the same vein. When they see someone cheating or shortchanging his father, and the father does nothing about it, they tell the boy that when he grows up, he should get back at people like that and be more of a man. He walks around town hearing the same thing: people who mind their own business are called fools and get no respect, while the busybodies are honored and applauded. The young man hears and sees all of this — and also hears his father's words and observes his way of life — and he's pulled in opposite directions. His father nourishes the rational part of his soul, while everyone else encourages the spirited and appetitive parts. Since he isn't naturally bad but has simply kept bad company, he's eventually pulled to a middle ground. He surrenders the kingdom within himself to the middle principle — competitiveness and spirit — and becomes arrogant and ambitious.
You've described his origin perfectly.
So now we have the second form of government and the second type of character?
We have.
Next, let's look at another man who, as Aeschylus puts it,
'Is set against another state' —
or rather, following our plan, let's start with the state.
By all means.
I believe oligarchy comes next.
And what exactly do you mean by oligarchy?
A government based on property qualifications, where the rich hold power and the poor are excluded.
I understand, he replied.
Should I start by describing how the transition from timocracy to oligarchy happens?
Yes.
Well, I said, you don't need special insight to see how one turns into the other.
How?
The hoarding of gold by private individuals is what ruins timocracy. They invent illegal ways to spend it — what do they or their wives care about the law?
True enough.
And then one person, seeing another getting rich, tries to keep up, and soon the whole citizen body is consumed with the love of money.
Likely enough.

And so they grow richer and richer. The more they think about making fortunes, the less they think about virtue. When riches and virtue are put on opposite sides of a scale, one always rises as the other falls.
True.
And as wealth and wealthy people gain honor in the State, virtue and virtuous people lose it.
Clearly.
And whatever is honored gets cultivated, while whatever is dishonored gets neglected.
Obviously.
So eventually, instead of being lovers of rivalry and glory, they become lovers of trade and money. They honor and look up to the rich man and make him ruler, while the poor man is despised.
That's what happens.

Then they pass a law setting a minimum property requirement for citizenship — higher in some places, lower in others, depending on how exclusive the oligarchy is. Nobody whose property falls below the threshold gets any share in government. They enforce these changes by force of arms if intimidation doesn't do the job.
Very true.
And that, broadly speaking, is how oligarchy is established.
Yes, he said. But what are the features of this form of government, and what are the defects we mentioned?

First of all, I said, think about the nature of that property qualification. Imagine if pilots were chosen based on their wealth, and a poor man were refused permission to steer even if he were the better pilot.
You mean they'd shipwreck?
Yes. And doesn't the same principle apply to governing anything?
I'd imagine so.
Including a city? Or would you exclude that?
No, he said. A city is the strongest case of all, since ruling a city is the greatest and most difficult task there is.
So this is the first major defect of oligarchy?
Clearly.
And here's another defect just as bad.
What's that?
The inevitable split: such a state isn't one state but two — one of the poor and one of the rich — living side by side and constantly conspiring against each other.
That's certainly just as bad.

Here's another shameful feature: they can't wage war properly.
