Now, using these examples, shall we investigate who this imitator really is?
If you like.
Here are three beds: first, the one that exists in nature, which is made by God — I think we can say no one else could be the maker.
No.
Second, the one the carpenter makes.
Yes.
And third, the one the painter makes.
Yes.
So there are three beds and three creators: God, the carpenter, and the painter.
Yes, three.
God, whether by choice or necessity, made one and only one bed in nature. Two or more such ideal beds have never been and never will be made by God.
Why not?
Because if he'd made even two, a third would appear behind them — the one they both derive from — and that would be the real bed, not the other two.
Very true, he said.
God knew this. Wanting to be the real maker of a real bed, not just a particular maker of a particular bed, he created one that is essentially and by nature one only.
So we believe.
Shall we call him the natural author or maker of the bed?
Yes, he replied — since through the natural process of creation, he is the author of this and all other things.
And the carpenter — is he also a maker of the bed?
Yes.
But would you call the painter a maker?
Certainly not.
Then what is he in relation to the bed?
I think we can fairly call him the imitator of what the other two make.
Good, I said. So you call the person who is three steps removed from nature an imitator?
Certainly, he said.
And the tragic poet is an imitator, and therefore — like all imitators — three steps removed from the truth and from reality?
So it appears.
We agree about the imitator, then. Now, about the painter: does he imitate the things that exist in nature, or only the creations of craftsmen?
The latter.
As they really are, or as they appear? That's still to be determined.
What do you mean?
When you look at a bed from different angles — straight on, at a slant, or from any other position — the bed appears different, though there's no actual difference. The same goes for everything else.
Yes, he said — the difference is only apparent.
Now here's the key question: is the art of painting designed to imitate things as they are, or as they appear? Is it an imitation of reality or of appearance?
Of appearance.

Then the imitator is a long way from the truth. He can reproduce anything because he touches only a small part of each thing — and that part is merely an image. For example, a painter can paint a cobbler, a carpenter, or any other craftsman without knowing the first thing about their trades. If he's a good painter, he could fool children or simple people into thinking they were looking at a real carpenter, shown from a distance.
Certainly.

So whenever anyone tells us he's found a man who knows all arts, all sciences, and everything else that anyone knows — and knows each one better than any specialist — we can only conclude that the informant is a naive soul who's been taken in by some wizard or actor, and mistook the appearance of knowledge for the real thing, being unable to distinguish knowledge from ignorance and imitation.
Very true.

So when people say that the tragedians — and Homer above all — know all the arts, all things human and divine, all virtue and vice, because a good poet must understand his subject to write well about it, we should consider whether they've been deceived by imitators. Perhaps they encountered these poets' works and didn't realize they were imitations three steps removed from truth — easy to produce without any real knowledge, because they're appearances, not realities. Or perhaps the poets do genuinely possess the knowledge they seem to display?
That question, he said, should definitely be examined.

Do you think that if someone could create the original as well as the copy, he'd seriously devote himself to making copies? Would he make imitation the ruling principle of his life, as if he had nothing higher in him?
I'd say not.

The real expert, who genuinely understood what he was imitating, would want to work with realities, not imitations. He'd prefer to be the subject of praise rather than its author — to leave behind real achievements rather than poems about them.
Yes, he said — that would bring far greater honor and profit.

Then let's not question Homer about medicine or the other arts his poems only touch on. Let's ask about the most important subjects — military strategy, politics, education, which are the noblest themes of his poetry. Let's say: 'Dear Homer, if you're only two steps from the truth about virtue, and not three — if you're a real knower and not just an image-maker — tell us: what state was ever better governed thanks to you? Sparta credits Lycurgus, and many cities honor other reformers. But what city claims you as its lawgiver?' Can he name one?
I don't think so, said Glaucon. Not even his biggest fans claim he was a legislator.
Is there any war on record that Homer conducted or helped win while he was alive?
None.
Any practical invention of his — something useful for the arts or for daily life, like those credited to Thales or Anacharsis?
Nothing at all.

Well, if he never served the public, was he at least a private guide or teacher? Did he have devoted students who loved his company and handed down a distinctive Homeric way of life, the way Pythagoras's followers maintain a way of life named after him?

Nothing of the sort. In fact, Socrates, Homer's companion Creophylus — whose name always makes people laugh — would be even more ridiculous for his foolishness if it's true that Homer was badly neglected during his own lifetime.

That is the tradition, I replied. But can you imagine, Glaucon, that if Homer had really been able to educate and improve people — if he'd had real knowledge and not been a mere imitator — that he wouldn't have gathered crowds of devoted followers? Protagoras and Prodicus and many others just have to whisper, 'You'll never manage your household or your state without us,' and people practically carry them around on their shoulders. Would Homer's contemporaries — or Hesiod's — have let them wander around as traveling poets if they could actually make people virtuous? Wouldn't they have clung to them like gold, and forced them to stay, or followed them everywhere until they'd learned enough?
Yes, Socrates, I think that's exactly right.

Then must we conclude that all these poets, starting with Homer, are only imitators? They copy images of virtue and everything else but never reach the truth. The poet is like the painter who can produce a convincing picture of a cobbler without knowing anything about cobbling — good enough to fool people who judge only by colors and shapes.
Quite so.

In the same way, the poet paints with words. He knows just enough about each subject to imitate it, and other people — equally ignorant — judge only by his words and think he speaks brilliantly about cobbling or warfare or anything else, so powerful is the natural enchantment of meter, harmony, and rhythm. But strip poetry of its musical coloring and recite it in plain prose, and you know how it looks. I'm sure you've noticed.
Yes, he said.
Like faces that were never really beautiful but only had the bloom of youth — once that bloom fades, you can see what they truly are.
Exactly.
Here's another point: the imitator — the image-maker — knows nothing of true reality. He knows only appearances. Right?
Yes.
Let's be thorough and not stop at half an explanation.
Go on.
A painter, we'd say, can paint reins and a bit.
Yes.
And a leather-worker and metalworker can make them.
Certainly.
But does the painter know the right form of reins and bit? For that matter, do the craftsmen who make them? Only the horseman who uses them actually knows what they should be like.
Very true.
And can we generalize this?
How?
For everything, there are three arts: the art of using, the art of making, and the art of imitating.
Yes.
And the excellence or beauty or rightness of any object — whether natural or man-made — is relative to the use for which it was designed.
True.

So the user has the greatest knowledge and must tell the maker what's good or bad about the product. A flute player tells the flute maker which flutes work well; he gives instructions, and the maker follows them.
Of course.
The one speaks with knowledge about the quality of the instrument; the other takes his word for it and does as he's told.
True.
The maker acquires correct belief about quality from the user who knows. But the user has actual knowledge.
True.
And the imitator? Will he have knowledge from using the thing, or correct belief from associating with someone who knows and taking instructions? Neither.
Neither.
So the imitator won't have true opinion any more than he has true knowledge about what he imitates.
I suppose not.
So the imitator will be brilliantly informed about his own creations — not.
Quite the reverse.
And yet he'll keep on imitating, without knowing what makes things good or bad. He'll simply imitate whatever looks good to the ignorant crowd.
Exactly.

So we're pretty well agreed: the imitator has no knowledge worth mentioning of what he imitates. Imitation is just a form of play. And the tragic poets, whether they write in iambic verse or in epic, are imitators of the highest degree.
Very true.
And haven't we shown that imitation deals with what is three steps removed from truth?
Certainly.
Now, which part of a person does imitation appeal to?
What do you mean?
Let me explain. The same object looks large when near and small when far away.
True.

And the same object appears straight out of water and crooked in it. Concave becomes convex through illusions of color. Every kind of confusion exists within us, and this is the weakness that the arts of conjuring and illusion exploit — working on us like magic.
True.
And the arts of measuring, counting, and weighing come to the rescue — replacing the apparent with the calculated. The seeming greater or less or heavier gives way before measurement and reason.
Very true.
And this must be the work of the calculating, rational part of the soul.
It must.
And when this rational part measures and determines that certain things are equal or unequal, and yet the senses report the opposite — we have a contradiction.
True.
But we said that the same part of the soul can't hold opposite opinions about the same thing at the same time.
And we were right.
So the part that disagrees with measurement is not the same as the part that agrees with it.
True.
And the part that trusts measurement and calculation is the better part of the soul.
Certainly.
And what opposes it is one of the soul's inferior elements.
No doubt.

This was the conclusion I was driving at: painting, and imitation in general, produces work far removed from truth. It is the companion and friend of a part within us that is equally removed from reason — and has no true or healthy purpose.
Exactly.
Imitation is an inferior thing that consorts with an inferior part of the soul and produces inferior offspring.
Very true.
And does this apply only to visual imitation, or also to what we call poetry?
The same probably applies to poetry.
Let's not rely on a probability from analogy with painting, I said. Let's examine directly whether the part of the mind that poetry appeals to is good or bad.
By all means.

We can put the question this way: imitation imitates people performing actions — voluntary or involuntary — which they believe have turned out well or badly, and they rejoice or grieve accordingly. Is there anything beyond this?
No, nothing else.

But in all these varied circumstances, is a person consistent with himself? Or is there, as with sight (where the eyes deliver contradictory reports about the same things), an internal conflict in how he lives? Though actually, I don't need to raise the question again — we already established that the soul is full of countless such contradictions at every moment.
And we were right, he said.
Yes, we were. But we left out something that needs to be added now.
What was that?
Didn't we say that a good man who suffers misfortune — losing a son, for instance, or something else he holds dear — will bear it more calmly than others?
Yes.
But will he feel no grief at all? Or should we say that while he can't help grieving, he'll moderate his grief?
The latter is more accurate, he said.
Now tell me: will he be more likely to fight and resist his grief when others are watching, or when he's alone?
It makes a big difference whether he's being observed or not.
When alone, he'll allow himself to say and do many things he'd be ashamed to have anyone see or hear.
True.
Within him, reason and law urge him to resist, while the feeling of his loss pushes him to surrender to sorrow.
True.
But when a person is pulled in two opposite directions at once, there must be two distinct principles within him.
Certainly.
One is prepared to follow the guidance of law.
What do you mean by that?

The law says that the best course is to endure misfortune patiently. We shouldn't give way to impatience, since we can't know whether such events are ultimately good or evil. Nothing is gained by anguish, and nothing human is really of such great importance. Besides, grief gets in the way of the very thing we most need in the moment.
What do we most need?

To take stock of what has happened and, like a dice player assessing a new throw, to arrange our affairs as reason thinks best. Not to behave like children who've taken a fall — clutching the injured part and wasting time in wailing — but to train the soul to apply the remedy quickly, to raise up what has fallen, and to cure the sick, replacing lamentation with the healing art.
Yes, he said. That's the right way to meet the blows of fortune.
And the higher principle is the one that follows reason's guidance?
Clearly.
While the other principle — the one that draws us toward grief and lamentation and can never get enough of them — we may call irrational, lazy, and cowardly?
Indeed we may.

Now this irrational, grief-loving element provides plenty of material for imitation. But the wise, calm temperament — being steady and nearly constant — is hard to imitate, and hard for a festival audience in a theater to appreciate, since the feeling being depicted is foreign to them.
Certainly.
So the imitative poet who wants to be popular is naturally drawn not to the rational principle in the soul, but to the emotional, unstable temperament, which is easy to imitate.
Obviously.

And now we can fairly place the poet alongside the painter. Like the painter, his creations have an inferior degree of truth. Like the painter, he appeals to an inferior part of the soul. So we're right to refuse him entry into a well-governed state, because he arouses, nourishes, and strengthens the emotional part of the soul while undermining reason. It's like giving power to the worst citizens and undermining the best. The imitative poet implants an evil constitution in the soul: he indulges the irrational part — the part that can't tell greater from less and thinks the same thing is now big, now small — manufacturing images far removed from truth.
Exactly.
But we haven't yet brought our heaviest charge: poetry's power to corrupt even good people. And that is truly alarming.
It certainly is, if it's true.

Listen and judge. When the best of us hear Homer or a tragedian depicting some hero drawing out his sorrows in a long speech, weeping and beating his breast — don't we delight in surrendering to sympathy? Don't we praise the poet who moves us most?
Of course — I know exactly what you mean.

But when grief strikes us personally, we pride ourselves on the opposite quality — staying quiet and patient. That, we say, is the manly part. The other behavior — the kind we enjoyed in the theater — we now consider womanly.
Very true, he said.
Is this praise consistent? Can we be right to admire in others what we'd despise in ourselves?
No, that doesn't seem reasonable.
Actually, I said, it's quite reasonable — from one perspective.
Which perspective?

Think about it: when misfortune hits us, there's a natural hunger to relieve our grief through weeping and lamentation — a desire our better nature, trained by reason, keeps in check. But the poets satisfy that desire for us. We let the sympathetic element loose because the suffering is someone else's, and we tell ourselves there's no shame in pitying a man who claims to be good and grieves extravagantly. The pleasure seems like a net gain — why should we be prudish and lose both the pleasure and the poem? But few people realize that what they absorb from other people's suffering seeps into their own lives. The grief that has gathered strength at the sight of others' misfortunes becomes hard to restrain in our own.
How very true!

The same applies to comedy. There are jokes you'd be ashamed to make yourself, but on the comic stage — or even in private — you find them hilarious and feel no disgust. It's the same pattern: a principle that reason once kept restrained — the urge to be funny — is now let loose in the theater, and before you know it you've become the comedian at home.
Very true, he said.

And the same goes for lust, anger, and all the other passions — desire, pain, pleasure — that accompany every action. Poetry feeds and waters them instead of drying them up. It lets them rule when they should be ruled, if we're ever to grow in happiness and virtue.
I can't deny it.

So, Glaucon, whenever you encounter Homer's admirers declaring that he educated Greece and that you should study him carefully and regulate your whole life according to him — love and respect these people, they mean well. Acknowledge that Homer is the greatest of poets and the first of tragedians. But stand firm: the only poetry to be admitted into our state is hymns to the gods and praise of good men. If you let in the honeyed Muse — whether in epic or lyric verse — then pleasure and pain will rule your state, not law and reason, which mankind has always recognized as best.
That is absolutely right, he said.

So let this be our defense, now that we've returned to the subject of poetry: we were right to banish this art from our state, given the tendencies we've identified. Reason required it. But lest she accuse us of harshness, let us tell her that there's an ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry — plenty of evidence for it in sayings like 'the yelping hound howling at her lord' and 'mighty in the vain talk of fools' and 'the mob of sages who've mastered Zeus' and 'the subtle thinkers who turn out to be beggars.' Nevertheless, let's assure our sweet friend Poetry and her sister arts of imitation that if she can prove her right to exist in a well-ordered state, we'll welcome her gladly — we feel her charm deeply. But we must not betray truth for charm. I suspect you feel her pull as much as I do, Glaucon — especially when she speaks through Homer.
I certainly do.
Shall we allow her to return from exile, then — on the condition that she defend herself in verse or some other meter?
Certainly.

And we can also allow her prose champions — people who love poetry but aren't poets themselves — to argue on her behalf: that she's not only pleasant but also useful to states and to human life. We'll listen sympathetically, because if this can be proved, we'll be the gainers — to have both delight and benefit from poetry.
Certainly, he said. We'd be the gainers.

But if her defense fails, my dear friend, then we must do what lovers do when they realize their passion is doing them harm: we must give her up, though not without a struggle. We're in love with this poetry — the education of our noble state implanted it in us — and we want her to appear at her best and truest. But as long as she can't justify herself, we'll chant this argument of ours as a counter-spell while we listen, guarding against falling back into the childish love that captivates the crowd. We know that poetry of this kind must not be taken seriously as if it touches the truth. The listener must fear for the city within himself and be on guard against her seductions, making our argument his law.
I quite agree, he said.

Yes, my dear Glaucon. The stakes are enormous — greater than they appear: whether a person becomes good or bad. Under the influence of honor, money, power, or even poetry, he must not neglect justice and virtue.
I've been persuaded by the argument, he said, and I believe anyone else would be too.
And yet we haven't even mentioned the greatest prizes and rewards that await virtue.
There are greater ones still? They must be inconceivably great.
Well, I said, what can really be great in such a short time? The whole span of a human life — seventy years, say — is surely a tiny thing compared to eternity.
A tiny thing? It's nothing, he replied.
Should an immortal being take this little space very seriously, rather than thinking about the whole of time?
The whole, obviously. But why do you ask?
Are you not aware, I said, that the soul of man is immortal and imperishable?
He stared at me in astonishment. No, by heaven! Are you really prepared to argue that?
I certainly am, I said — and so should you. There's no great difficulty in proving it.
I see great difficulty. But I'd like to hear you make light work of it.
Listen, then.
I'm listening.
There's something you call good and something you call evil?
Yes, he replied.
Would you agree that the evil element is what corrupts and destroys, while the good element is what preserves and benefits?
Yes.

And everything has its own specific evil and its own specific good? Ophthalmia is the evil of the eyes, disease of the body, mildew of grain, rot of timber, rust of metal. Almost everything has an inherent evil that attacks it.
Yes, he said.
And whatever is attacked by its inherent evil is damaged, and if the attack is complete, it's destroyed?
True.
So each thing is destroyed by its own inherent evil. If that doesn't destroy it, nothing else will. Goodness certainly won't destroy it, and neither will what's neutral.
Certainly not.
So if we find something whose inherent evil can damage but never completely destroy it, then we know that thing is indestructible.
That seems right.
Well, I said — is there an evil that corrupts the soul?
Yes, he said — all the evils we just reviewed: injustice, intemperance, cowardice, ignorance.

But does any of these actually dissolve or destroy the soul? Be careful here — don't make the mistake of thinking that an unjust man who's caught perishes because of his injustice. Think of the body: disease, the body's own evil, wastes and destroys it. Everything we mentioned is destroyed by its own inherent corruption. Is that right?
Yes.
Now consider the soul the same way. Do injustice and other evils, by dwelling in the soul, waste and consume it? Do they ultimately destroy it and separate it from the body?
Certainly not.
And yet it would be absurd to suppose that something could be destroyed from outside by an alien evil, when it can't be destroyed from within by its own.
It would, he replied.

Consider this, Glaucon: bad food doesn't destroy the body directly. Staleness, decomposition, and other bad qualities in the food are confined to the food itself. If bad food brings about disease in the body, we say the body was destroyed by its own evil — disease — triggered by the food. But we'd never say the body itself was destroyed by the badness of the food, since body and food are different things.
Very true.

By the same principle: unless some bodily evil can produce an evil in the soul, we shouldn't suppose that the soul can be destroyed by any evil that belongs to something external and different from itself.
That's reasonable, he said.

Then either we refute this conclusion, or — as long as it stands — we must never say that fever, or the knife, or even cutting the whole body into tiny pieces can destroy the soul. Not unless someone proves that these bodily injuries make the soul more unjust or more wicked. If an external evil that belongs to something else cannot destroy the soul when the soul's own evil cannot, then the soul is indestructible.
And surely, he replied, no one will ever prove that people's souls become more unjust as a result of dying.

But suppose someone bravely denies the soul's immortality and claims that the dying really do become worse. Well, if that were true, then injustice would be like a fatal disease — people who caught a heavy dose would die of it naturally, sooner or later, rather than being executed by others as punishment. Injustice would be its own death sentence.

In that case, he said, injustice wouldn't be so terrifying — it would just deliver the unjust from their evil. But I suspect the truth is the opposite: injustice kills others when it gets the chance, but keeps the unjust man very much alive — and wide awake too. Its home is the opposite of a house of death.

Right, I said. If the soul's own inherent evil — its own vice and wickedness — can't kill it, then an evil designed to destroy something else is hardly going to destroy the soul, or anything other than what it was meant for.
Hardly.
And if nothing can destroy the soul — neither its own evil nor any external evil — then the soul must exist forever. And if it exists forever, it must be immortal.
It must.

Let us accept that conclusion, I said. And if it's true, then the number of souls must always be the same. They can't decrease (since none are destroyed) and they can't increase (since any increase in immortal beings would have to come from mortal ones, and eventually everything would become immortal).
Very true.
But we can't believe that — reason won't permit it — any more than we can believe the soul in its truest nature is full of variety, difference, and internal contradiction.
What do you mean? he said.
The soul, having been proven immortal, can't be composed of many parts — it must be the most beautifully simple of compositions.
Certainly not a compound.

Our argument proves its immortality. But to see the soul as it truly is — not as it appears now, marred by its union with the body and other afflictions — you must look at it with the eye of reason in its original purity. Then its beauty will be revealed, and justice and injustice and everything we've discussed will become far clearer. What we've said about the soul so far is true of how it appears in its present condition. But we've been looking at it in a state comparable to that of the sea-god Glaucus, whose original form can barely be recognized because his limbs are broken and crushed by the waves, and encrusted with shells and seaweed and barnacles until he looks more like a monster than his natural self. That's how we see the soul too, disfigured by countless evils. But that's not where we should look, Glaucon.
Where, then?

At its love of wisdom. Notice what it reaches for, what company it seeks — its kinship with the immortal, the eternal, the divine. Consider what it would become if it followed that higher principle completely, carried by divine impulse out of the ocean where it now dwells, freed from the rocks and shells and earthly growths that cling to it. Then you'd see its true nature — whether it has one form or many, and what that nature really is. For now, I think we've said enough about its present condition and the forms it takes in this life.
True, he replied.

And so, I said, we've fulfilled the terms of our argument without resorting to the rewards and reputations of justice, as you said Homer and Hesiod do. We've shown that justice in its own nature is best for the soul in its own nature. Let a person do what is just, whether or not he wears the ring of Gyges — and even if he adds the helmet of Hades to that ring.
Very true.
And now, Glaucon, there can be no harm in also listing the rewards that justice and the other virtues bring to the soul from gods and men, both in life and after death.
Certainly not, he said.
Will you pay me back what you borrowed from the argument?
What did I borrow?

The assumption that the just man should appear unjust and the unjust just. You said that even if the truth couldn't escape the notice of gods and men, we should make that assumption for the sake of argument, so that pure justice could be weighed against pure injustice. Remember?
I'd be greatly to blame if I'd forgotten.

Well, now that the case is decided, I claim on justice's behalf that her true reputation — the one that gods and men give her — should be restored. She's been shown to confer genuine benefits on those who possess her. Let what was taken from her be given back, so she may win the prize of appearance that is also rightfully hers.
The claim is just, he said.
First, then: the gods know the true nature of both the just and the unjust.
Granted.
And knowing them, one must be the friend of the gods and the other their enemy, as we agreed from the start.
True.
And the friend of the gods may be expected to receive every good thing from them — except whatever suffering is the necessary consequence of past wrongs?
Certainly.

So we must believe this about the just man: whether he suffers poverty, sickness, or any other apparent misfortune, all things will work out for his good in the end — in this life and after death. For the gods don't neglect anyone who genuinely strives to become just and to become as godlike as a human being can, through the pursuit of virtue.
Yes, he said. If he's like God, God surely won't neglect him.
And of the unjust, we may assume the opposite?
Certainly.
So these are the prizes that the gods give to the just.
That's my belief.

And what about their treatment by other human beings? Look at things as they truly are, and you'll see that clever unjust people are like runners who sprint well from start to finish but then can't make it back again. They start fast but end up looking foolish, slinking off with their ears drooping and no crown on their heads. But the true runners complete the course, win the prize, and are crowned. And isn't that how it usually goes for the just? At the end of every endeavor and of life itself, they win the reputation and the prizes that humanity has to give.
True.

Then you'll let me say about the just what you were saying about the unjust: as they grow older, they become rulers in their city if they choose. They marry whom they please and give their children to whom they please. Everything you said about the unjust, I now say about the just. And of the unjust, I say that most of them, even if they escape in youth, are found out in the end and look ridiculous in their old age — despised by strangers and citizens alike. They're beaten, and then come the things you rightly called too crude to mention — racking, burning, and the rest. You can take it as said. But will you let me assume these things are true?
Certainly, he said. What you say is true.
These, then, are the prizes, rewards, and gifts that the just receive from gods and men during this life — in addition to the inherent goods that justice itself provides.
Yes, he said, and they are noble and lasting.

And yet all of these, I said, are nothing in number or magnitude compared to what awaits both the just and the unjust after death. You need to hear about those, so that both receive the full account owed them by our argument.
Speak, he said. There are few things I'd rather hear.

I won't tell you a tale like those Odysseus tells Alcinous, I said. But this too is a tale of a brave man: Er, son of Armenius, a Pamphylian. He was killed in battle, and when the dead were collected ten days later — already decomposing — his body alone was found untouched by decay. He was carried home for burial. On the twelfth day, as he lay on the funeral pyre, he came back to life and described what he had seen in the other world. He said that when his soul left his body, it traveled with a great company of souls to a mysterious place where there were two openings in the earth, close together, and two corresponding openings in the sky above. Between them sat judges, who sent the just upward through the right-hand opening in the sky, with tokens of their judgments fastened in front of them, and the unjust downward through the left-hand opening in the earth, with tokens fastened on their backs. When Er approached, they told him he was to be a messenger, carrying a report of the other world back to the living. He was to see and hear everything. He watched souls departing through both pairs of openings after receiving their sentences. And through the other two openings, souls were arriving: from the earth, dusty and worn from travel; from heaven, clean and radiant. They gathered in a meadow like people at a festival. Those who recognized each other embraced and exchanged stories — the ones from below weeping as they recalled their thousand-year journey underground, the ones from above describing heavenly delights and visions of inconceivable beauty. The full story would take too long, Glaucon, but the essence was this: for every wrong they'd done, each soul suffered tenfold punishment — once per hundred years, since a human life was reckoned at a hundred years, so that each crime was punished ten times in a thousand years. And the rewards for goodness, justice, and holiness were in the same proportion. He said more about children who died young, and about the punishments for impiety toward gods and parents and for murder, which I won't repeat. He mentioned being present when one spirit asked another: 'Where is Ardiaeus the Great?' This Ardiaeus had been a tyrant in Pamphylia a thousand years before Er's time, who had murdered his aged father and elder brother and committed many other terrible crimes. The answer was: 'He hasn't come and never will.' Er described one of the most terrifying sights they witnessed: they were at the mouth of the passage, about to ascend after completing their time below, when Ardiaeus appeared with several others, mostly tyrants and great criminals. They thought they were about to emerge — but the opening let out a roar whenever these incurably wicked souls or any who hadn't been punished enough tried to ascend. Savage, fiery-looking men who were standing by seized them, bound them hand and foot, threw them down, flayed them, dragged them along roads of thorns, and proclaimed their crimes to everyone they passed, declaring they were being taken to be cast into Tartarus. Of all the terrors they'd experienced, Er said, nothing compared to the dread each soul felt at that moment — the terror of hearing the roar. And when there was silence, the joy of passing through was beyond measure. Such were the punishments and rewards — and there were corresponding blessings.

After the spirits had spent seven days in the meadow, on the eighth they had to move on. Four days later they came to a place where they could see, stretching from above, a straight beam of light like a pillar, running through all of heaven and earth, brighter and purer than a rainbow. After another day's journey they reached it, and there, at the center of the light, they saw the ends of heaven's chains hanging down — for this light is the belt that holds the universe together, like the cables under the hull of a ship. From these ends extends the Spindle of Necessity, on which all the heavenly revolutions turn. Its shaft and hook are made of steel, its whorl partly of steel and partly of other materials. The whorl is shaped like an ordinary whorl on earth, but imagine a large hollow whorl scooped out, with smaller ones nested inside it — eight in all, fitting together like a set of bowls. Their rims show on top, forming one continuous whorl from below. The spindle passes through the center of the eighth. The outermost whorl has the broadest rim, then the sixth, fourth, eighth, seventh, fifth, third, and second in decreasing order. The outermost is spangled with stars; the seventh (the sun) is brightest; the eighth (the moon) reflects the seventh's light; the second (Saturn) and fifth (Mercury) are yellow; the third (Venus) is whitest; the fourth (Mars) is reddish; the sixth (Jupiter) is second in whiteness. The whole spindle revolves in one direction, but the seven inner circles move slowly in the opposite direction. The eighth moves fastest, then the seventh, sixth, and fifth together, then (in reverse motion) the fourth, then the third, then the second. The spindle turns on the knees of Necessity. On the upper rim of each circle sits a Siren, each singing a single note, and the eight together produce one perfect harmony. Around them, seated at equal intervals on thrones, are the three Fates — Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos — daughters of Necessity, robed in white with garlands on their heads. Their voices accompany the Sirens' harmony: Lachesis sings of the past, Clotho of the present, Atropos of the future. Clotho occasionally touches the outer circle with her right hand to assist its revolution; Atropos touches the inner ones with her left; and Lachesis touches both in turn, first with one hand, then the other.

When Er and the spirits arrived, they had to go straight to Lachesis. First a prophet arranged them in order. Then he took lots and samples of lives from Lachesis's knees, mounted a high platform, and spoke: 'Hear the word of Lachesis, daughter of Necessity. Mortal souls, a new cycle of mortal life begins. No spirit will be assigned to you — you will choose your own spirit. Let the one who draws the first lot choose first, and the life he chooses will be his destiny. Virtue has no master: each person will have more or less of it depending on how much he honors or neglects it. The responsibility belongs to the chooser — God is blameless.' After speaking, the prophet scattered the lots among them all (except Er, who wasn't allowed to choose), and each picked up the lot nearest to him and saw his number. Then the prophet laid out samples of lives on the ground — far more lives than souls, of every possible kind. There were lives of every animal and every human condition: tyrannies (some lasting a lifetime, others broken off in poverty and exile), lives of famous men and women renowned for beauty, strength, athletic glory, or noble birth, and lives of the obscure and humble. But no life came with a fixed character — the soul would necessarily change according to which life it chose. Everything else was mixed in: wealth and poverty, health and sickness, and the various conditions between. Here, my dear Glaucon, lies the supreme danger of our existence — and therefore the utmost care is needed. Each of us should set aside all other knowledge and seek only to learn how to distinguish a good life from a bad one, and always and everywhere to choose the better. He should understand how all the factors we've discussed — beauty, wealth, birth, strength, knowledge, all the soul's gifts both natural and acquired — work together or against each other to affect virtue. From all this, he should be able to judge which life makes the soul more just and which makes it more unjust. Everything else should be set aside. We've seen that this is the best choice both in life and after death. A person must carry with him into the next world an adamantine faith in truth and justice, so that even there he won't be dazzled by wealth or seduced by evil into tyranny or crime — inflicting terrible harm on others and suffering even worse himself. He must know how to choose the middle path, avoiding extremes as far as possible, both in this life and in all the lives to come. That is the road to happiness.

And according to the messenger, this is what the prophet said at the time: 'Even the last to choose, if he chooses wisely and lives well, can expect a happy life — not a bad one. Let the first not be careless, and let the last not despair.' When he finished speaking, the soul with the first pick came forward and immediately chose the greatest tyranny. Blinded by folly and greed, he hadn't thought things through and didn't notice at first that his chosen life included the fate of devouring his own children, among other horrors. When he had time to reflect and saw what was in store, he beat his breast and wailed — forgetting the prophet's warning. Instead of blaming himself, he blamed luck and the gods and everything else. He was one of the souls who had come from heaven, having lived his previous life in a well-ordered state — but his virtue was only a matter of habit, not philosophy. And this was true of many who came from heaven: never having been tested by suffering, they made poor choices. The souls who came from earth, having suffered themselves and witnessed others' suffering, were more careful. Due to this inexperience and the randomness of the lottery, many souls exchanged good fates for bad or bad for good. But if someone had always dedicated himself to genuine philosophy whenever he arrived on earth, and if his lot hadn't been absolutely last, the messenger reported that he would be happy both here and on his journey between lives — traveling the smooth heavenly road rather than the rough underground one. The spectacle of the choosing was most remarkable — sad and comic and strange — because most souls chose based on their experience in their previous life. Er saw the soul that had been Orpheus choose the life of a swan, out of hatred for women (since women had killed him); he saw the soul of Thamyras choose to be a nightingale; he saw birds choosing human lives and musicians choosing to be birds. The soul with the twentieth lot chose a lion — it was Ajax, son of Telamon, who refused to be human again because of the injustice done to him in the dispute over Achilles' armor. After him came Agamemnon, who also chose a non-human life — an eagle — because his sufferings had made him hate the human race. In the middle of the choosing came Atalanta, who couldn't resist the glory of being a male athlete. Then came Epeus, son of Panopeus, passing into the nature of a skilled craftswoman. Far back among the last, the buffoon Thersites was putting on the shape of an ape. And finally came the soul of Odysseus, who had drawn the very last lot. Cured of all ambition by the memory of his former labors, he wandered around for a long time looking for the quiet life of an ordinary man with no public responsibilities. He found it at last, lying in a corner where everyone else had ignored it. When he picked it up, he said he would have chosen the same even if he'd had the first pick. Animals changed into other animals and into humans too — the good animals into gentle creatures, the evil ones into savage ones, in every kind of combination.

After all the souls had chosen their lives, they went in the order of their lots to Lachesis, who sent each one on its way with the guardian spirit it had chosen. This spirit led the soul first to Clotho, who drew it beneath the revolution of her spindle, confirming the destiny each had chosen. After being fastened to the spindle, the spirit carried the soul to Atropos, who spun the thread and made it irreversible. Then, without looking back, they passed beneath the throne of Necessity. When all had gone through, they traveled on in scorching heat across the Plain of Forgetfulness — a barren wasteland without trees or grass. Toward evening, they camped by the River of Unmindfulness, whose water no vessel can hold. Everyone was required to drink a certain amount. Those not saved by wisdom drank more than they should, and as each one drank, he forgot everything. After they had gone to sleep, around the middle of the night, there came thunder and an earthquake, and in an instant they were all swept upward to their births in every direction, like shooting stars. Er himself was prevented from drinking the water. How he returned to his body, he couldn't say. He only knew that he suddenly woke up in the morning and found himself lying on the funeral pyre.

And so, Glaucon, the tale has been saved and has not perished, and it may save us too, if we heed it. If we believe it, we'll cross the River of Forgetfulness safely and keep our souls undefiled. If you'll take my advice, we'll hold that the soul is immortal and capable of enduring all evil and all good, and we'll always pursue the upward path, practicing justice with wisdom in every way we can — so that we may be friends both to ourselves and to the gods, both while we remain here and when we receive our rewards like victors making their rounds to collect their prizes. And so, both here and in the thousand-year journey we've described, we shall fare well.
